doctrine_entities.title: Synthetic system substitution
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Using synthetic fixtures as substitutes for available system.
doctrine_entities.statement: Using synthetic fixtures as substitutes for available system.

scope_limit.text: Refusing synthetic substitution does not make the real basis correct, complete, or strong, and it does not forbid synthetic fixtures where they are declared as such. It only stops a fabricated input from carrying a real basis's weight; this example is reader illustration and never counts as support for the rule.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of building a real conclusion on a made-up stand-in input when genuine, shareable material was right there to use, so the fake input quietly lends the conclusion strength it never earned.

analogy.text: A lab keeps a bag of practice 'dummy' blood for training, but when a real patient test is needed the technician uses a dummy bag instead of the available real sample and reports the result as a genuine reading.

maps.doctrine: the synthetic fixture standing in for real material
maps.analogy: the practice dummy blood bag

maps.doctrine: the available real material
maps.analogy: the real patient sample that was on hand

maps.doctrine: the real claim that inherits unearned strength
maps.analogy: the result reported as a genuine patient reading

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a stand-in must not be passed off as the real input when the real input was available; it does not say practice dummy bags are useless, and it does not establish that the real sample, once used, would give a correct or complete reading.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: Readers can tell whether a stated result rests on something real and shareable or on a convenient placeholder, so they can judge how much to lean on it.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a stand-in is fine because it looks identical to the real thing on the page. The tempting wrong belief is that looking the same means it can carry the same weight.

deep_reading.text: AP-12 is the failure AX-1, AX-4, and AX-8 jointly refuse: substituting a synthetic fixture for available real material and then letting a real claim ride on it. A synthetic stand-in has no derivation from anything real (so AX-1's checker has nothing to recompute), it is not the content hash of any real basis (so AX-4 cannot tell when it has drifted from the thing it stands for), and it carries no real provenance (so AX-8's label is fabricated at the door rather than propagated). It is tempting because a synthetic fixture is convenient and looks identical to a real one on the page, and the system itself admits synthetic fixtures for shape and negative cases; the line AP-12 polices is narrower, when real material exists, a synthetic substitute must not silently inherit a real basis's strength.

formal_statement.reads: A claim is grounded on a synthetic basis while a real basis was available, the stand-in's content hash differs from the real basis's hash (it was not derived from the real material), and the claim is still allowed to carry more than bottom strength.

the synthetic fixture it is grounded on
the real material was available to read
the real material that was available
the content hash of that real basis
the evidence strength the claim is allowed to carry
bottom: the strength a fabricated input may carry

relationship_triad.governs: The basis boundary, where a claim is grounded on a real or a fabricated input.
relationship_triad.requires: Grounding a load-bearing claim on available real material, or holding the claim at bottom and labelling the input synthetic when only a fixture stands in.
relationship_triad.refuses: Substituting a synthetic fixture for available real material and letting the claim inherit a strength the real basis never granted.

doctrine_entities.title: Generated-result record source inversion
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Treating generated result records as hand-authored source.
doctrine_entities.statement: Treating generated result records as hand-authored source.

scope_limit.text: Keeping generated records bound to their basis does not make either the record or the source correct, and this example illustrates the rule without supporting it. Refusing the inversion only preserves lineage; it does not establish that the basis it points back to is itself true or complete.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of treating an auto-generated summary record as if it were the hand-written original, then editing or quoting that summary as the source while the real source it was built from is left behind and no longer matches.

analogy.text: Scribbling a correction onto a library's catalogue card and then citing the card as the book, when the card was only ever copied from the book and the book itself still says something different.

maps.doctrine: the generated record derived from a source
maps.analogy: the catalogue card copied from the book

maps.doctrine: the hand-authored source it should defer to
maps.analogy: the actual book on the shelf

maps.doctrine: editing or citing the record as origin
maps.analogy: writing on the card and citing the card as the book

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a copied card must stay below the book and be redone from it, never used as the origin; it stops there and does not establish that the book itself is correct or up to date.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: It keeps a generated view from quietly outranking the thing it was built from, so a reader knows which artifact is the real origin and which is just a downstream copy.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That whichever copy is already sitting in front of you, with a confident verdict on it, is the thing to edit and cite. The tempting wrong belief is that the handy artifact is the source.

deep_reading.text: AP-13 is the lineage confusion that AX-4 and AX-11 exist to refuse: mistaking a generated result record for the hand-authored source it was derived from. A generated record is a function of a basis, so its identity is the hash of that basis, and its authority can never exceed the basis it recomputes from; the moment it is read as source, it is cut loose from that basis, so drift no longer forces a recompute and a hand-edit to the record becomes an orphan with nothing underneath it. It is tempting because a generated record often looks authored, carries a confident verdict, and is the artifact already on disk, so the cheaper move is to cite it or edit it in place rather than fix the source and regenerate. The repair is to keep the kinds apart by construction: source is hand-authored and content-addresses its outputs, a generated record stays below its basis and is rebuilt from it, and a parity check refuses the record whenever it has drifted from the source it claims to project.

formal_statement.reads: A generated artifact, derived from a basis by a builder, is rejected when it is treated as if it were hand-authored source.

symbols.meaning: r is a generated artifact
a generated artifact such as a result record or projection
the generator from basis to artifact
the content basis r is derived from
r is treated as hand-authored source

relationship_triad.governs: The boundary between a generated record and the hand-authored source it derives from.
relationship_triad.requires: Keeping a generated record bound to its basis by hash and rebuilt from source, so it is recomputed rather than edited or cited as origin.
relationship_triad.refuses: Treating a generated result record as hand-authored source.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings material in by manifest and content digest, so each imported copy stays bound to the original it was derived from and a basis change forces a recompute rather than letting the copy stand in as source.

counterexample.text: A generated result record is edited directly and then cited as the origin for a verdict, while the source it was built from is left behind and no longer matches it.

doctrine_entities.title: Public-authority inflation
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Letting public docs imply a hosted service, external service access, source-file mutation, financial or trading decisions, deployment postu…
doctrine_entities.statement: Letting public docs imply a hosted service, external service access, source-file mutation, financial or trading decisions, deployment posture, affiliation or endorsement, or whole-system equivalence that no admissible witness backs.

scope_limit.text: Blocking inflated public-authority language does not establish that any specific authority is in fact held; it only refuses the unbacked implication. The example is reader illustration and never counts as support that the system is hosted, deployed, affiliated, or deployment-posture.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting a public page's wording imply powers the system does not have, such as being a hosted, ready product, having an outside partner, changing its own source, making financial decisions, or being the same thing as the larger source system, when nothing behind the page backs any of that.

analogy.text: Labeling a local prototype as a live production endpoint. The label may help a reader see what the prototype resembles, but it cannot grant the uptime, permissions, or partnerships that only the real production system carries.

maps.doctrine: the public page implying an authority
maps.analogy: the 'production endpoint' label on the prototype

maps.doctrine: the inflated set of unbacked powers
maps.analogy: the uptime, permissions, and partnerships the prototype does not actually have

maps.doctrine: demoting the claim to its bounded scope when no witness backs it
maps.analogy: relabeling it an honest 'local prototype' until a real deployment exists

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a label must not promise a status nothing backs; it does not say the prototype is bad, and removing the inflated label does not settle whether the system could be deployed either way.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: A reader can trust that what a public page says about itself, like being hosted or ready or affiliated, is limited to what the system can actually back, not free-floating prose.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That impressive-sounding wording is harmless because it costs nothing and usually looks right. The tempting wrong belief is that stating a power is the same as holding it.

deep_reading.text: AP-14 is the inflation the evidence floor exists to refuse: a public page quietly granting itself an authority it cannot back. The danger is that all seven implied authorities (a hosted service, access to an external service, permission to mutate the source, financial or trading decisions, deployment posture, an affiliation or endorsement, or equivalence with the whole private system) are stated for free in prose, while the witness that would actually hold each one is absent. The failure is the unbacked implication, not the implication itself: a backed authority may be stated at its bounded scope. It bites across three floors at once: AX-5, because an in-scope claim with no admissible witness must fail closed rather than read as granted; AX-8, because a public-authority implication is private-adjacent material that may reach a public sink only through a declared transform, not by being asserted at the page; and AX-12, because the system's own copy is held to the same evidence floor it imposes on any other work. The repair is to state only the authority a witness backs, and to demote or refuse the public claim the moment the witness is missing.

formal_statement.reads: If a public artifact lets a reader infer an authority from the inflated set and no admissible witness backs that authority, the claim is demoted to its bounded scope or refused. The bad thing is the unbacked implication, not implication itself.

symbols.meaning: a public doctrine artifact or doc

an implied authority

relationship_triad.requires: Stating only the authority an admissible witness backs, and demoting or refusing the public claim when the witness is absent.
relationship_triad.refuses: Letting public copy imply a hosted service, external service access, source-file changes, financial or trading decisions, deployment posture, affiliation or endorsement, or whole-system equivalence that nothing holds.

doctrine_entities.statement: Using field vocabulary such as proof, verifier, information flow, world model, or benchmark integrity when the public mechanism only validates a result record or projection shape.

scope_limit.text: Refusing mechanism theater does not upgrade the mechanism. It keeps the words honest; the underlying check is still only as strong as what it computes.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of using strong words like 'verifier' or 'world model' for something that only checks the shape of a record, not the claim those words promise.

analogy.text: Calling a quick glance at a passport photo a 'full background check'. The name promises far more scrutiny than the glance actually performs.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That an impressive name reflects an impressive check. The name has to be earned by what the mechanism actually decides.

deep_reading.text: AP-15 is the overclaim the system polices in its own packaging. It is mechanism theater: using heavy field words, proof, verifier, information flow, world model, benchmark integrity, when the public mechanism behind them only checks that a record has the right shape. It is tempting because the vocabulary impresses, and the gap between "checks a schema" and "proves a property" is invisible to a casual reader. The repair is to name what the mechanism actually computes, hold the claim to that, and reserve the strong words for the few places that earn them, such as a real verifier run.

doctrine_entities.title: Receiver inflation
doctrine_entities.summary_line: Displaying a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed runtime effect without evidence of the effect relation.
doctrine_entities.statement: Displaying a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed runtime effect without evidence of the effect relation.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of showing an action's intended destination as if the action had already landed there, when nothing has actually checked that it reached the receiving end.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: A reader can tell apart 'this was sent toward a known target' from 'this was confirmed to have landed', instead of mistaking an intention for a witnessed result.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That because the destination is known in advance, showing it as reached is as good as confirming it. The tempting wrong belief is that knowing where something is headed is the same as seeing it arrive.

deep_reading.text: AP-16 is the failure AX-8 exists to refuse, applied to effects rather than labels: presenting the intended receiver of an action as if it were the witnessed result. A pipeline declares that a value reached a sink, that a write landed in memory, or that a route was taken, and the page renders that declared target as an observed runtime effect, when nothing carried the effect relation across the steps between source and receiver. It is tempting because the downstream target is usually known in advance, so showing it costs nothing and almost always looks right, while the gap between an intended reach and a witnessed one is invisible to a reader. The repair is the same shape AX-8 imposes on provenance: the effect relation has to be carried and observed at the receiver, not asserted from the sending side, and absent that witness the honest display is a declared target marked as unobserved, held below the strength a real observation would carry.

formal_statement.reads: Displaying an effect of a source s on a downstream receiver r as observed, while no witness establishes the effect relation from s to r.

relationship_triad.refuses: Rendering a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed effect with no evidence that the effect relation held.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting a generated page or summary overrule the real contract it was only meant to describe.

analogy.text: Treating a news article about a law as if it were the law itself, and acting on the article when the two disagree.

analogy.boundary: The article-versus-law picture shows a summary cannot outrank its source; it does not capture that the summary must also be recomputed and demoted when the source it describes drifts.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: A readable summary is easy to trust, so letting it win over the source quietly replaces the real rule with a description of it.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That the clearest version is the authoritative one. The source stays authoritative; the summary only points at it.

deep_reading.text: AP-17 is the inversion P-15 exists to prevent: a projection quietly becoming the authority. It happens when a markdown page, a generated card, an atlas row, or a compact summary is cited as the source of truth, overriding the executable contract it was generated from. It is tempting because the projection is the readable thing, so people reach for it, and over time the source it came from is forgotten. The repair is to keep the projection below its source by construction: recompute from the contract, and demote the projection the moment its basis drifts.

formal_statement.reads: If a projection's authority would exceed its source's, reject it: a generated view can expose source authority but never raise it.

public_glossary.label: Plectis
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis is this project's declared public name. The name does not define a general category or imply affiliation, endorsement, or identity with similarly named external entities.
public_glossary.short_definition: Plectis—named from the Latin *plectere*, to weave or entwine—is the current public name for the human-facing map, site, reader packets, and canonical public source repository drawn over this source-linked AI workflow system.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Plectis—named from the Latin *plectere*, to weave or entwine—is the current public name for the human-facing map, site, reader packets, and canonical public source repository drawn over this source-linked AI workflow system.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis is the public identity for everything shown on these pages and the open source slice behind them. It is the name carried by the landing page, the components and paper modules, the reader handoff surfaces, and the published repository. The system was previously called Microcosm, and that earlier name still appears in lineage notes and in technical identifiers such as package names, schema ids, and historical URLs. Authority for what the system actually is rests in the source substrate, the standards, the validators, and the dissemination gates, not in the name itself.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When you see Plectis, read it as the public identity of the whole system and its public source slice. Where you encounter the older name Microcosm in identifiers or links, treat it as the same project under its earlier name.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Plectis names the public surface and its source repository, but the surface is a map; the working machinery and the recorded state that authority rests on live in the substrate beneath it.
public_glossary.scope_note: Plectis covers the public-facing identity: the landing page, glossary, site routes, reader packets, and the canonical public source repository. A reader meets it as the name of the project across every page of this site and on the source and licence page.
public_glossary.example: The "Source and licence" page presents Plectis as the public identity over the published, source-open repository, alongside the licence and the naming lineage from Microcosm.

example_route.label: Source & license
example_route.gloss: see the public identity and the open source repository it names

public_glossary.non_example: Do not use Plectis as proof that package ids, old URLs, or source paths were already renamed; the name is the public identity only, and the earlier Microcosm name still lives on in those technical surfaces.

relationships.gloss: Plectis is the current human-facing public label; Microcosm remains a historical and technical compatibility label.
The Plectis name is governed through the existing Plectis/Microcosm standard while compatibility identifiers remain supported.
Cold readers should see Plectis as the public name while still resolving Microcosm compatibility identifiers.
Plectis identity claims must be checked against current source, generated projections, and release gates.

source_refs.gloss: Machine-readable authority for the Plectis public name and Microcosm compatibility boundary.
Doctrine roof for the source-open substrate now presented publicly as Plectis.
Curated landing surface where the human-visible public name is published.

public_glossary.label: component
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Component means one governed public system object in Plectis. It does not claim that every software, physical, or organizational component has this record shape.
public_glossary.short_definition: A component is one bounded unit of working machinery with a defined job, explicit inputs and outputs, and a claim limit, called a component in public copy and an organ in source identifiers.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A component is one bounded unit of working machinery with a defined job, explicit inputs and outputs, and a claim limit, called a component in public copy and an organ in source identifiers.
public_glossary.card_definition: The system is built as a set of these units rather than one large program, and each one is presented on its own card. A component card names the unit, says what it does, gives the evidence line that backs it, links to its source route, and marks where its scope stops. Each component can be opened and inspected on its own.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Take a component as one bounded unit doing one job, and read its evidence line and scope limit to see what it is responsible for and where that responsibility ends.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Component is a naming boundary, not a separate object: it lets the object model be read on the public pages without inheriting the internal working vocabulary, and the source registry, atlas, object map, and evidence profiles decide what each component is allowed to claim.
public_glossary.scope_note: Component covers the reader-facing units that make up the system, encountered across the public site wherever a unit is named, carded, or linked, with the full set gathered on the components page.
public_glossary.example: The Cold Reader Route Map is one component: a single unit whose job is to lay out a route through the system for someone arriving without prior context, shown on its own card with its evidence line and source route.

example_route.label: Cold Reader Route Map
example_route.gloss: open one live component card

public_glossary.non_example: A component is not a marketing feature and not the whole system in miniature. It is a single unit of running code with a stated boundary, and the public word does not mean every underlying source identifier has been renamed from organ.

relationships.gloss: Components are the public object units exposed by Plectis.
Component is the public copy translation for legacy Microcosm object vocabulary.
Each component needs an explicit limit on what its evidence supports.

source_refs.gloss: Public-site builder translates source object vocabulary into component-facing copy.
Current source atlas still carries legacy object ids.

public_glossary.label: scope limit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A scope limit is the claim ceiling imposed by one item’s evidence; it is not necessarily the project’s work scope, permission boundary, or schedule.
public_glossary.short_definition: A scope limit—also called a claim ceiling or authority ceiling—is the explicit boundary between what a unit's evidence establishes and what the unit is not allowed to assert.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A scope limit—also called a claim ceiling or authority ceiling—is the explicit boundary between what a unit's evidence establishes and what the unit is not allowed to assert.
public_glossary.card_definition: Every component, evidence class, and published packet on this site carries a scope limit. It marks the edge of what the supporting evidence covers, so that a real result stays a claim about exactly what was checked and does not stretch into launch readiness, whole-system correctness, hosted-service behaviour, professional advice, or private runtime state. A local fixture can pass while the scope limit still rules out any wider guarantee.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result is shown, read its scope limit to see how far the evidence reaches. The result holds only within that boundary, and nothing beyond it is being claimed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A scope limit does not weaken evidence; it protects it by blocking unsupported elevation. The component digest, the claim-ceiling index, the question routes, and the evidence pages all check this boundary before an answer is permitted to make a broader claim.
public_glossary.scope_note: Scope limits appear wherever a result, component card, digest row, evidence page, or agent answer separates what is shown from what is not shown. The same boundary is recorded in source identifiers as a claim ceiling or authority ceiling.
public_glossary.example: The doctrine card "Bind authority to transaction scope" is a scope limit in action: a unit's authority is tied to the bounded transaction it ran, so its claim cannot extend past what that transaction actually covered.

example_route.label: Bind authority to transaction scope
example_route.gloss: open the doctrine card that ties a claim to its bounded scope

public_glossary.non_example: A scope limit is not a flaw, a hedge, or an admission that a result is weak. It is the precise statement of how far one verified result reaches, leaving everything outside that line unclaimed rather than quietly assumed.

relationships.gloss: Each component carries a scope limit.
Public Plectis copy stays honest by keeping scope limits close to evidence.
A scope limit must be read against current public records, not stale memory.

source_refs.gloss: Builder emits scope-limit copy, claim-ceiling index, and canonical question routes.
Component records carry per-object boundary fields consumed by public projections.

public_glossary.label: evidence class
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An evidence class fixes what kind of support a record provides and which inferences it licenses; it is not a confidence score or a declaration that the underlying claim is true.
public_glossary.short_definition: An evidence class names the kind of support behind a result—such as a source-linked row, fixture pass, local tool run, or review packet—without implying that every claim made from that support is true.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An evidence class names the kind of support behind a result—such as a source-linked row, fixture pass, local tool run, or review packet—without implying that every claim made from that support is true.
public_glossary.card_definition: When a card or result on this site is marked as backed, its evidence class is the category of that backing. The classes distinguish, for example, a result whose support is a link to a source row, one whose support is a fixture that passed, one whose support is a tool that ran locally, and one whose support is a recorded review. Each class carries its own ceiling on what may be claimed from it, so two results can both be supported while resting on very different kinds of evidence.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check which evidence class a result carries, and read it as a statement about the kind of support, not the strength of every conclusion. A class sits next to a scope limit that names what that support does not establish.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The governing list of classes is kept in the source slice and the site builder's claim-ceiling projection, so a class is a fixed vocabulary entry rather than a free-form label, and it keeps a local fixture or a generated record from being read as wider authority.
public_glossary.scope_note: Evidence class covers the typed backing attached to public results, cards, and packets. A reader meets it on result and component pages where a claim is shown alongside the category of support that stands behind it, and most directly on the evidence page that sets out what a pass proves.
public_glossary.example: On the evidence page, a result marked as fixture-backed carries the fixture-pass evidence class: its support is a test fixture that ran and passed, which is a different and narrower kind of backing than a row linked directly to a source file.

example_route.label: What the pass proves (evidence)
example_route.gloss: see results sorted by the kind of support behind them

public_glossary.non_example: An evidence class is not a quality score or a rank that makes one result better than another, and a high or strong-sounding class is not proof of launch readiness, security, or whole-system correctness. It names the kind of support, not a verdict.

relationships.gloss: Evidence type must be read with the claim boundary.
A record can carry an evidence class describing the support it contains.
Plectis public copy uses evidence classes to avoid overclaiming.

source_refs.gloss: Source registry for component evidence classes.
Builds evidence labels, ranks, profiles, and claim-ceiling routes into the public site.

public_glossary.label: record
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Record means a governed stored result or receipt in this system. It does not by itself carry legal-record status, evidentiary sufficiency, or truth authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: A record is a concrete, durable, independently inspectable artifact—such as a result row, receipt, generated output, review packet, or verification entry—that preserves what was checked, produced, or routed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A record is a concrete, durable, independently inspectable artifact—such as a result row, receipt, generated output, review packet, or verification entry—that preserves what was checked, produced, or routed.
public_glossary.card_definition: A record is the inspectable object a page points to when it refers to something more solid than a sentence. Each record carries what produced it and where its authority stops, and it sits below its owning source rather than replacing it. Records are how narrative pages connect to source authority: a reader can open the actual result row, receipt, ledger, or generated projection behind a statement.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a page points you to a record, open it and read what it actually preserves and where its scope ends. A record holds a checkable object; it does not make a claim true merely by existing.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In this system a record may be a source row, a generated projection, a receipt, a ledger entry, or a public packet. Each is durable and reopenable, and each ranks below the source that produced it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers concrete source and generated artifacts across the site: result rows, receipts, generated JSON outputs, review packets, ledgers, and verification entries. A reader meets records wherever a page links out to something inspectable rather than describing it in prose.
public_glossary.example: The doctrine card "Generated-result record source inversion" concerns exactly this: a generated record, such as a result file emitted by a tool, must stay subordinate to the source that produced it rather than being treated as the authority itself.

example_route.label: Generated-result record source inversion
example_route.gloss: open a rule about how generated records relate to their source

public_glossary.non_example: A record is not a paragraph of explanatory text and not a claim that becomes true by being written down. It is a concrete artifact, row, or generated output that someone can reopen and check.

relationships.gloss: A record can name the support type behind it.
A record's claim boundary must travel with it.
A generated record is not stronger than its source authority.

source_refs.gloss: Generated public index of components, paper modules, glossary terms, and evidence profiles.
Builds public records from source rows and generated projections.

public_glossary.label: substrate
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Substrate means the live files, records, or runtime state on which this system operates. It is a local systems metaphor, not a biological, chemical, or philosophical substrate claim.
public_glossary.short_definition: A substrate is the underlying body of files, routes, recorded state, and tools that the system operates on, distinct from the pages and summaries projected over that source material.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A substrate is the underlying body of files, routes, recorded state, and tools that the system operates on, distinct from the pages and summaries projected over that source material.
public_glossary.card_definition: The substrate is everything the public pages are generated from: the source files, the standards, the recorded state, the validators, and the tools that act on them. It is the concrete, inspectable layer beneath any summary, route, or evidence view. A generated page can describe or point into the substrate, but it does not own the source records, package identifiers, or state transitions that live there.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is called the substrate, treat it as the lower source layer that a page is reporting on, and look to it rather than the page when you need the actual file or record.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The substrate is what keeps a generated page honest about its own status: the page makes a map, digest, or evidence view, while the substrate remains the authority that owns the source records, validators, identifiers, and state changes underneath.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the source layer of the whole system: files, standards, ledgers, recorded state, and tooling. A reader meets it wherever the pages distinguish the generated public view from the source it was derived from.
public_glossary.example: The Source and license page is the entry point into this substrate, opening onto the source files and records that the rest of the site is generated from.

example_route.label: Source & license
example_route.gloss: open the source layer the pages are generated from

public_glossary.non_example: A substrate is not a vague word for the whole project, and not a mystical layer behind it. It is the specific, inspectable set of files and records that the pages are generated from.

relationships.gloss: Source authority rests in substrate-owned records and tools.
Plectis is a public map over source substrate.
A record is one inspectable artifact inside or generated from substrate.

source_refs.gloss: Doctrine roof for the source-open substrate concept.
Type A operating seed that distinguishes live substrate from chat.

public_glossary.label: source authority
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Source authority means the local source-of-record relationship for a claim or artifact. It does not imply institutional, legal, academic, or moral authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: Source authority is the artifact, standard, tool, or ledger that owns a fact more strongly than anything generated from it: the place where the truth is held, beneath any page, summary, or AI answer that merely reports it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Source authority is the artifact, standard, tool, or ledger that owns a fact more strongly than anything generated from it: the place where the truth is held, beneath any page, summary, or AI answer that merely reports it.
public_glossary.card_definition: Every generated surface on this site, a page, a digest, an AI summary, is a projection of something lower down. The source authority is that lower thing: a source file, a standard, a validator, a ledger, or a generated sidecar with an ownership contract. When prose, HTML, or a summary may have drifted, the source authority is where the actual claim lives and where a fact is settled. A projection can route to its source authority, but summarising a fact does not make the summary the owner of it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a page makes a claim, the source authority is the artifact it stands below; treat that artifact, not the page, as the place the fact is owned.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This is the rule that keeps generated public surfaces honest: they are useful because they route, compress, and display, and they stay accurate by naming the lower artifact or tool that owns each claim and refusing to assert anything beyond it.
public_glossary.scope_note: Source authority appears wherever a public page describes itself as a map, projection, record, or digest, and points to the underlying file, standard, validator, or ledger that holds the fact. It marks the boundary between a generated surface and the material it is drawn from.
public_glossary.example: The vocabulary registry standard is a source authority: a glossary row on this site can cite it for the meaning of a term while the row itself remains a projection that owns nothing.

example_route.label: Generated-result record source inversion
example_route.gloss: open the anti-pattern that fires when a generated record is mistaken for the source that owns the fact

public_glossary.non_example: Source authority is not a generated page, a digest, or an AI answer. Those are projections; they hold authority only when a governing standard explicitly names them as the owner of the fact.

relationships.gloss: Records point to the authority that owns their claim.
Plectis public pages stay below source authority.
Authority and scope must be named together for public claims.

source_refs.gloss: Defines system vocabulary rows as projections below cited source authority.
Emits source refs and authority boundaries into public packets.

public_glossary.label: organ (source identifier)
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Organ is a retained source/storage compatibility identifier. It is not the preferred public object name, a biological claim, or proof that a storage rename has completed.
public_glossary.short_definition: An organ is the source-code name for one self-contained unit of working machinery with a defined job, explicit inputs and outputs, and a recorded claim limit, presented as a component on public pages.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An organ is the source-code name for one self-contained unit of working machinery with a defined job, explicit inputs and outputs, and a recorded claim limit, presented as a component on public pages.
public_glossary.card_definition: The system is built as a set of these units rather than one large program. Each organ does one job, such as mapping a route, running a check, importing source material, or generating a page, and can be opened and inspected on its own. Each one carries its own boundary and a record of what it is allowed to assert, so a unit's reach is fixed and visible rather than implied.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a source path or identifier names an organ, read it as one bounded unit doing a single job; the same unit appears on the public pages as a component.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Organ is the source-level and runtime name for these units, kept stable in file paths, identifiers, and compatibility records; component is the same thing under its public label.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers every bounded unit the system is assembled from. A reader meets it in source paths and identifiers such as organ_registry.json, and meets the same units as components throughout the public pages, where each can be opened on its own.
public_glossary.example: A concrete organ is the Source Projection Import Protocol, a unit that brings source material across into the public slice; it is listed and openable among the components.

example_route.label: Source Projection Import Protocol
example_route.gloss: browse the units, each openable on its own

public_glossary.non_example: An organ is not a biological metaphor and not a marketing feature. It is a unit of running code with a stated boundary.

relationships.gloss: Component is the preferred reader-facing word.
Organ ids may appear in the public source slice.
Source-level organ records still need claim boundaries.

source_refs.gloss: Source-level registry that still uses organ ids.
Source atlas consumed by public component projections.

public_glossary.label: check result
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Witness means a source-linked check result or verification record in this system. It is not a legal witness and does not by itself establish proof beyond its stated evidence class.
public_glossary.short_definition: A witness is the durable record that one specific check ran and what it found, shown in public copy as a check result or verification record.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A witness is the durable record that one specific check ran and what it found, shown in public copy as a check result or verification record.
public_glossary.card_definition: When a statement on this site claims it is supported, the witness is the concrete artifact behind that support: the output of a validator, a test, or a source-row check, naming exactly what was examined and what held. It is evidence for one bounded statement, not a verdict on the whole system.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read what a witness actually checked before relying on it. It vouches for that one claim and nothing wider.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Each witness carries its scope limit with it: the command or record that produced it, the exact thing it examined, and the boundary of what that result does and does not cover.
public_glossary.scope_note: Witness covers the evidence layer of the system: the checkable records that sit behind supported claims on components, doctrine cards, and the evidence page, where the public label is check result or verification record.
public_glossary.example: On the evidence page, the record of what a passing check examined, such as a source-row check or a validator run, is a witness: it names the command and the rows it inspected and the one claim that result supports.

example_route.label: What the pass proves (evidence)
example_route.gloss: see the records that stand behind a passing check

public_glossary.non_example: A witness is not legal testimony, a mathematical proof on its own, or a guarantee that the whole system is correct. It records that one named check passed.

relationships.gloss: Verification record is the safer reader-facing object.
A check result can carry an evidence class.
A witness/check result must not exceed its claim boundary.

source_refs.gloss: Axiom support routes use witness-like evidence vocabulary.
Scrubs public copy toward check results and verification records.

evidence_commands.reason: Inspect a generated support record when present.

public_glossary.label: navigable
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Navigable means a cold reader can discover, select, open, and verify an artifact through supported routes; it is stronger than merely being searchable or linked somewhere.
public_glossary.short_definition: A navigable term, record, or page carries at least one concrete anchor, source reference, relationship link, command, or pointer that takes a reader from its summary to the underlying object or evidence.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A navigable term, record, or page carries at least one concrete anchor, source reference, relationship link, command, or pointer that takes a reader from its summary to the underlying object or evidence.
public_glossary.card_definition: Across Plectis, an object is treated as navigable when it can be opened, cross-referenced, checked, and traced back to its source instead of only being named. A navigable component, for example, links to the source file that defines it, the standards it answers to, and the check that confirms it. The opposite is a dead term: a word that sounds meaningful but offers no route to anything concrete.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is described as navigable, expect a real link, anchor, or command behind it, and follow that route to the source if you want to confirm the claim yourself.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Navigability is how the system separates a real surface from a decorative one: a navigable concept can be selected, opened, related to others, and bounded by what it is allowed to claim, while anything that cannot route to a source, record, or owner is counted as a gap.
public_glossary.scope_note: The property applies to glossary rows, components, records, and pages throughout the site, and is most visible on the architecture map, where each part connects through to the source material it stands for.
public_glossary.example: The architecture map is a navigable surface: each area and component on it links through to the source files, standards, and checks it represents, so you can move from the overview down to the exact material behind any box.

example_route.label: How it fits together (architecture map)
example_route.gloss: follow a map whose every part routes to its source

public_glossary.non_example: Navigable does not mean important, prominent, or well written. A heading can look significant and still be non-navigable if it offers no anchor, owner, or source reference to follow.

relationships.gloss: Navigable objects need routes.
Navigability prevents cold readers from guessing.
Records make route targets inspectable.

source_refs.gloss: Navigation theory behind routeable, inspectable surfaces.
Generated public graph carrying routes and anchors.

public_glossary.label: above and beyond
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Inside ai_workflow this means bounded durable follow-through, not overwork, speculative expansion, or permission to exceed the user's scope.
public_glossary.short_definition: In ai_workflow, above and beyond means bounded follow-through that makes the requested result durable, then stops at a named boundary.
public_glossary.reader_preview: In ai_workflow, above and beyond means bounded follow-through that makes the requested result durable, then stops at a named boundary.
public_glossary.card_definition: It describes a finished pass that did the immediately useful follow-through, not one that wandered off into new scope. When a task surfaces something that would otherwise go stale or be hard for the next person to find, the extra work is to make that one result durable: name the boundary, do the smallest improvement that prevents rediscovery, run a focused check, and leave evidence. The boundary is part of the trait: the work has a source case, a place it belongs, a check, and a clear stopping point.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a pass is described this way, take it to mean the result was made durable and was bounded, not that scope was expanded; the record of what was checked tells you how far the follow-through actually reached.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It is the active form of care and standards held together: care protects whoever reads the result next, and the safety condition is that the extra work stays bounded, with a recorded stopping point rather than an open-ended campaign.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers how a unit of work is judged complete across the system, and it appears wherever a pass reports what it finished and what it deliberately left for later, most directly on the surfaces that audit whether a pass closed its loop honestly.
public_glossary.example: The Agent Completion Faithfulness Audit is a concrete instance: it is the check that compares what a pass claims it finished against what it actually closed, which is the boundary that above and beyond stays inside.

public_glossary.non_example: Above and beyond is not speculative scope expansion or doing more than was asked for its own sake. It is bounded follow-through that makes one result durable and then stops at a named boundary.

public_glossary.label: accept
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, audit is narrower than an ordinary review: it checks faithfulness between a report and an execution record. It does not judge whether the underlying work was correct.
public_glossary.short_definition: To accept something is to admit, approve, receive, or treat it as satisfying a stated condition.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To accept something is to admit, approve, receive, or treat it as satisfying a stated condition.
public_glossary.card_definition: Acceptance may concern input validity, a proof step, a publication gate, or a proposed result. It should be tied to an actor or checker and a rule rather than treated as universal endorsement.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is accepted, identify the accepting authority, criteria, scope, and resulting permissions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Acceptance under one interface or test does not establish correctness, safety, or approval outside that boundary.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers validation, workflow, proof, review, and data-ingestion decisions.
public_glossary.example: The JSON parser accepts a registry file when its syntax is valid JSON.
public_glossary.non_example: A parser accepting syntax does not mean every definition is accurate.

public_glossary.label: access
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, bundle means a component's exported evidence package—source bodies, fixtures, and result records—not an arbitrary group of files.
public_glossary.short_definition: Access is the ability and permission to reach, open, or use a page, file, tool, or service.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Access is the ability and permission to reach, open, or use a page, file, tool, or service.
public_glossary.card_definition: Access answers whether a reader can get to something, not whether that thing is complete, correct, or safe to rely on. Public access, repository access, and tool access are separate permissions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat access as a reachability condition and check authority, evidence, and license separately.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A route can exist without being accessible because it needs an account, network, local checkout, or permission that the current reader does not have.
public_glossary.scope_note: Access covers the stated reader, object, route, and permission conditions.
public_glossary.example: A public glossary page has anonymous web access, while a private working file does not.
public_glossary.non_example: Being able to open a file does not prove that its claims are correct.

public_glossary.label: accountability layer
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Here, accountability layer names the records and routes around a mechanism that make one claim inspectable. It is not the only accepted use of the phrase, and it does not imply that the wider system is public or independently verified.
public_glossary.short_definition: The accountability layer is the set of evidence records, result records, source links, and scope limits that lets a reader trace what a mechanism ran and where the resulting claim stops.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The accountability layer is the set of evidence records, result records, source links, and scope limits that lets a reader trace what a mechanism ran and where the resulting claim stops.
public_glossary.card_definition: This layer sits around a mechanism rather than replacing it. It connects the visible claim to the recorded run or replay, the source that owns it, the kind of evidence attached to it, and the boundary beyond which that evidence says nothing.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the accountability layer to follow a claim back to evidence and source; do not treat the page that presents those links as the authority itself.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The layer makes a claim inspectable by preserving provenance and limits together. A record without a source route or a scope limit is not enough to establish accountable public evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the public records and routes that make one mechanism or claim traceable. It does not mean that every part of the larger system is public or independently verified.
public_glossary.example: A result record that names its command, evidence class, source file, and scope limit participates in the accountability layer.
public_glossary.non_example: A confident summary with no source or result record is not an accountability layer.

relationships.gloss: Records preserve what a mechanism or check produced.
Evidence classes state what kind of support a record carries.
Scope limits prevent a local record from becoming a wider claim.

public_glossary.label: action
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, check means an executable command tied to a stated claim and persistent result record, not merely informal inspection or a checklist item.
public_glossary.short_definition: An action is a discrete operation performed by a person, agent, program, or tool that can change state or produce an observable effect.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An action is a discrete operation performed by a person, agent, program, or tool that can change state or produce an observable effect.
public_glossary.card_definition: Actions differ from intentions and suggestions because something actually happens. Their authorization, target, and result should be recorded when they affect durable state.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Verify who or what acted, on which target, under what permission, and with what outcome.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A multi-step task may contain many actions but become valid only when its transaction and closeout conditions are satisfied.
public_glossary.scope_note: An action covers the named operation, actor, target, time, and execution conditions.
public_glossary.example: Writing a generated glossary file is an action performed by the site builder.
public_glossary.non_example: Describing a command without running it is not the action the command would perform.

public_glossary.label: actor axes
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: These are local actor-classification axes. They are not personality types, intelligence rankings, capability tiers, or a universal taxonomy of agents.
public_glossary.short_definition: Actor axes keep separate how an actor accesses the system, what it can do, how it is invoked, and what role it plays.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Actor axes keep separate how an actor accesses the system, what it can do, how it is invoked, and what role it plays.
public_glossary.card_definition: Rather than ranking actors on one scale from weak to strong, the system measures them along several axes at once. The primary axis is substrate authority, which marks whether an actor has live, direct access to the system's own files and tools (Type A) or works from an interface, an API, an injected copy of context, or the public web without that direct access (Type B). The other axes, including capability tier, invocation surface, topology role, evidence access, purpose lane, and reasoning budget, are recorded separately so that being clever, being expensive, and being delegated never get confused with having authority over the real material.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When an actor is described by where it sits on these axes, read each axis on its own. A capable or costly actor is not automatically one with direct authority over the system, and a delegated helper with live access can hold more authority than a powerful service that only sees a copy.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The decisive axis is substrate authority: a tool-using agent with live access to the repository counts as Type A, while operator dashboards, bridges, hosted models, and anything reasoning over injected or public context count as Type B unless they too hold live access to the private material.
public_glossary.scope_note: Actor axes appear wherever the system labels who or what is acting, including handoffs between a Type B service and a Type A agent, prompt and route descriptions, and the documentation for working through a coding agent.
public_glossary.example: A coding agent running with live access to the repository is an actor that sits at the Type A end of the substrate-authority axis, with a high capability tier and a delegated topology role, all distinguished at once by the axes.

example_route.label: With a coding agent
example_route.gloss: see a Type A actor, a coding agent with live repository access, in use

public_glossary.non_example: Actor axes are not a single ranking of actors from least to most powerful, and substrate authority is not the same as intelligence or cost. An actor can be highly capable or expensive yet still sit on the Type B side because it lacks direct access to the system's real files and tools.

relationships.gloss: Type A is substrate_type=type_a under actor axes.
Type B is substrate_type=type_b under actor axes.
Bridge is one Type B surface, not the whole Type B concept.

public_glossary.label: admitted proof step
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, a claim is a separately registered assertion whose wording can be compared with evidence; ordinary assertions outside that contract remain ordinary prose.
public_glossary.short_definition: An admitted proof step is a gap left deliberately in a proof: a step assumed rather than proved, which the proof checker accepts on request and flags.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An admitted proof step is a gap left deliberately in a proof: a step assumed rather than proved, which the proof checker accepts on request and flags.
public_glossary.card_definition: It is the single most important number to check in any formal corpus. One admitted step in the wrong place can carry an entire result, so a large corpus with an admission may establish less than a small one without. Formal systems make this checkable rather than a matter of trust, because the checker records every admission.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the admitted-step count first. Everything downstream of an admission is assumed, not proved.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The reason to publish the count rather than the intention is that admissions are normal during development and easy to leave behind. The number is a fact about the corpus as shipped.
public_glossary.scope_note: The count describes the corpus at the measured commit.
public_glossary.example: This corpus reports zero admitted proof steps and zero added axioms.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: affordance row
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Here, an affordance row is a navigation record for one selectable artifact, not a database row, spreadsheet row, or visual layout primitive.
public_glossary.short_definition: An affordance row is one selectable navigation entry that says what an artifact is, why to open it, and where its source evidence lives.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An affordance row is one selectable navigation entry that says what an artifact is, why to open it, and where its source evidence lives.
public_glossary.card_definition: The system organises navigation as rows, not as monolithic documents. Each affordance row is the atomic unit of that navigation surface: it states one option, the next thing an agent or reader could open, along with enough structured detail to decide whether to open it. A row can be shown at different depths, from a one-line flag through a fuller card to a detailed view with the exact command that produced its evidence, so a choice can be made from a budgeted menu instead of by searching through source files.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When you meet an affordance row, read it as one option on a menu: it tells you what the thing is, what opening it costs, and what backs it, so you can decide your next read without scanning the underlying files.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The row compresses choice rather than content: it turns "what can I do with this artifact" into source-derived structure, with each row being projectable at several depths, linked to its evidence, marked with a lifecycle state, and typed by what it is allowed to claim.
public_glossary.scope_note: Affordance rows underlie the system's browse and navigation surfaces, where each artifact kind, components, paper modules, doctrine cards and others, is listed as rows at varying depths. They appear wherever the public pages or internal tools present a menu of things to open rather than a raw file listing.
public_glossary.example: The Navigation Hologram Route Plane is the component that emits the system's artifacts as these rows and projects them as a navigable menu, so it is a working instance of affordance rows in use.

example_route.label: Navigation Hologram Route Plane
example_route.gloss: open the component that turns artifacts into navigable rows

public_glossary.non_example: An affordance row is not a row in a spreadsheet or database table, and not a styling choice for laying text out in lines. It is a structured navigation entry that bundles one option's identity, cost, evidence, edges, and state.

public_glossary.label: agent
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An agent is a software-controlled worker that can interpret instructions, inspect context, use permitted tools, and produce or change artifacts.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An agent is a software-controlled worker that can interpret instructions, inspect context, use permitted tools, and produce or change artifacts.
public_glossary.card_definition: On this site, an agent is not a person and not an autonomous authority. It acts through a bounded tool and permission surface, and its outputs still require source checks and validation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Judge an agent by the evidence and permissions attached to its actions, not by how fluent its explanation sounds.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Different agents may have different contexts, tools, runtimes, and mutation rights even when they use the same underlying model.
public_glossary.scope_note: Agent covers the software worker active in one declared task, environment, and permission set.
public_glossary.example: A coding agent can inspect the repository, edit a claimed file, and run its focused tests.
public_glossary.non_example: A chat answer with no tool access is not evidence that an agent executed the described command.

public_glossary.label: agent reliability and safety
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Agent reliability and safety is the question of whether an AI agent's report of what it did matches what it actually did, and whether it stays inside the limits it was given.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Agent reliability and safety is the question of whether an AI agent's report of what it did matches what it actually did, and whether it stays inside the limits it was given.
public_glossary.card_definition: An agent can say it committed a fix, ran a test, or finished a task, in fluent prose, with none of it having happened. Reliability work checks the report against the record the action would have left. Safety work checks the second half: whether the agent stayed inside its sandbox, refused what it should refuse, and did not quietly widen its own permissions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A component in this area checks a specific failure it can reproduce. None of them establishes that an agent is reliable in general.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It is the largest area of the public release, with 20 components. The worked example on the landing page belongs to it: an audit that runs real git and pytest against notes carrying three planted forgeries, and is required to name each refusal.
public_glossary.scope_note: Reliability here means agreement between a claim and its evidence for a checked case, not dependability of the underlying model.
public_glossary.example: Reading an agent's close-out note against the commits and test runs it cites.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: agent seed
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Agent seed is the local agent-authored synthesis substrate; it is not operator voice, a random seed, training data, or a public research seed by default.
public_glossary.short_definition: An agent seed is the durable, attributed record of an AI agent's own observations, synthesis, and drift signals, kept separate from raw seed so agent interpretation cannot be mistaken for the operator's original words.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An agent seed is the durable, attributed record of an AI agent's own observations, synthesis, and drift signals, kept separate from raw seed so agent interpretation cannot be mistaken for the operator's original words.
public_glossary.card_definition: When a coding agent working inside this system learns something worth keeping, such as a pattern it noticed or a correction it made, it deposits that into an agent seed rather than into the operator's raw seed. The deposit is stamped with the agent that wrote it and the sources it drew on. It is treated as useful but lower authority than the operator's own statements of intent, so the system can retain what an agent learned without that material being mistaken for the operator's voice.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Take an agent seed as an AI agent's recorded reasoning, attributed to that agent, not as the operator's intent. It carries who wrote it and what it drew on, so weigh it accordingly.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Keeping agent-authored synthesis in its own seed is what lets the system absorb an agent's learning while the operator's raw seed stays the higher authority on intent, with neither layer impersonating the other.
public_glossary.scope_note: Agent seed names the attributed AI-authored layer of the system's substrate, sitting alongside the operator-voice raw seed. A reader meets it on the pages about agent reliability and about how agent observations feed back into the system's doctrine.
public_glossary.example: The Voice To Doctrine Self Improvement Loop is the component that carries agent-authored seed material onward, taking what an agent recorded and folding it into the system's standing doctrine while preserving who wrote it.

example_route.label: Voice To Doctrine Self Improvement Loop
example_route.gloss: see where agent-authored seed material feeds back into doctrine

public_glossary.non_example: An agent seed is not the operator's own voice and not source authority on intent. It is also not the agent's private working memory: it is durable, attributed material meant to be kept, distinct from the raw seed that records the operator directly.

relationships.gloss: Agent seed is attributed agent voice, not operator voice.
Agent learning can be routed upward through the right lane.

public_glossary.label: agent trace
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, an agent trace is captured session-event evidence used to audit an agent’s report; it is not the report itself, a complete record beyond the capture surface, or a verdict that the work was correct.
public_glossary.short_definition: An agent trace is the recorded sequence of what an AI agent actually did during a session: the calls it made, the files it touched, and the order it did them in.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An agent trace is the recorded sequence of what an AI agent actually did during a session: the calls it made, the files it touched, and the order it did them in.
public_glossary.card_definition: An agent's own account of its work is a summary written by the thing being audited. The trace is the record underneath it, and the two can disagree. Keeping the trace separate is what makes it possible to check whether a reported action occurred, which is a different question from whether the report is plausible.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Compare an agent’s closeout with the captured trace, but read the trace only within its instrumentation coverage: it is evidence for recorded events, not proof that every action was observed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This is the same discipline the rest of the site applies to itself: prose describing a run is not the run. An agent is simply a case where the prose is unusually convincing.
public_glossary.scope_note: An agent trace establishes the events captured by the named tracing surface during one session. It does not by itself establish completeness, intent, correctness, or the absence of unrecorded activity.
public_glossary.example: The closeout faithfulness audit compares what a session reported against what its trace shows it did.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: AI-native
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary uses AI-native in a broad architectural sense and does not certify one universal definition. The label does not establish model quality, autonomy, safety, or correctness.
public_glossary.short_definition: AI-native describes a system or workflow designed around AI agents doing bounded, inspectable work through explicit tools, records, permissions, and checks.
public_glossary.reader_preview: AI-native describes a system or workflow designed around AI agents doing bounded, inspectable work through explicit tools, records, permissions, and checks.
public_glossary.card_definition: The phrase describes architecture, not intelligence or correctness. Agents are expected to inspect, build, maintain, route, or validate artifacts, while human direction, source authority, and separate checks still constrain the result.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read AI-native as a description of how the workflow is organized, never as proof that the workflow is autonomous, reliable, or correct.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The system makes agent context, tool access, durable state, handoffs, and validation first-class because agent work must survive beyond one chat and remain open to inspection.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers workflow architecture built around agent execution. It does not establish model quality, autonomy, safety, or correctness.
public_glossary.example: A workflow in which an agent reads a source route, claims a file, performs a bounded change, runs a validator, and leaves a result record is AI-native.
public_glossary.non_example: Adding a chat box to an otherwise unchanged application does not by itself make the application AI-native.

relationships.gloss: Agents are working actors inside an AI-native workflow.
Runtime records distinguish actual agent execution from prose description.
Agent involvement does not create authority by itself.
Independent checks bound agent-produced results.

public_glossary.label: algorithm
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps for transforming specified inputs into outputs.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps for transforming specified inputs into outputs.
public_glossary.card_definition: An algorithm describes the procedure independently of one programming language or implementation. Correctness, termination, and efficiency are separate properties that need their own arguments or measurements.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask what inputs the algorithm accepts, what output it promises, and under which assumptions it terminates.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Two implementations can realize the same algorithm while differing in performance, numerical behavior, and failure handling.
public_glossary.scope_note: An algorithm covers the declared input domain, steps, and output contract.

public_glossary.non_example: A vague strategy such as “try likely options” is not an algorithm until its steps and stopping condition are specified.

public_glossary.label: allowed
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Allowed describes an action, value, or state that a governing rule or authority permits within stated conditions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Allowed describes an action, value, or state that a governing rule or authority permits within stated conditions.

public_glossary.short_definition: An anchor is a stable reference point used to attach, locate, or route related material.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An anchor is a stable reference point used to attach, locate, or route related material.

public_glossary.label: annex
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Here annex means curated external prior art adapted into the local doctrine graph, not merely an appendix attached to a document.
public_glossary.short_definition: An annex is a curated account of reusable patterns from an external framework, repository, or document, translated into this system's vocabulary without importing the outside source as local authority.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An annex is a curated account of reusable patterns from an external framework, repository, or document, translated into this system's vocabulary without importing the outside source as local authority.
public_glossary.card_definition: Annexes live under the `annexes/` directory and hold shape-level notes about external sources: what problem each one solves and which patterns are worth borrowing. They exist so that before a piece of machinery is built from scratch, the system can check whether the same shape has already been solved elsewhere and translate the idea in, rather than re-deriving it or forking another project's structure. Each annex is a reference point for a pattern, never a binding rule the system must obey.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat an annex as a pointer to outside prior art, not as part of the system's own authority. It tells you where a pattern came from and how it was adapted, not what the system is required to do.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The governing discipline is adapt, do not adopt: an external primitive is compared against the local one and a more coherent version is synthesised when the evidence supports it, so the system can learn from open work without taking on its ontology.
public_glossary.scope_note: Annex covers the layer of curated external references the system draws on for design patterns and prior art. A reader meets it in the import and drift-control area and wherever a component records that its shape was informed by outside work.
public_glossary.example: The Pattern Binding Contract is a concrete instance: a component that governs how a borrowed external pattern is bound into the system's own form before it is allowed to take effect.

public_glossary.label: answer

public_glossary.short_definition: An answer is a response intended to resolve or address a question, request, or problem.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An answer is a response intended to resolve or address a question, request, or problem.
