Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.label: environment
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An environment is the surrounding operating system, tools, versions, configuration, permissions, and external services under which a command or program runs.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An environment is the surrounding operating system, tools, versions, configuration, permissions, and external services under which a command or program runs.
public_glossary.card_definition: The environment is part of a result even when the source code is unchanged. A check may pass locally and fail elsewhere because a dependency, platform feature, permission, or network service differs, so reproducible work records the relevant environment instead of assuming it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Compare environments before treating different run results as evidence about the code alone.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Environment capture can range from a version list to a locked container or toolchain; the necessary detail depends on which surrounding conditions can affect the result.
public_glossary.scope_note: Environment covers the declared execution context for one build, command, or deployed service.
public_glossary.example: A cold-clone check records the operating system and Lean toolchain used to build the public proof corpus.
public_glossary.non_example: The repository contents alone do not fully describe the environment in which they run.

public_glossary.label: epistemic control plane
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The epistemic control plane governs how evidence changes belief and permitted action; it is not an infrastructure control plane, a knowledge base, or a source of truth by itself.
public_glossary.short_definition: An epistemic control plane is a proposed runtime form of the Workingness Instrument that connects the system's current beliefs and acknowledged unknowns to actions that are allowed, blocked, or routed for review.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An epistemic control plane is a proposed runtime form of the Workingness Instrument that connects the system's current beliefs and acknowledged unknowns to actions that are allowed, blocked, or routed for review.
public_glossary.card_definition: It works as a chain: evidence sets the status of a claim, the status of that claim sets which actions are permitted, and any unresolved uncertainty stops a change from being made. It would draw together the recorded checks, judgments, appeals, and projection comparisons into claim rows and matching action boundaries, so that the system only acts where its own beliefs are backed and holds back where they are not. Today it exists as a stated target and an alias; the written-up artifact behind it is the Workingness Instrument paper module and a candidate standard.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat it as a planned bridge from self-observation to safe action, not a shipped runtime: where you meet it, expect a description of how belief is meant to gate action, with the live writer still to be built.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The core rule it encodes is that changing evidence changes a claim's status, changing status changes the allowed actions, and an open question blocks any mutation until it is settled.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the runtime layer that would govern action by belief status across the system; a reader meets it in architecture and runtime descriptions and as the forward-looking name for the Workingness Instrument.
public_glossary.example: The Workingness Instrument, written up as a paper module and a candidate standard, is the concrete artifact this term points at: the authored design that an epistemic control plane would one day run as live machinery.

example_route.label: How it fits together (architecture map)
example_route.gloss: see where this runtime layer would sit in the system

public_glossary.non_example: An epistemic control plane is not an already-running gate that currently decides every action, and it is not a general phrase for the system's overall safety. It is one specific, still-to-be-built layer that would link belief status to permitted action.

relationships.gloss: The control plane is the runtime realization of the instrument contract.
It would bound what apply lanes may consume from judgments and appeals.
It operationalizes truth maintenance as action permissions.

source_refs.gloss: Defines the control-plane target and explicitly marks runtime writer as not yet built.

public_glossary.label: equality
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An equality is a statement that two expressions denote the same value or object under the stated assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An equality is a statement that two expressions denote the same value or object under the stated assumptions.
public_glossary.card_definition: Equality is exact and symmetric: if a = b, either side can replace the other where the expression is defined. Numerical approximations use a different relation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the domain, assumptions, and whether the symbol denotes exact equality or an approximation.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Proofs of equality may proceed by calculation, algebraic rewriting, extensionality, or showing both sides satisfy a unique characterization.
public_glossary.scope_note: An equality covers the two expressions, domain, and assumptions stated around it.
public_glossary.example: The equality 12 = 3 × 4 witnesses that 3 divides 12.
public_glossary.non_example: Two decimal approximations that look alike are not necessarily exactly equal.

public_glossary.label: equation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An equation is an equality containing one or more unknowns whose allowed values are to be found or constrained.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An equation is an equality containing one or more unknowns whose allowed values are to be found or constrained.
public_glossary.card_definition: In the Plectis papers, equations are exact mathematical constraints, not formatted approximations. They may define a quantity, express a recurrence, or state the equality from which a proof derives a denominator or integrality condition; the permitted values depend on the declared number system.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the variables, domain, hypotheses, and equivalence of each transformation before treating a displayed equation as solved.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A Lean theorem can machine-check an equation and the transformations applied to it, but the surrounding prose still has to identify why that formal equality represents the intended Erdős problem.
public_glossary.scope_note: An equation covers the expressions, unknowns, domain, and constraints stated in its formulation.
public_glossary.example: In a denominator argument, an equation obtained by assuming a series rational converts an infinite sum into an exact relation among integers.
public_glossary.non_example: An identity true for every allowed value is not an equation asking for unknown solutions in the same sense.

public_glossary.label: equivalence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, evaluator means a read-only measuring component that emits a report and does not repair its subject; broader software usage may use evaluator more generally.
public_glossary.short_definition: An equivalence is a proved two-way relationship in which each of two statements implies the other under the same stated hypotheses.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An equivalence is a proved two-way relationship in which each of two statements implies the other under the same stated hypotheses.
public_glossary.card_definition: Equivalent statements may look very different while carrying exactly the same truth conditions. Proving only one direction gives an implication or reduction, not an equivalence.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For an equivalence, locate both directions and verify that their hypotheses and domains match.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Equivalences are valuable because they let a problem move into a representation with better tools without changing what would count as a solution.
public_glossary.scope_note: An equivalence covers the two named statements under their common hypotheses and domain.
public_glossary.example: An irrationality question may be equivalent to the impossibility of an eventually periodic digit pattern.
public_glossary.non_example: Similarity, shared examples, or a one-way implication does not establish equivalence.

public_glossary.label: Paul Erdős
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: This registry only explains how the external term appears here. The external owner, specification, or primary source controls when exact meaning matters.
public_glossary.short_definition: Paul Erdős (1913–1996) was a Hungarian mathematician known for posing and solving problems across number theory, combinatorics, and discrete mathematics.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Paul Erdős (1913–1996) was a Hungarian mathematician known for posing and solving problems across number theory, combinatorics, and discrete mathematics.
public_glossary.card_definition: The six numbered Erdős problems discussed here are questions associated with Erdős and indexed by the independently maintained Erdős Problems database. A label such as “Erdős #249” identifies that database entry; it is not a claim that Erdős assigned the number himself.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read “Erdős #n” as a database identifier for a mathematical problem associated with Paul Erdős.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Erdős worked extensively through collaboration and left a large body of questions that continue to organize research; the site covers only the six explicitly listed problems and makes no claim about the rest.
public_glossary.scope_note: This entry covers the person and the meaning of his name in the numbered problem labels used on this site.
public_glossary.example: “Erdős #257” means problem 257 in the cited Erdős Problems catalogue.
public_glossary.non_example: Erdős is not the author of this site, and the catalogue number is not a theorem number or difficulty ranking.

public_glossary.label: error
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An error is a detected condition in which data, reasoning, behaviour, or execution differs from what is valid or expected.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An error is a detected condition in which data, reasoning, behaviour, or execution differs from what is valid or expected.
public_glossary.card_definition: Errors may be defects in the system, invalid inputs, incorrect assumptions, measurement mistakes, or explicit diagnostic values. An error message is evidence about the detector's view, not automatically the root cause.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read an error with the operation, input, expected condition, observed condition, and source that detected it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Useful diagnosis separates symptom, cause, and impact so repair targets the owning layer rather than the nearest visible message.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers software, data, proof, process, and factual errors.
public_glossary.example: Invalid JSON syntax produces a parser error that identifies where parsing stopped.
public_glossary.non_example: An outcome someone dislikes is not necessarily an error if it satisfies the stated rules.

public_glossary.label: establish
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To establish something is to provide sufficient basis for it to be accepted as present, true, valid, or operative within a stated standard.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To establish something is to provide sufficient basis for it to be accepted as present, true, valid, or operative within a stated standard.
public_glossary.card_definition: What establishes a fact depends on the claim: observation may establish presence, a proof may establish a theorem, and a successful gate may establish conformance. The verb should not erase those different evidence standards.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result establishes a claim, identify the claim, standard, evidence chain, and boundary beyond which the establishment does not extend.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Establishing one premise or property can support further reasoning without automatically establishing every downstream conclusion.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers evidence-to-claim relationships explicitly reported by the site.
public_glossary.example: A complete link check establishes that all examined internal href targets existed at that generated state.
public_glossary.non_example: A plausible explanation does not establish a universal mathematical statement.

public_glossary.label: evaluator
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An evaluator is a read-only component that measures something and reports, without changing what it measured.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An evaluator is a read-only component that measures something and reports, without changing what it measured.
public_glossary.card_definition: Separating measurement from repair matters because a tool that both judges and fixes can quietly redefine the standard it is judging against. An evaluator emits a report and stops, leaving the decision about what to do with it outside itself.
public_glossary.reader_rule: An evaluator reports. If a tool also repairs what it measures, ask what its measurement means.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The independence is what makes an evaluator's number worth reading. A measurement produced by the thing being measured is not a measurement.
public_glossary.scope_note: An evaluator establishes what it measured at the time it ran.
public_glossary.example: The term-layer evaluator measures vocabulary coverage across the site and writes reports; it changes no page.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: evidence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Evidence is a source, observation, check result, or record that supports a specific claim within a stated scope and can be inspected independently of that claim.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Evidence is a source, observation, check result, or record that supports a specific claim within a stated scope and can be inspected independently of that claim.
public_glossary.card_definition: Evidence is the backing under a statement, not the statement itself. Its strength depends on what produced it, whether the record is current, and whether its scope actually matches the claim being made.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask which exact claim the evidence supports, how it was produced, and where its coverage stops.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same artifact can be strong evidence for one narrow assertion and irrelevant to a broader one; a passing fixture run may establish that a validator handles those fixtures while saying nothing about real-world performance.
public_glossary.scope_note: Evidence covers only the claim, cases, source version, and conditions named by its producing record.
public_glossary.example: A result record from a local check is evidence that the declared fixtures passed at the recorded commit.
public_glossary.non_example: A confident summary or repeated assertion is not evidence merely because it sounds precise.

public_glossary.label: exact
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Exact describes correspondence or value with no permitted difference under the stated representation and comparison rule.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Exact describes correspondence or value with no permitted difference under the stated representation and comparison rule.
public_glossary.card_definition: Exactness is stricter than approximation but remains relative to what is compared. Two rendered pages can look the same while their bytes differ, and two numbers can be mathematically equal despite different textual forms.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When exact is claimed, identify the representation, normalization, and equality rule used for comparison.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Exact results can still be irrelevant or stale; exactness addresses difference, not purpose, authority, or freshness.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers equality of values, identifiers, files, copies, and match conditions.
public_glossary.example: An exact identifier lookup requires every normalized character to agree.
public_glossary.non_example: A visually similar screenshot is not an exact byte-for-byte copy of HTML.

public_glossary.label: exact rational arithmetic
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Exact rational arithmetic works with fractions as pairs of whole numbers rather than as decimal approximations, so rounding error cannot enter.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Exact rational arithmetic works with fractions as pairs of whole numbers rather than as decimal approximations, so rounding error cannot enter.
public_glossary.card_definition: It is slower than floating-point arithmetic and answers a different question. A floating-point computation shows a value is close to something; an exact rational computation shows it is that something, for the case computed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Exactness removes rounding error from a finite computation. It does not extend that computation to cases it did not run.
public_glossary.deep_definition: One Plectis component recomputes an Erdős certificate in exact rational arithmetic and compares the result against the checked-in value. A pass establishes that the recorded certificate is the one the arithmetic produces, for that certificate.
public_glossary.scope_note: Applies to computations over the rationals; irrational quantities are not represented exactly this way.
public_glossary.example: One third plus one sixth is stored as one half, not as 0.5000000001.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: example
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An example is a concrete instance chosen to show how a definition, method, or claim applies.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An example is a concrete instance chosen to show how a definition, method, or claim applies.
public_glossary.card_definition: Examples make an abstract idea easier to inspect by supplying actual values, objects, or steps. They illustrate a rule but normally do not prove it for every possible case.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use an example to understand the mechanism, not to infer universal coverage.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A counterexample has the stronger logical role of disproving a universal claim, whereas an ordinary positive example only demonstrates one instance.
public_glossary.scope_note: An example covers the specific instance and conditions it presents.
public_glossary.example: Showing one component's command, input, and result is a worked example of the component contract.
public_glossary.non_example: One successful run is not proof that every input or environment succeeds.

public_glossary.label: exclude
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To exclude something is to deliberately leave it outside a set, scope, result, permission, or process.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To exclude something is to deliberately leave it outside a set, scope, result, permission, or process.
public_glossary.card_definition: Exclusion depends on a boundary and a rule for membership. It may protect privacy, remove invalid cases, narrow a claim, or identify an omission that weakens coverage.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is excluded, check the criterion, reason, and whether the exclusion is reflected in downstream counts and claims.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An exclusion can make a result more precise while also limiting who or what the result represents.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers filtering, scoping, access, validation, and publication boundaries.
public_glossary.example: The public glossary excludes a historical compatibility name from its active public count.
public_glossary.non_example: An item accidentally missed by a scan was omitted, not deliberately excluded.

public_glossary.label: executable cross-section
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Executable cross-section is a local ai_workflow/Plectis construct for the published runnable selection. No generally accepted external category, whole-system coverage, or equivalence with an unpublished system is claimed.
public_glossary.short_definition: An executable cross-section is a bounded public slice of a larger system whose included components, checks, source, and result records can be run and inspected independently.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An executable cross-section is a bounded public slice of a larger system whose included components, checks, source, and result records can be run and inspected independently.
public_glossary.card_definition: An executable cross-section is the public middle ground between a description and a complete system release. Plectis selects mechanisms whose code, fixtures, validation commands, source links, and result records can stand together and be rerun by a cold reader. That makes the selected behavior inspectable rather than merely narrated. The selection remains a boundary: omitted mechanisms, private inputs, live orchestration, and the behavior of the larger working system do not inherit evidence from the runnable slice.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Judge the executable cross-section by the components and records it actually publishes; do not infer that it represents or proves the unpublished remainder.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The important distinction is not size but evidential closure. A cross-section is executable only when the included source, inputs, commands, expected negatives, and durable records are sufficient to inspect the selected mechanism without private context. It is still a projection because the act of selecting that closed slice does not establish equivalence with everything outside it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the published runnable selection and its recorded checks. It excludes unpublished components, private data, and claims about whole-system behaviour.
public_glossary.example: Plectis is an executable cross-section because its public components can be cloned, run locally, and inspected through their result records.
public_glossary.non_example: A video of a private application is not an executable cross-section because the viewer cannot run or inspect the demonstrated mechanism.

relationships.gloss: An executable cross-section is a source slice with runnable checks and records.
The slice consists of bounded public components.
The slice cannot establish claims about material outside its public boundary.
Runnable mechanisms are the unit demonstrated by the slice.

source_refs.gloss: Names Plectis as the public executable cross-section.
Projects runnable components and their public boundaries into the site.

public_glossary.label: execution
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Execution is the act of carrying out instructions, a command, a program, a plan, or a defined procedure.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Execution is the act of carrying out instructions, a command, a program, a plan, or a defined procedure.
public_glossary.card_definition: Execution turns a description into an actual run with inputs, environment, effects, and output. It therefore carries operational consequences that merely reading or proposing the instructions does not.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Before execution, verify the target, authority, side effects, and rollback or containment conditions appropriate to the action.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An execution can complete mechanically while failing its intended higher-level purpose, so outcome validation remains separate.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers command, program, workflow, test, and proof-checking runs.
public_glossary.example: Executing the builder reads source data and writes generated public files.
public_glossary.non_example: Displaying a command in a code block does not execute it.

public_glossary.label: exit code
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An exit code is the number a command returns when it finishes: zero means it succeeded, anything else means it failed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An exit code is the number a command returns when it finishes: zero means it succeeded, anything else means it failed.
public_glossary.card_definition: This is the smallest honest unit of evidence on the site. A check that returns exit 0 passed; one that returns anything else failed. A pass is only worth reading if the check could have failed, because a repository where nothing ever fails is usually a repository whose checks stopped discriminating.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the exit code, not the surrounding prose. Zero passed; anything else did not.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The useful question about a green run is whether the check was capable of going red. These checks have gone red before: one lane was found silently skipped in July and fixed in the release that followed, and that correction is recorded beside the current run.
public_glossary.scope_note: An exit code reports the outcome of one run of one command.
public_glossary.example: The landing page's cold rerun lists four commands and the exit code each one returned.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: expand
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To expand something is to increase its extent, detail, coverage, or explicit content.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To expand something is to increase its extent, detail, coverage, or explicit content.
public_glossary.card_definition: Expansion can add new material or reveal detail that was already compressed or hidden. The operation should preserve the identity and boundaries of the subject it expands.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a view expands, distinguish newly authored content from previously available detail that is merely being displayed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: More detail can improve understanding but can also increase noise, so expansion should remain tied to a reader need or coverage goal.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers growth of definitions, views, datasets, scope, and public coverage.
public_glossary.example: Adding ordinary terms expands the glossary's vocabulary coverage.
public_glossary.non_example: Repeating the same sentence at greater length does not meaningfully expand its information.

public_glossary.label: expected
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Expected describes a result or condition predicted, required, or treated as normal under stated assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Expected describes a result or condition predicted, required, or treated as normal under stated assumptions.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis uses expected in two distinct ways: a schema or test can require an exact value, while a model or prior run can merely predict one. Both are compared with an observation, but only the first is a conformance condition; the second can be wrong without making the system invalid.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the source of the expectation—contract, fixture, model, convention, or historical baseline—before classifying a mismatch.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Keeping expected separate from observed lets checks report honest deltas. A fixture mismatch can be a regression, an intended source change, stale generated output, or a bad expectation; the comparison alone does not choose the cause.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers predicted and required states in tests, builds, interfaces, and research.
public_glossary.example: A generated-site check expects byte-identical HTML from the current registry and builder; a performance estimate may only predict a likely runtime.
public_glossary.non_example: An outcome is not expected merely because it happened once before.

public_glossary.label: explain
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, a fixture is a committed, usually synthetic check input that makes a public run reproducible. It is not production data or a general test environment.
public_glossary.short_definition: To explain something is to make its meaning, cause, mechanism, or reasoning understandable by connecting it to relevant facts and relationships.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To explain something is to make its meaning, cause, mechanism, or reasoning understandable by connecting it to relevant facts and relationships.
public_glossary.card_definition: An explanation answers why, how, or what something means rather than merely restating that it exists. Its depth should match the reader's question and distinguish evidence from interpretation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Judge an explanation by whether it identifies the relevant relationship and remains consistent with the available evidence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Explanations can be useful at several levels, but a simpler account must not contradict or conceal the deeper mechanism it compresses.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers reader-facing accounts of concepts, results, failures, and system behaviour.
public_glossary.example: A glossary card explains a term by defining it and marking its boundary with examples.
public_glossary.non_example: Repeating a technical label in different words does not necessarily explain it.

public_glossary.label: exponent
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An exponent states how many times a base is multiplied by itself, so `b^n` uses base `b` and exponent `n`.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An exponent states how many times a base is multiplied by itself, so `b^n` uses base `b` and exponent `n`.
public_glossary.card_definition: Exponents index the terms in several series on this site. Choosing which exponents are included changes the support, while their least common multiple can control repeating arithmetic patterns.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Distinguish the exponent that selects a power from the value of the power itself.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The arithmetic relationship among exponents—divisibility, gaps, and least common multiples—often matters more than their individual size.
public_glossary.scope_note: Exponent covers the power index in the named expression, sequence, or support.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #257 sums `1/(2^n-1)` over an infinite set of positive exponents `n`.
public_glossary.non_example: The exponent `n` is not the same number as the power `2^n`.

public_glossary.label: export
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An export is an artifact or data package deliberately produced from one environment for use in another.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An export is an artifact or data package deliberately produced from one environment for use in another.
public_glossary.card_definition: Exporting selects and transforms allowed material across a boundary, often removing private paths or unsupported fields. The exported copy remains traceable to its source and build.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Inspect the export policy, source fingerprint, and omissions before treating the package as complete.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An export can preserve content faithfully while changing paths, labels, or format to fit the destination's access and safety constraints.
public_glossary.scope_note: An export covers the fields, artifacts, source revision, and destination declared by its producing process.
public_glossary.example: The AI reader packet is an export of the public site content for another assistant.
public_glossary.non_example: Copying an entire private working tree without a release boundary is not a governed public export.

public_glossary.label: external
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: External describes something originating, operating, or existing outside the boundary currently being discussed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: External describes something originating, operating, or existing outside the boundary currently being discussed.
public_glossary.card_definition: The relevant boundary may be a repository, organization, process, network, or public site. External does not mean untrusted by definition, but it does mean authority and availability must be checked separately.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Whenever material is external, identify the boundary it sits outside and the conditions under which it enters or influences the system.
public_glossary.deep_definition: External dependencies can change independently, so provenance, versioning, and failure handling matter even when the source is reputable.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers outside websites, services, packages, people, and evidence relative to the named system boundary.
public_glossary.example: A linked mathematical biography hosted by another institution is an external source.
public_glossary.non_example: A generated page inside the public site is not external merely because a reader opens it in a browser.

public_glossary.label: factor
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A factor is one quantity or expression multiplied with others to form a product.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A factor is one quantity or expression multiplied with others to form a product.
public_glossary.card_definition: For integers, saying d is a factor of n usually means d divides n. In algebra, factors can be expressions whose product expands to the original expression.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify whether factor refers to integer divisibility, algebraic factorisation, or a multiplicative term.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Factorisation exposes multiplicative structure and can make divisibility, roots, cancellation, and proof obligations easier to see.
public_glossary.scope_note: Factor covers the product and algebraic domain named in context.
public_glossary.example: 3 and 4 are factors in the product 3 × 4 = 12.
public_glossary.non_example: A summand in 3 + 4 is not a factor because the operation is addition.

public_glossary.label: factorisation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Factorisation is the expression of an integer or algebraic object as a product of simpler factors, especially the unique prime factors of a positive integer.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Factorisation is the expression of an integer or algebraic object as a product of simpler factors, especially the unique prime factors of a positive integer.
public_glossary.card_definition: Prime factorisation exposes divisibility structure that addition or decimal notation hides. Arithmetic functions such as the totient depend directly on which primes divide a number and with what multiplicities.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result uses factorisation, check which object is being factored and whether the factors are required to be prime or merely nontrivial.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Some certificate algorithms deliberately avoid factoring large integers because repeated modular checks can verify the needed property more cheaply.
public_glossary.scope_note: Factorisation covers the named integer, polynomial, or algebraic expression and the permitted factor class.
public_glossary.example: Euler's totient can be computed from the prime factorisation of its input.
public_glossary.non_example: Writing a number as `1 × n` is formally a product but not the nontrivial factorisation usually sought.

public_glossary.label: failure
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A failure is an outcome in which a required function, condition, check, or expectation is not satisfied.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A failure is an outcome in which a required function, condition, check, or expectation is not satisfied.
public_glossary.card_definition: Failures can arise from defects, invalid inputs, unavailable dependencies, unsafe conditions, or incorrect expectations. Classifying the cause matters because each class has a different repair path.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a failure with the operation attempted, expected condition, observed result, and evidence that locates the cause.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A failure result is information about a boundary; it should not be generalized to unrelated operations or causes without evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers test, build, proof, runtime, process, and publication failures.
public_glossary.example: A missing link target causes an internal-link validation failure.
public_glossary.non_example: A deliberate rejection of unsafe input is successful protection, not necessarily a system failure.

public_glossary.label: failure class propagation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Failure-class propagation tests whether one local break recurs across sibling surfaces before widening the repair; it is not permission to apply one fix everywhere.
public_glossary.short_definition: Failure-class propagation tests whether one local break recurs on sibling surfaces, then repairs only the proven class boundary.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Failure-class propagation tests whether one local break recurs on sibling surfaces, then repairs only the proven class boundary.
public_glossary.card_definition: When something fails in one place, that failure is taken as evidence about one location and as a question about others: does the same cause sit in sibling files, standards, routes, tests, or generated records. Failure class propagation answers that question by scanning those siblings, stating exactly where the pattern holds and where it stops, and then making a fix that covers the proven extent and no more. A deliberate decision not to widen counts as a valid outcome when it records what was checked and why widening would currently cause harm.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When you see a fix described as failure class propagation, read what siblings were scanned and where the boundary was drawn: it claims to have repaired a bounded class, not every instance everywhere and not just the one case that was first noticed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It carries a fixed set of parts: the concrete local case, the sibling scan, the class boundary, the counter-force against overgeneralising, the plane that owns the repair, and the validation. A no-op or deferred repair is sound only when it names what was examined and why holding back is the right call for now.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers how the system turns a local defect into a bounded, checked repair across related surfaces. A reader meets it in the doctrine and in components such as the Pattern Binding Contract, where a local pattern is bound to its proven extent with a stated boundary rather than patched once or expanded without limit.
public_glossary.example: The Pattern Binding Contract is a concrete instance: it takes an observed pattern, binds it to the sibling surfaces where the same shape genuinely recurs, and fixes the extent of the binding so the repair neither stops at the first case nor spreads past where the pattern holds.

example_route.label: Pattern Binding Contract
example_route.gloss: open the component that binds a local pattern to its proven class with a stated boundary

public_glossary.non_example: Failure class propagation is not patching only the one spot that broke, and it is not turning a single bug into an unbounded sweep across the whole system. It is a bounded repair sized to the siblings that were actually checked.

relationships.gloss: Moves a local failure into a bounded reusable class across the lattice.
Annexes can pressure the class hypothesis when the primitive is unsettled.
Old failure evidence remains evidence; live substrate decides current repair.
The local-to-general skill chooses the plane home.

source_refs.gloss: Procedural packet for local-to-general and failure-class closeout.

public_glossary.label: false
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: False describes a proposition that is not true or a boolean value representing the negative branch of a two-valued condition.
public_glossary.reader_preview: False describes a proposition that is not true or a boolean value representing the negative branch of a two-valued condition.
public_glossary.card_definition: In logic, falsity concerns the truth of a proposition; in software, false is a value interpreted by a program under a condition. A failed check can provide evidence of falsity but may instead indicate an invalid test or environment.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Distinguish the proposition or condition being denied from the mechanism that reported false.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Showing a universal statement false requires one valid counterexample, while showing an observed field false only reports its encoded value.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers logical and programmatic uses made explicit by the surrounding statement.
public_glossary.example: The comparison 2 = 3 is false in ordinary integer arithmetic.
public_glossary.non_example: A missing value is not automatically the boolean value false.

public_glossary.label: falsifiable
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A claim is falsifiable when there is a specific observation or run that would show it is wrong.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A claim is falsifiable when there is a specific observation or run that would show it is wrong.
public_glossary.card_definition: It is a property of how a claim is stated, not of whether it is true. A claim nobody can test is not thereby safe; it is outside the reach of evidence.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask what result would refute the claim. If nothing would, the claim is not doing evidential work.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The stated position for this site is that the private frontend is not falsifiable by a reader and should not be trusted, while the public repositories are: the commands are given, the fixtures are included, and a disagreement between a claim and its record is visible.
public_glossary.scope_note: Ordinary usage from philosophy of science, applied here to software claims.
public_glossary.example: A component's claim is falsifiable because you can run its check and compare.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: Farey sequence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A Farey sequence lists, in increasing order, every fraction in lowest terms whose denominator is at most a chosen bound.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A Farey sequence lists, in increasing order, every fraction in lowest terms whose denominator is at most a chosen bound.
public_glossary.card_definition: Two neighbours in a Farey sequence cannot be arbitrarily close: their separation is fixed by their denominators. So if a target number is shown to lie strictly between two neighbours, it cannot equal any fraction whose denominator is inside the bound.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A Farey exclusion rules out denominators up to its bound and says nothing whatever about denominators above it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The Erdős #249 work uses a 240-bit Farey window to exclude every reduced denominator through 79,639,646,646,701,375,323,355,774,875,831,053, roughly 7.96 times ten to the thirty-fourth. The problem remains open because no argument covers the denominators beyond that bound.
public_glossary.scope_note: A Farey window is a finite exclusion. It never becomes an irrationality proof by being extended further.
public_glossary.example: The Farey sequence of order three is 0/1, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 1/1.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: field

public_glossary.short_definition: A field is one named slot in a structured record, holding a value with an expected meaning and format.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A field is one named slot in a structured record, holding a value with an expected meaning and format.
public_glossary.card_definition: Fields let producers and readers refer to facts precisely instead of relying on position or prose. A schema may require a field, restrict its type, or explain when it can be empty.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Interpret a field through the schema or contract that defines its name and allowed value.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A field's presence proves only that a value was recorded, not that the value is true or current.
public_glossary.scope_note: A field covers one named property within the record and schema that own it.
public_glossary.example: A result record may have fields for status, source revision, command, and timestamp.
public_glossary.non_example: A sentence that happens to mention a value is not automatically a structured field.

public_glossary.short_definition: A file is a named sequence of stored bytes addressed at a path and interpreted according to a format or program.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A file is a named sequence of stored bytes addressed at a path and interpreted according to a format or program.
public_glossary.card_definition: Files are containers: one may hold code, prose, structured data, an image, or generated output. Its extension and location help identify the format but do not guarantee content or authority.

public_glossary.non_example: A route or database record is not necessarily a filesystem file.

public_glossary.short_definition: A finding is a conclusion or observed condition produced by an investigation, audit, experiment, or analysis.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A finding is a conclusion or observed condition produced by an investigation, audit, experiment, or analysis.
public_glossary.card_definition: Findings connect a method and evidence to a stated result. They may be positive, negative, tentative, or limited, and should retain the conditions under which they were derived.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a finding with its source process, evidence, confidence, scope, and any unresolved alternative explanation.

public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers audit, research, diagnostic, and measurement results.
public_glossary.example: A vocabulary audit finding can report that a high-frequency word has no governed definition.
public_glossary.non_example: An unsupported suspicion is not yet a finding.

public_glossary.label: finite
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Finite means containing or requiring only a limited number of elements, steps, or operations.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Finite means containing or requiring only a limited number of elements, steps, or operations.
public_glossary.card_definition: A finite object can in principle be exhausted by counting or enumeration, even when it is too large to inspect practically. Finiteness is a structural property, not a claim of small size.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Do not confuse finite with computationally easy or already enumerated.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Many proofs separate finite verification from infinite generalization because checking every member is possible only after a finite bound is justified.
public_glossary.scope_note: Finite covers the collection, process, or bound named in the statement.
public_glossary.example: A computation checking all denominators up to a fixed bound is finite.
public_glossary.non_example: A billion-element set is still finite despite being too large for convenient manual inspection.

public_glossary.label: finite computation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A finite computation is a terminating calculation over a bounded set of inputs that produces an exact or explicitly approximate result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A finite computation is a terminating calculation over a bounded set of inputs that produces an exact or explicitly approximate result.
public_glossary.card_definition: Finite computations can settle individual cases, verify certificates, and discover patterns. They do not settle an infinite family unless a proof shows that the bounded cases exhaust every possibility.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the computed range and the theorem, if any, that connects it to the general claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Formal projects often turn large computations into compact certificates so the trusted checker verifies the result without trusting the generator's implementation.
public_glossary.scope_note: A finite computation covers its declared inputs, algorithm, numeric exactness, and execution record.
public_glossary.example: The corpus checks thousands of finite denominator-order cases while the universal irrationality problem remains open.
public_glossary.non_example: Computing many cases is not a proof that every remaining case behaves the same way.

public_glossary.label: fit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Fit is the degree to which something satisfies the needs, constraints, or shape of a particular purpose or context.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Fit is the degree to which something satisfies the needs, constraints, or shape of a particular purpose or context.
public_glossary.card_definition: Fit is relational: a method can be excellent yet unsuitable for a specific task, budget, audience, or evidence standard. The relevant requirements must therefore be named.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When the site says something fits, identify the purpose and constraints against which the fit was judged.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Fit does not imply universal superiority; it means the option aligns with one stated situation better than relevant alternatives.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers suitability of tools, routes, formats, evidence, and explanations for named uses.
public_glossary.example: A one-sentence definition fits a hover card better than a long technical essay.
public_glossary.non_example: A tool being powerful does not mean it fits every task.

public_glossary.label: fixture
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A fixture is the fixed input a check runs against: a small, committed file standing in for the real data, chosen so the same run produces the same result on any machine.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A fixture is the fixed input a check runs against: a small, committed file standing in for the real data, chosen so the same run produces the same result on any machine.
public_glossary.card_definition: Every component here ships with its inputs rather than reaching for live data. That is what makes a check repeatable on a stranger's laptop: the fixture is in the repository, so the run does not depend on the private system, a network call, or the state of anyone's machine. It also fixes what the check can establish. A component passing against a fixture has been shown to work on that input, which is a smaller claim than working on production data, and the scope limit says so.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a check passes, look at the fixture it ran against. The result holds for that input; it is not a statement about data the fixture does not contain.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Fixtures are why the public repository can be checked at all without the private system. They are deliberately synthetic: shipping real data would leak the substrate this system does not publish. The trade is explicit rather than hidden - a synthetic input buys reproducibility and costs realism, and the component's scope limit records which of the two you are being sold.
public_glossary.scope_note: Fixtures appear wherever a component states an input. A passing run against a fixture establishes the fixture case, never whole-system correctness.
public_glossary.example: A component that classifies evidence ships a fixture file of sample rows; running the check reads that file, writes a result record, and proves the classifier behaves as claimed on those rows.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: follow
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To follow is to come after, proceed along, result from, or act according to something already given.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To follow is to come after, proceed along, result from, or act according to something already given.
public_glossary.card_definition: The intended sense depends on context: a conclusion follows from premises, a reader follows a route, and a task follows a rule. Each describes a directed relationship rather than simple proximity.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify what leads and which relationship makes the later item count as following it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Sequence alone does not establish dependence; a later event follows in time but may not follow logically or causally.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers ordered navigation, rule compliance, and stated consequence.
public_glossary.example: A validation step follows the build step in the publication process.
public_glossary.non_example: Two adjacent paragraphs do not necessarily follow from one another logically.

public_glossary.label: forecasting
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Forecasting here means predicting a future value, such as a market series, and then measuring whether the prediction was better than an obvious alternative.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Forecasting here means predicting a future value, such as a market series, and then measuring whether the prediction was better than an obvious alternative.
public_glossary.card_definition: The measurement is the harder half. Any method looks good on the run that was chosen for it, so a forecast-skill claim has to survive tests built to catch that: comparing named methods, correcting for how many were tried, and resampling the series in a way that keeps its structure.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A forecast-skill claim covers the data it was tested on. It is not a claim about future markets.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The components in this area run Diebold-Mariano, Hansen's superior predictive ability test, and a stationary bootstrap over synthetic market fixtures. Synthetic means the statistical machinery is shown to run and refuse as specified, not that any live market was predicted.
public_glossary.scope_note: Nothing here is investment advice or a claim about tradeable performance.
public_glossary.example: Comparing a forecast against a benchmark and reporting whether the difference is larger than chance.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: formal
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Formal describes something expressed through explicit rules and symbols precise enough for rule-governed checking.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Formal describes something expressed through explicit rules and symbols precise enough for rule-governed checking.
public_glossary.card_definition: A formal statement removes selected ambiguities by giving its objects and allowed operations exact meaning. Formality can support machine checking, but it does not by itself guarantee that the formal statement captures the intended real-world question.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is called formal, identify the language, rules, and checker that give the description its precision.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Formality concerns how a claim is represented and checked; truth, relevance, and correspondence to the intended subject remain separate questions.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers rule-governed mathematical and software descriptions, not ceremonial or stylistic formality.
public_glossary.example: A Lean theorem declaration is formal because its meaning is fixed by Lean's language and kernel.
public_glossary.non_example: Carefully worded prose is not formal merely because it sounds rigorous.

public_glossary.label: formal mathematics
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Formal mathematics is mathematics written so a machine can check it: every definition and step expressed in a language a proof assistant verifies, rather than in the usual prose of a paper.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Formal mathematics is mathematics written so a machine can check it: every definition and step expressed in a language a proof assistant verifies, rather than in the usual prose of a paper.
public_glossary.card_definition: An ordinary paper is checked by referees reading it. Formal mathematics is checked by software, which is unforgiving about steps a human reader would grant. The translation is substantial work and often reveals that a published argument covers slightly less than it appeared to, which is the main reason to bother.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result is described as formal, look for the source. The formal statement is the claim; the prose is commentary.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The gap between a formal statement and its description is where overstatement survives machine checking untouched, which is why the wording is registered and checked separately.
public_glossary.scope_note: Formalisation establishes what was formalised. Nothing follows about the parts left in prose.
public_glossary.example: Two of the covered problems have full reasoning papers alongside the formal sources.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: formal proof
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A formal proof is a mathematical argument encoded in a precise language so a proof checker can verify every inference from the stated definitions, axioms, and hypotheses.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A formal proof is a mathematical argument encoded in a precise language so a proof checker can verify every inference from the stated definitions, axioms, and hypotheses.
public_glossary.card_definition: Formalization removes hidden appeals to intuition by requiring each step to type-check against explicit rules. It guarantees that the encoded statement follows inside the formal system, not that the statement was translated from informal mathematics exactly as intended.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the formal statement and hypotheses as carefully as the fact that its proof checker accepted it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Trust is concentrated in the definitions, formal statement, axioms, elaborator boundary, and small proof-checking kernel rather than spread across a long human argument.
public_glossary.scope_note: A formal proof establishes its exact formal statement under its declared axioms and hypotheses in the recorded toolchain.
public_glossary.example: A Lean theorem with no admitted steps is a formal proof of the proposition written in its declaration.
public_glossary.non_example: A detailed paper proof or successful numerical experiment is not automatically a formal proof.

public_glossary.label: fraction
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A fraction is a number written as one integer numerator divided by a nonzero integer denominator.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A fraction is a number written as one integer numerator divided by a nonzero integer denominator.
public_glossary.card_definition: The numerator is the top integer and the denominator is the bottom integer. A fraction is reduced when those integers share no common factor greater than one, making the denominator canonical up to sign.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When denominator properties matter, check that the fraction has first been reduced.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Exact fraction arithmetic preserves numerator and denominator structure that floating-point approximations discard, which is essential in irrationality and multiplicative-order arguments.
public_glossary.scope_note: Fraction covers the stated numerator-denominator representation, including whether it is reduced.
public_glossary.example: A finite reciprocal sum can be computed exactly as a reduced fraction `P/Q`.
public_glossary.non_example: A decimal approximation is not the exact fraction unless the equality is separately established.

public_glossary.label: frontend
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The frontend is the part of a system a person looks at and clicks: its screens, as opposed to the machinery underneath.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The frontend is the part of a system a person looks at and clicks: its screens, as opposed to the machinery underneath.
public_glossary.card_definition: The frontend here is not published. It appears in the recorded videos so a reader can see what the operator sees, while the components and their checks, which are the part that can be verified, are the part released. The split is stated rather than implied.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Video of a frontend shows that it exists and how it behaves. It is not a check anyone else can run.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Demonstration and evidence are different currencies. A recording is persuasive and unfalsifiable; a check is dull and repeatable.
public_glossary.scope_note: Recordings establish what was on screen when they were made.
public_glossary.example: Three videos show the frontend at three lengths; the repository checks provide the validation records.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: full
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Full describes material or coverage presented without the omissions made by a named shorter, filtered, or partial form.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Full describes material or coverage presented without the omissions made by a named shorter, filtered, or partial form.
public_glossary.card_definition: Full is always relative to a defined whole. A full card may include every card field while still being only one projection of a much larger source.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is called full, identify the collection or schema whose parts are claimed to be included.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Completeness at one layer does not imply completeness at every layer, so a full report can remain bounded by its inputs and measurement method.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers expanded views, complete field sets, and unfiltered outputs within a stated boundary.
public_glossary.example: A full glossary card shows definition, rule, scope, example, and non-example.
public_glossary.non_example: A page is not a full account of the system merely because it is long.

public_glossary.label: function
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A mathematical function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input in its domain.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A mathematical function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input in its domain.
public_glossary.card_definition: A function is specified by its domain, codomain, and assignment rule, not only by a formula. Different formulas can define the same function on a stated domain.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the domain and output type before applying or comparing functions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Functions can take numbers, sets, sequences, or other functions as inputs and can be studied through properties such as injectivity, monotonicity, continuity, or multiplicativity.
public_glossary.scope_note: A function covers the input domain, output codomain, and assignment rule declared in context.
public_glossary.example: Euler's totient function assigns to n the number of positive integers up to n that are coprime to n.
public_glossary.non_example: A relation that gives two different outputs for the same input is not a function unless the output itself is a set.

public_glossary.label: gate
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A gate is a rule-controlled checkpoint that permits or blocks a later action according to declared evidence or conditions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A gate is a rule-controlled checkpoint that permits or blocks a later action according to declared evidence or conditions.
public_glossary.card_definition: Gates turn requirements into enforceable boundaries: a release gate may require tests, source checks, and safety scans before publication. A gate should explain both its decision and repair route.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read which evidence the gate consumes and which action its result controls.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A passing gate licenses only the downstream action named by its contract, not a broader claim that the whole artifact is correct.
public_glossary.scope_note: A gate covers the input conditions and downstream permission declared by its rule.
public_glossary.example: A link-integrity gate can block publication when an internal anchor does not resolve.
public_glossary.non_example: A warning with no effect on any action is not a blocking gate.

public_glossary.label: generalise-up-propagate
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Generalise/up-propagate is the two-step move from a local lesson to its smallest honest durable owner; it does not promote every observation into doctrine or overwrite source authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: Generalise-up-propagate is the move of taking a lesson learned in one local piece of work and carrying it upward into a durable, system-wide rule, while stating exactly how far that lesson applies and where it does not.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Generalise-up-propagate is the move of taking a lesson learned in one local piece of work and carrying it upward into a durable, system-wide rule, while stating exactly how far that lesson applies and where it does not.
public_glossary.card_definition: When work on one part of the system reveals something worth keeping, generalise-up-propagation does two things at once: it preserves the original case as evidence, and it names the broader invariant that case revealed. The general rule it produces carries an applicability boundary and a not-when boundary, so a single instance is never written up as if it held everywhere. It also records which layer of the system owns the new rule, so the lesson lands in a definite home rather than floating loose.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When you meet a rule that arrived this way, check the boundary it states: it was promoted from one concrete case, and it holds only within the limits recorded alongside it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It answers three questions about a local finding: what invariant the case actually revealed, which layer of the system should own that invariant, and how broadly it can be stated without claiming more than the single case supports.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers how knowledge moves from specific work into shared doctrine across the system. A reader meets it in the doctrine and propagation rules, where local findings are turned into bounded, reusable invariants.
public_glossary.example: Axiom AX-8, provenance propagation and non-interference, is one such durable rule: a lesson about keeping a record of where a result came from, raised to a system-wide invariant with its own stated limits.

example_route.label: Provenance propagation and non-interference
example_route.gloss: open the doctrine rule this propagation produced

public_glossary.non_example: Generalise-up-propagation is not the same as simply saving or filing a note. It does not assume one case proves a universal truth: the broader rule is only valid with its applicability and not-when boundaries attached.

relationships.gloss: Adds portable invariant and boundary discipline.
Lattice transposition is the named form for cross-plane portable-invariant routing.
Schema-grade generalizations can become standards.
Procedure-grade generalizations can refine skills.

public_glossary.label: Git

public_glossary.short_definition: Git is the version-control system most software projects use to record every change to their files as a numbered commit.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Git is the version-control system most software projects use to record every change to their files as a numbered commit.
public_glossary.card_definition: Because every commit has an identifier derived from its contents, a claim can be pinned to an exact state of a repository rather than to whatever the project looks like today.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A commit identifier names one snapshot. A branch name does not, because the branch moves.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Several checks here run real Git commands against a sample repository rather than reading a description of what Git would have said. The receipts record how many calls were made.

public_glossary.example: The audit rerun was pinned to plectis at commit 9539695.

public_glossary.short_definition: GitHub is an online service for hosting Git repositories and presenting their code, history, issues, releases, and web-published artifacts.
public_glossary.reader_preview: GitHub is an online service for hosting Git repositories and presenting their code, history, issues, releases, and web-published artifacts.
public_glossary.card_definition: This site links GitHub repositories so readers can inspect the public source and its revision history. GitHub hosts the material but does not author, verify, or endorse its mathematical or software claims.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use GitHub to locate and inspect the repository, then rely on the repository's own evidence and licenses.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A GitHub URL can identify a moving branch, an exact commit, a file view, a release, or a hosted page, and those routes provide different levels of version precision.
