public_glossary.label: Lean
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Lean is a proof assistant: software that checks a mathematical proof step by step and refuses it if any step does not follow.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Lean is a proof assistant: software that checks a mathematical proof step by step and refuses it if any step does not follow.
public_glossary.card_definition: A proof written in Lean is checked by machine rather than by a reader's judgement. That removes a specific class of error, the plausible step that turns out not to hold, and it is why a Lean-checked result carries more weight than a written argument of the same length. It does not remove every error: Lean confirms the proof establishes the statement written in the source, and whether that statement is the interesting one is a human question.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For a Lean result, read the formal statement rather than the summary. Lean checked the statement, not the description of it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Machine checking moves the risk rather than deleting it. What remains is whether the formal statement means what the prose says it means, which is exactly the proof boundary.
public_glossary.scope_note: Lean establishes that a proof is valid for the statement as written.
public_glossary.example: The Erdos problem work here is written in Lean, so each theorem's range is exactly what the source states.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: Lean kernel
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The Lean kernel is the small fixed core of the Lean proof assistant that decides whether a completed proof is accepted.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The Lean kernel is the small fixed core of the Lean proof assistant that decides whether a completed proof is accepted.
public_glossary.card_definition: Everything else in Lean, including tactics, automation, and the Mathlib library, only produces a candidate proof. The kernel is what checks it, and it is deliberately small so that trusting Lean means trusting that one component.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Kernel acceptance means the written formal statement was proved. It does not mean the English sentence printed beside that statement says the same thing.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The alignment between a formal statement and its public wording is an authored judgement, checked separately. Beyond the kernel, this corpus also runs Comparator, an independent checker, over nineteen propositions declared apart from their proofs.
public_glossary.scope_note: Distinct from the Plectis kernel, which on this site means the command-line control layer agents read.
public_glossary.example: A proof the Lean kernel accepts is machine-checked; its accompanying prose is not.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: Lean's standard axioms
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice are the three axioms Lean assumes beyond its core logic: propositional extensionality, the soundness of quotient types, and the axiom of choice.
public_glossary.reader_preview: propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice are the three axioms Lean assumes beyond its core logic: propositional extensionality, the soundness of quotient types, and the axiom of choice.
public_glossary.card_definition: Essentially all of Mathlib rests on these three, so a proof that uses only them is standing on ordinary mathematical foundations rather than on anything the author added.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A count of added axioms means axioms beyond these three. A non-zero count means the proof assumed something extra, which has to be read and judged.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The corpus reports 0 added axioms and 1 admitted proof step, the latter in ExternalVerification/Challenge.lean. An admitted step is a different thing from an added axiom: it is a gap left open inside a proof rather than an assumption introduced for it.
public_glossary.scope_note: These are Lean's axioms, not axioms specific to this work.
public_glossary.example: Comparator reports that the checked proofs use no axioms beyond these three.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: least common multiple
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The least common multiple of a set of whole numbers is the smallest number all of them divide into exactly.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The least common multiple of a set of whole numbers is the smallest number all of them divide into exactly.
public_glossary.card_definition: It appears here as the quantity governing when a repeating pattern comes back into alignment. Several results turn on the least common multiple of a set of exponents, because that number determines the period at which the structure of a sum repeats.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Where a least common multiple appears, it is usually setting the period of something.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Least common multiples grow quickly, which is what makes the periods involved large enough to be hard to search directly.
public_glossary.scope_note: A result about a least common multiple covers the set it is taken over.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #269 concerns the running least common multiples of numbers built from a fixed set of primes.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: Lebesgue measure
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Lebesgue measure is the standard way of assigning a length to a set of numbers, extended to sets far more broken up than an interval.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Lebesgue measure is the standard way of assigning a length to a set of numbers, extended to sets far more broken up than an interval.
public_glossary.card_definition: Measure and topology disagree on what counts as small. A set can contain no interval at all and still have positive measure, and a dense set can have measure zero. The two answer different questions about the same set.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Measure says how much of the line a set fills. It does not say whether the set contains any particular number.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The set of subsums of the sum of one over two to the n minus one is compact, nowhere dense, and of Lebesgue measure exactly one, which is Lean-checked. Being nowhere dense and of positive measure at once is the substance of that statement. It leaves open whether one half is one of those subsums over an infinite support, which is a separate question about membership.
public_glossary.scope_note: A measure statement about a set is not a membership statement about a point in it.
public_glossary.example: The rational numbers are dense in the line and have Lebesgue measure zero.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: lemma
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A lemma is a proved supporting statement introduced mainly for use in proving a later theorem or organizing an argument.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A lemma is a proved supporting statement introduced mainly for use in proving a later theorem or organizing an argument.
public_glossary.card_definition: Lemma describes the statement's role, not its difficulty or truth status. In a formal library a lemma is checked in exactly the same way as a theorem and may be mathematically substantial.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a lemma's exact statement and dependencies rather than assuming it is minor because of the label.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Breaking a proof into lemmas exposes reusable structure, gives the proof checker smaller obligations, and makes later results' dependency chains inspectable.
public_glossary.scope_note: A lemma establishes its own stated proposition under its declared hypotheses.
public_glossary.example: A denominator lemma may prove the exact reduced form needed by the main irrationality argument.
public_glossary.non_example: A useful observation is not a lemma until it has a stated proposition and proof.

public_glossary.label: lemniscate
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A polynomial lemniscate is the set of points in the plane where a polynomial has one fixed size, so it is a level curve of the polynomial's absolute value.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A polynomial lemniscate is the set of points in the plane where a polynomial has one fixed size, so it is a level curve of the polynomial's absolute value.
public_glossary.card_definition: For a small threshold the curve is a set of separate loops around the roots; as the threshold grows the loops merge. Where and how they merge is what Erdős #1041 asks about.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A lemniscate is fixed by the polynomial and the chosen level, so a statement about one level is not a statement about the family.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Erdős #1041 asks about short connections inside polynomial lemniscates. The Lean work formalises a no-connection criterion, the exact translation ray-collision locus, finite-line avoidance, and a root-retention bound. The global topology and length gluing remain open.
public_glossary.scope_note: Polynomial lemniscate in the complex plane, not only the classical figure-of-eight curve.
public_glossary.example: The set where the absolute value of z squared minus one equals one half.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: library
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A software library is a reusable collection of code and interfaces intended to be called by other programs or modules.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A software library is a reusable collection of code and interfaces intended to be called by other programs or modules.
public_glossary.card_definition: Libraries supply shared functionality so each project does not reimplement it. Using a library introduces a dependency on its version, behavior, license, and compatibility.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Record the exact library version and interface assumptions when a result depends on it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A library can be source code, a compiled package, or a formal collection of definitions and theorems, but in each case consumers rely on a maintained external contract.
public_glossary.scope_note: A library covers the APIs, definitions, and version exposed by its named package.
public_glossary.example: Mathlib is the Lean library supplying many standard mathematical definitions and theorems.
public_glossary.non_example: A directory of unrelated helper files is not automatically a coherent library.

public_glossary.label: license
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A license is a permission granted under stated terms to use, copy, modify, distribute, or otherwise act on protected material.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A license is a permission granted under stated terms to use, copy, modify, distribute, or otherwise act on protected material.
public_glossary.card_definition: A license defines allowed uses and conditions but does not transfer every right or guarantee the material's quality. Different files or dependencies can have different licenses.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Before reusing material, check the applicable license, its scope, attribution duties, and compatibility with the intended use.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Public availability is not the same as permission to reuse; access and licensing are separate questions.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers software and content permissions explicitly attached to the relevant material.
public_glossary.example: An open-source license may permit redistribution provided its conditions are followed.
public_glossary.non_example: A publicly visible page is not automatically free of copyright restrictions.

public_glossary.label: limit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A limit is a boundary or restriction; in Plectis, the surrounding phrase distinguishes a scope limit, mathematical limit, or service rate limit.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A limit is a boundary or restriction; in Plectis, the surrounding phrase distinguishes a scope limit, mathematical limit, or service rate limit.
public_glossary.card_definition: Unqualified limit is a routing word, not one local technical object. In evidence pages it marks where a claim stops; in mathematics it is a value approached by a sequence or function; in runtime prose a rate limit caps requests over time. Plectis uses scope limit and mathematical limit when precision matters.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the noun phrase around limit before following the definition; never transfer conclusions between scope, analytic, and rate limits.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The senses share the ordinary idea of a boundary but have different authorities and checks: scope contracts govern claims, proofs govern mathematical limits, and provider or service policies govern rate limits.
public_glossary.scope_note: This row disambiguates the ordinary word; qualified term rows own the precise Plectis and mathematical senses.
public_glossary.example: A scope limit bounds a claim, a mathematical limit describes convergence, and a rate limit bounds request volume.
public_glossary.non_example: A provider rate limit is not an evidence boundary and not the limit of a sequence.

public_glossary.label: line
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, map means a generated view derived from the material it describes, with coverage and freshness receipts. It is narrower than the ordinary visual or geographic senses.
public_glossary.short_definition: A line is a sequence of text or source characters separated from neighbouring sequences by a line boundary or displayed as one row.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A line is a sequence of text or source characters separated from neighbouring sequences by a line boundary or displayed as one row.
public_glossary.card_definition: Lines support editing, diagnostics, and citation, but visual wrapping can make one stored line appear as several displayed lines. Meaning often spans several lines.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use line references with a specific file or document version so the location remains interpretable.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Line position is a convenient locator, not a stable identity when earlier edits can shift later lines.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers stored source lines, displayed text lines, and line-based diagnostic locations.
public_glossary.example: A parser error may identify line 42 of a JSON file.
public_glossary.non_example: A sentence is not necessarily one line because it can wrap or span line breaks.

public_glossary.label: lineage
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: This is the standard mathematical sense used when Plectis discusses convergence. Evidence or process boundaries use scope limit instead.
public_glossary.short_definition: Lineage is the recorded chain of origins and transformations through which an artifact or claim came to exist.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Lineage is the recorded chain of origins and transformations through which an artifact or claim came to exist.
public_glossary.card_definition: Lineage connects a current result to its source material, intermediate versions, builders, and prior names. It lets a reader distinguish inherited material from newly authored or transformed material.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Follow lineage when you need to know where something came from and which transformations may have changed it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Lineage establishes ancestry, not correctness; a faithfully traced claim can still be wrong at its source.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers documented origin and transformation paths for files, concepts, results, and public pages.
public_glossary.example: A generated glossary entry has lineage back to its registry row and the site builder.
public_glossary.non_example: A timestamp alone is not lineage because it does not identify origins or transformations.

public_glossary.label: link
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A link is an actionable reference that takes a reader from the current surface to another page, file, anchor, or external resource.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A link is an actionable reference that takes a reader from the current surface to another page, file, anchor, or external resource.
public_glossary.card_definition: A link supplies a route, while its text and relationship explain why the destination matters. It does not by itself establish support, equivalence, or authority.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the destination and relationship before treating a link as evidence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Internal links are validated against generated routes and anchors; external links also depend on the continued availability and meaning of another site.
public_glossary.scope_note: A link covers the declared source, destination, and relationship at the time it was generated.
public_glossary.example: A glossary term link opens the matching definition card.
public_glossary.non_example: Two nearby paragraphs are not linked merely because they discuss similar subjects.

public_glossary.label: list
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A list is an ordered or unordered collection of separate items presented under a shared purpose or rule.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A list is an ordered or unordered collection of separate items presented under a shared purpose or rule.
public_glossary.card_definition: Lists support enumeration and scanning but may omit relationships beyond membership and order. Completeness depends on the list's stated source and inclusion boundary.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a list by identifying what qualifies as an item, whether order matters, and whether the list claims completeness.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A list can be a projection over richer records, so each item may have deeper fields not visible in the compact display.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers navigation, evidence, term, file, result, and membership collections.
public_glossary.example: The glossary index lists each preferred term label alphabetically.
public_glossary.non_example: Several examples are not a complete list unless the page says they exhaust the category.

public_glossary.label: live
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Live describes a currently operating or directly accessible state rather than a static copy, simulation, or historical snapshot.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Live describes a currently operating or directly accessible state rather than a static copy, simulation, or historical snapshot.
public_glossary.card_definition: Live material can change while it is being observed, and actions against it may affect the real system. That makes freshness, authority, and mutation safety more important than for a detached copy.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat live access as current but mutable, and verify what actions the interface is authorized to perform.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A live reading is temporally closer to current truth, but it can still be partial, inconsistent during change, or misinterpreted.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers active repository state, running services, and current operational records.
public_glossary.example: A tool querying the current work ledger reads live coordination state.
public_glossary.non_example: A saved report from yesterday is a snapshot, not live state.

public_glossary.label: living system posture
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Living-system posture means maintaining the repository as an evolving, interdependent substrate whose feedback updates its records and routes; it does not claim biological life, autonomy, or production readiness.
public_glossary.short_definition: Living system posture is the stance that every page, result, doctrine row, raw quote, or runtime claim is dated evidence from one system state rather than a timeless fact, so present truth must be checked against the live source and its freshness.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Living system posture is the stance that every page, result, doctrine row, raw quote, or runtime claim is dated evidence from one system state rather than a timeless fact, so present truth must be checked against the live source and its freshness.
public_glossary.card_definition: The system changes continuously, so a claim that held when it was written can later be out of date while the record of it stays on file. Living system posture keeps both halves separate: the past claim is preserved as a record of what was true then, and current authority comes from the live files and the surface that tracks how fresh each thing is. Reading something under this posture means asking what was true when it was written, what is true now, what changed, and which check proves it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat any record on this site as carrying a date and a state of the system, not as a permanent truth: it tells you what held when it was made, and a current claim is confirmed against the live source and its freshness check.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Different layers go stale in different ways: a generated summary can lag its source, a recorded result can describe wiring that has since moved, and an early piece of doctrine can predate the rule that now governs it. The posture makes the gap between then and now something you can locate and check rather than something hidden.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers how every dated artifact on the site should be read, from recorded results and generated pages to doctrine and raw quotes. A reader meets it wherever a record states what a pass found or what the system once contained, and the live question is whether that record still describes the system today.
public_glossary.example: The evidence page, "What the pass proves", is a concrete instance: it sets out what a given pass actually checked and found at the time it ran, which is the kind of dated record that living system posture asks you to read as evidence from that moment rather than as a standing guarantee.

example_route.label: What the pass proves (evidence)
example_route.gloss: see a dated record of what a pass actually checked and found

public_glossary.non_example: Living system posture is not a claim that the system is unstable or that nothing on the site can be trusted, and it does not mean old records are discarded. It is the practice of reading each record as tied to a time and confirming current claims against the live source.

relationships.gloss: The local case becomes a portable currentness boundary.
Moves stale-claim lessons into the plane that owns currentness checks.
Derived surfaces stay useful only when refreshed and validated.
Worker jobs must carry current source fingerprints and receipts.
Standards and companions must reflect current file-type shape.
Cold agents need currentness posture before trusting old routes or receipts.

source_refs.gloss: Owning skill for preserving local case, portable invariant, and boundary before plane-home routing.

public_glossary.label: llms.txt
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: llms.txt is a plain-text file at the root of a site that tells an AI assistant where the site's readable content is.
public_glossary.reader_preview: llms.txt is a plain-text file at the root of a site that tells an AI assistant where the site's readable content is.
public_glossary.card_definition: It is the counterpart of robots.txt for assistants: rather than restricting crawling, it points at the files worth reading and says what each one is for.
public_glossary.reader_rule: It is a routing file. It carries no claim that an assistant reading it has run anything.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It is offered here alongside the AI packet and the reviewer brief as a direct route for readers whose buttons fail or who have JavaScript off.
public_glossary.scope_note: An emerging convention rather than a ratified standard.
public_glossary.example: An assistant can be pointed at llms.txt to find the public files.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: load
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To load something is to bring data, code, configuration, or a resource into a program or environment so it can be used.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To load something is to bring data, code, configuration, or a resource into a program or environment so it can be used.
public_glossary.card_definition: Loading may read from disk, network, memory, or a package system and can fail because the source is absent, invalid, unauthorized, or incompatible. Loaded state may persist only for the current run.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When material is loaded, identify its source, version, validation, and lifetime in the receiving environment.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Loading provides availability to a consumer but does not change the source's authority or guarantee safe interpretation.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers reading files, importing modules, retrieving resources, and initializing runtime state.
public_glossary.example: The public-site builder loads the term registry before constructing glossary rows.
public_glossary.non_example: A file existing on disk is not loaded into a running program until the program reads it.

public_glossary.label: local
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Local describes something situated within the current machine, repository, scope, or immediate context rather than a broader or remote one.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Local describes something situated within the current machine, repository, scope, or immediate context rather than a broader or remote one.
public_glossary.card_definition: The relevant boundary must be named: local to a function differs from local to a repository or computer. Local access is often direct, but it does not automatically grant authority over the material.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When local is used, identify the containing boundary and whether outside dependencies still influence the result.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A local result can be correct within its boundary while failing to generalize or match deployed conditions.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers machine, repository, file, process, and proof-context locality.
public_glossary.example: A browser preview served from the developer's machine is a local site preview.
public_glossary.non_example: A cloud service reached from the local machine is not itself local.

public_glossary.label: locus
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A locus is a specific place where a feature, rule, effect, or piece of evidence resides or becomes observable.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A locus is a specific place where a feature, rule, effect, or piece of evidence resides or becomes observable.
public_glossary.card_definition: In software and documentation, a locus may be a file, function, field, route, or generated section. Naming it makes responsibility and inspection more precise than referring to the whole repository.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a locus to point to the smallest stable place that owns or demonstrates the relevant behaviour.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An effect can have several loci, such as one source definition, one builder transformation, and one public projection.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers identifiable source, runtime, evidence, and display locations.
public_glossary.example: The first-use underline rule has its styling locus in the public site's stylesheet.
public_glossary.non_example: Naming the repository root is not a useful locus for a rule owned by one function.

public_glossary.label: machine-checked
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Machine-checked means a result has been verified by software rather than accepted on a reader's judgement.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Machine-checked means a result has been verified by software rather than accepted on a reader's judgement.
public_glossary.card_definition: It is the strongest evidence class on this site, and also the narrowest. A machine-checked theorem is settled for exactly the statement checked, which is often a smaller claim than the surrounding description suggests. Reading the statement rather than the headline is the whole discipline.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Machine-checked applies to the formal statement. Check what that statement actually says.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The label is worth distrusting when it appears near prose rather than near a source reference, because that is where the range quietly widens.
public_glossary.scope_note: Machine checking establishes the checked statement only.
public_glossary.example: A theorem proved for all bases at least two is machine-checked for that range, and for nothing wider.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: machine-readable
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Machine-readable means structured so a program can use it directly, rather than written as prose a program would have to interpret.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Machine-readable means structured so a program can use it directly, rather than written as prose a program would have to interpret.
public_glossary.card_definition: A page of prose describing a proof corpus can be read by a person and only guessed at by a program. The same content as structured data can be queried: which results depend on this one, which are still conditional, what has already been ruled out. That is the difference between a corpus you must read to use and one you can ask.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Machine-readable is about form, not truth. Structured data can be structured and wrong.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Publishing the structure rather than only the prose is what lets someone else's tool check a claim without reimplementing the reading.
public_glossary.scope_note: Machine-readable form establishes nothing by itself; the content still has to be right.
public_glossary.example: The claim registry and the semantic corpus are machine-readable; the papers describing them are not.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: manifest
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A manifest is a structured inventory that lists the artifacts in a release or build together with the metadata needed to identify and check them.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A manifest is a structured inventory that lists the artifacts in a release or build together with the metadata needed to identify and check them.
public_glossary.card_definition: A manifest answers what was included and often records paths, hashes, roles, sizes, or source revisions. It is an inventory, not the content or proof of correctness of every listed item.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the manifest to establish membership and identity, then inspect the listed artifact for substance.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Manifests make omissions and unexpected additions mechanically detectable because the declared collection can be compared with disk or build output.
public_glossary.scope_note: A manifest covers the artifacts and metadata included in its declared build or release.
public_glossary.example: The site content manifest lists every generated public file and its source-bound metadata.
public_glossary.non_example: A directory listing without governed roles or identity metadata is not necessarily a release manifest.

public_glossary.label: map
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A map here is a generated view over a body of material, built from that material rather than written alongside it, showing what is in it and how the parts connect.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A map here is a generated view over a body of material, built from that material rather than written alongside it, showing what is in it and how the parts connect.
public_glossary.card_definition: Several things on this site are called maps: the architecture map over the components, the semantic map over the proof corpus, the site map for machine readers. They share a form rather than a subject. Each is regenerated from what it describes, so it cannot quietly disagree with it, and each is meant to be entered at any point rather than read from the start.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A map is regenerated from its subject. If it disagrees with the subject, the map is stale.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The distinction from documentation is that documentation is written and maps are derived. Written documentation ages silently; a derived map either regenerates or shows as stale, which is why the maps carry the coverage and orphan counts that let you check them.
public_glossary.scope_note: A map covers what it was generated over, as of its last build.
public_glossary.example: The semantic map over the Lean corpus indexes every declaration and records how the statements relate.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: match
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A match is a correspondence that satisfies stated comparison criteria.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A match is a correspondence that satisfies stated comparison criteria.
public_glossary.card_definition: Matching may compare text, identifiers, structures, values, or expected outcomes. The result is only as meaningful as the criteria and tolerance used to decide correspondence.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When two things match, check which features were compared and whether exact or approximate agreement was required.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Objects can match on one property while differing on others, so a match does not imply identity unless the criteria require complete equality.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers explicit comparisons made by search, validation, routing, and tests.
public_glossary.example: An identifier matches a registry row when their normalized values are equal.
public_glossary.non_example: Two pages sharing a colour do not thereby match in content.

public_glossary.label: mathematical limit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A mathematical limit is the value a sequence or function gets arbitrarily close to as its index or input approaches a stated point or infinity.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A mathematical limit is the value a sequence or function gets arbitrarily close to as its index or input approaches a stated point or infinity.
public_glossary.card_definition: In the Plectis mathematics, limits turn infinite processes into exact statements. Saying a_n tends to L means that every requested tolerance is eventually met; it does not require any term to equal L, and it is separate from calling a claim boundary a limit.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the varying object, target value, direction of approach, and quantified notion of closeness.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For the infinite series discussed in the papers, convergence establishes that partial sums have a limit, while irrationality asks what kind of number that limit is. A long numerical prefix can suggest the value but cannot replace the quantified proof.
public_glossary.scope_note: This row covers analytic limits of sequences, functions, and series; scope limit covers evidence or process boundaries.
public_glossary.example: For a convergent reciprocal series, its sum is the mathematical limit of its partial sums even though no finite partial sum contains the whole series.
public_glossary.non_example: A scope limit is a claim boundary, not a mathematical limit.

public_glossary.label: mathematics
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Mathematics is the study of abstract structures, quantities, patterns, and logical relationships through definitions, conjectures, proofs, and computation.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Mathematics is the study of abstract structures, quantities, patterns, and logical relationships through definitions, conjectures, proofs, and computation.
public_glossary.card_definition: This site focuses on number-theoretic problems and distinguishes informal exposition, computational evidence, and machine-checked formal proof. Those are complementary ways of doing and communicating mathematics.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Match each mathematical claim to the kind of argument or evidence that supports it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Mathematical certainty applies to conclusions proved from explicit assumptions within a formal or accepted logical framework, not automatically to interpretations, significance, or empirical claims.
public_glossary.scope_note: Mathematics here covers the published problems, definitions, proofs, computations, and explanatory papers.
public_glossary.example: The Erdős papers study questions about integers, sequences, series, and arithmetic functions.
public_glossary.non_example: A numerical pattern observed in examples is not by itself a mathematical proof.

public_glossary.label: Mathlib
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: This registry only explains how the external term appears here. The external owner, specification, or primary source controls when exact meaning matters.
public_glossary.short_definition: Mathlib is the community-maintained mathematical library for Lean, providing reusable definitions, theorems, tactics, and notation.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Mathlib is the community-maintained mathematical library for Lean, providing reusable definitions, theorems, tactics, and notation.
public_glossary.card_definition: The formal mathematics in this project can depend on Mathlib instead of rebuilding standard foundations. Exact proof reproduction therefore pins a compatible Lean and Mathlib revision.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat imported Mathlib theorems as checked dependencies and record the revision used by the build.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Mathlib's breadth makes formalization faster, but an imported result still has an exact statement whose hypotheses and types must match the local proof.
public_glossary.scope_note: Mathlib covers the library revision and modules imported by the named Lean project.
public_glossary.example: A proof may import Mathlib's number-theory definitions before stating a project-specific theorem.
public_glossary.non_example: Mathlib is not a collection of informal papers and does not make every mathematical claim on this site machine-checked.

public_glossary.label: mean
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To mean something is to signify, express, entail, or be interpreted as that thing within a language or context.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To mean something is to signify, express, entail, or be interpreted as that thing within a language or context.
public_glossary.card_definition: Meaning connects a sign, statement, or action with what a reader should understand from it. The same form can mean different things under different definitions or contexts; arithmetic mean is a separate mathematical use.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Resolve what something means from its governing definition and context rather than from appearance alone.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Meaning may be conventional, formally specified, or inferred from use, and those sources can disagree unless the system names which one governs.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers semantic interpretation of words, symbols, statuses, and actions.
public_glossary.example: In this registry, public means available to the stated outside audience under stated access conditions.
public_glossary.non_example: Two words looking similar does not prove that they mean the same thing.

public_glossary.label: measurement
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A measurement is a value obtained by applying a defined procedure or instrument to an observed object or process.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A measurement is a value obtained by applying a defined procedure or instrument to an observed object or process.
public_glossary.card_definition: Measurements need units, method, conditions, uncertainty, and provenance to be interpreted. Repeating a measurement can test stability without proving a universal law.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read what was measured, how, when, with which units, and under which conditions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Computed metrics and physical measurements share a result shape but differ in error sources: one depends on code and input data, the other also depends on instruments and observation conditions.
public_glossary.scope_note: A measurement covers the object, method, units, environment, and observation time recorded with it.
public_glossary.example: A benchmark can measure how long one command takes on a stated machine.
public_glossary.non_example: An estimate copied from prose without a producing method is not an inspectable measurement.

public_glossary.label: mechanism
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Mechanism means a governed doctrine or implementation operator backed by local sources. It is not automatically a proven causal mechanism in the scientific sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: A mechanism is an account of how something in the system happens: how an object moves, transforms, routes, validates, or changes state, stated as the actual flow of inputs, steps, and outputs rather than as a label.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A mechanism is an account of how something in the system happens: how an object moves, transforms, routes, validates, or changes state, stated as the actual flow of inputs, steps, and outputs rather than as a label.
public_glossary.card_definition: A mechanism names the working path behind a piece of doctrine or behaviour: what goes in, what is done to it, what comes out, what authority governs it, and how it can fail. It ties an idea to running code, a standard, or a runtime surface, so a claim about how the system behaves can be traced to the steps that actually carry it out.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a mechanism is described, follow it down to the inputs, steps, and outputs it names, and check that those steps are grounded in real code or standards rather than asserted in the abstract.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A mechanism is meant to bind meaning to flow: inputs, transformations, outputs, authority, validation, failure modes, and the relationships between the parts. A description that names a behaviour without those moving parts is a slogan, not a mechanism.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the "how it works" layer that connects concepts, principles, skills, standards, and code. A reader meets it across the doctrine pages, where each rule is expected to be backed by an explanation of the process that carries it out.
public_glossary.example: The Executable Doctrine Grammar component is a mechanism: it is the surface that requires a piece of doctrine to be run as actual steps before it is treated as authoritative, so the rule is bound to a working process rather than to wording alone.

example_route.label: Executable Doctrine Grammar
example_route.gloss: open the component that turns a rule into runnable steps

public_glossary.non_example: A mechanism is not a slogan or a name for a behaviour on its own. Calling something a routing or validation step does not make it a mechanism until the inputs, steps, outputs, and failure modes are spelled out and grounded in real code or standards.

relationships.gloss: Mechanisms are doctrine nodes.
Mechanisms describe movement around concepts.

source_refs.gloss: Mechanism schema standard.
Concept/mechanism curation workflow.

public_glossary.label: menu
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A menu is a presented set of choices from which a reader or operator can select an action or destination.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A menu is a presented set of choices from which a reader or operator can select an action or destination.
public_glossary.card_definition: Menus compress an available option space into labels and groupings. Their quality depends on whether the choices are understandable, reachable, and appropriate to the current context.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a menu as a choice surface and verify that its labels lead to the destinations or actions they promise.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A menu can hide options through grouping or filtering, so it should not be assumed to enumerate every possible action unless declared complete.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers web navigation menus and structured operational choice surfaces.
public_glossary.example: The documentation menu lets a reader choose the glossary or architecture area.
public_glossary.non_example: A decorative list with no selectable choices is not a functional menu.

public_glossary.label: Mersenne number
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A Mersenne number is one less than a power of two: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, and so on.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A Mersenne number is one less than a power of two: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, and so on.
public_glossary.card_definition: Erdős #257 asks about sums of reciprocals of these numbers, taken over a chosen set of exponents. At a general whole-number base b the same construction uses b to the n minus one instead.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Base two is the critical case for these questions, not a representative one, so a result at base two does not automatically extend to other bases.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The reduced denominator of a finite subsum over Mersenne numbers has multiplicative order exactly the least common multiple of the support, which is Lean-checked. That is a statement about finite supports and does not settle the infinite case.
public_glossary.scope_note: Mersenne number here means two to the n minus one for any n, not only the prime ones.
public_glossary.example: 31 equals two to the fifth minus one.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: metabolism
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Metabolism is a local metaphor for governed substrate upkeep and repeated state transitions. It is not biological metabolism and makes no biological claim.
public_glossary.short_definition: Metabolism is the governed upkeep loop that refreshes derived artifacts from their authoritative sources and records the checks.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Metabolism is the governed upkeep loop that refreshes derived artifacts from their authoritative sources and records the checks.
public_glossary.card_definition: Where ordinary navigation reads what is already there, metabolism is the layer that produces and refreshes it. It watches the authoritative source material, queues bounded pieces of work, populates or rebuilds derived surfaces such as generated summaries and indexes, checks the results, and records what it did. It is durable upkeep, not a one-off answer: enforcing standards, refreshing generated views, and repairing scaffolding all run here. It is bounded by design and halts at the point where a human or a higher authority must decide.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something on this site is described as metabolized, take it as a surface that the upkeep loop generated and last refreshed, not source material edited by hand.
public_glossary.deep_definition: There are two kinds: deterministic metabolism handles fixed, well-defined refresh once the rules exist, while the judgement-bearing kind handles unsettled cases such as naming a new concept or resolving a contradiction before any automatic refresh can take over.
public_glossary.scope_note: Metabolism covers the maintenance and refresh machinery beneath the system, spanning the lane that turns raw operator notes into structured records, the always-on runtime, and the periodic rebuilds of generated pages. A reader meets it whenever a page notes that a surface is generated, populated, or kept in sync rather than authored directly.
public_glossary.example: The Engine Room Metabolism Runtime is a concrete instance: the working machinery that runs these upkeep loops over the underlying material and keeps derived surfaces current.

example_route.label: Engine Room Metabolism Runtime
example_route.gloss: open the runtime that runs the upkeep loops

public_glossary.non_example: Metabolism is not a biological metaphor and not a vague word for activity in general. It is the specific, bounded machinery that refreshes derived surfaces and records what it changed.

relationships.gloss: Unsettled grammar and authority decisions are Type A metabolism.
Bounded population and checking are Type B metabolism.
Metabolism keeps projections fresh so navigation can read instead of recompute.
Metabolic population should follow the governing standard or profile.
Raw-seed metabolism turns voice substrate into distill, route, and apply work.
Metabolism needs routing to decide which queued work should move next.
Kernel and docs-route expose metabolism status and authority packets.
A metabolism route gap is evidence for upward vocabulary or route refinement.

source_refs.gloss: Resident metabolismd runtime and queue substrate.
Theory roof for row metabolism, navigation boundaries, and provider row jobs.
Daemon and CLI surface for runtime metabolism.
Always-on metabolism governance code.

public_glossary.label: metadata-only
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Metadata-only means a record carries declared shape, counts, digests, and verdicts without the input bodies; it is not a universal guarantee that no sensitive information exists or permission to publish.
public_glossary.short_definition: Metadata-only describes a record that carries the shape and verdict of a run but none of the content it read: counts, classes, digests and outcomes, without the bodies behind them.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Metadata-only describes a record that carries the shape and verdict of a run but none of the content it read: counts, classes, digests and outcomes, without the bodies behind them.
public_glossary.card_definition: This is what lets a run over private inputs still produce something publishable. The record says how many rows were classified and how, or that a body matched its declared digest, without reproducing the row or the body. It is a deliberate reduction, and it is checkable in its own right: the build refuses a record that has let content leak into a field meant to hold only shape.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a metadata-only record as evidence about a run, never as the data the run saw.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The guarantee is enforced rather than promised. Result-record fields are checked for body leakage on every build, and a record carrying content where it should carry shape raises a specific failure code instead of passing quietly.
public_glossary.scope_note: A metadata-only record establishes only the declared shape and outcome of its run. It neither exposes the underlying content nor proves that every possible private field was excluded unless the named leakage and public-safety checks also passed.
public_glossary.example: A classifier run over non-public rows writes counts and class labels; the rows themselves never enter the record.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: method
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A method is an ordered way of carrying out an analysis, computation, proof, or construction.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A method is an ordered way of carrying out an analysis, computation, proof, or construction.
public_glossary.card_definition: A method explains how a result was reached so another reader can inspect or repeat it. The method can be valid even when a particular implementation or input is flawed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate the method from the evidence that one execution of it succeeded.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Methods range from informal reasoning strategies to exact algorithms; their reproducibility depends on how fully their inputs, steps, and assumptions are stated.
public_glossary.scope_note: A method covers the stated inputs, steps, assumptions, and intended output.
public_glossary.example: Clearing denominators is a method for turning a rational equality into an integer statement.
public_glossary.non_example: A result with no account of how it was obtained does not document a method.

public_glossary.label: missing
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Missing describes something required, expected, or referenced that is not present or cannot be found in the relevant place.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Missing describes something required, expected, or referenced that is not present or cannot be found in the relevant place.
public_glossary.card_definition: Missingness depends on an expectation and a search boundary. A value can be absent by design, unavailable because of access, or lost through a defect, and those cases need different responses.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is reported missing, check what should exist, where the search looked, and whether absence was permitted.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Failure to observe an item is evidence of absence only when the observation method and coverage are strong enough.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers absent files, fields, links, evidence, definitions, and results within stated collections.
public_glossary.example: A glossary audit reports a requested term as missing when no registry row has its identifier.
public_glossary.non_example: A private file is not missing merely because a public reader cannot access it.

public_glossary.label: model
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A model is a deliberately simplified representation or computational system used to describe, predict, classify, or generate outcomes about something else.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A model is a deliberately simplified representation or computational system used to describe, predict, classify, or generate outcomes about something else.
public_glossary.card_definition: On this site, “model” may mean an AI model, a mathematical representation, or a structured data model; the nearby qualifier determines which. Every model omits detail and has a domain where its outputs are meaningful.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify what the model represents, how it was produced, and where its assumptions stop.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Model outputs are observations about the model's behavior, not direct facts about the represented world unless validation connects the two.
public_glossary.scope_note: A model covers the entities, assumptions, inputs, and output interpretation declared for that model.
public_glossary.example: An AI model can propose code, while a validator independently checks the resulting artifact.
public_glossary.non_example: A model is not the represented system itself and is not automatically an authority on it.

public_glossary.label: module
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A module is a bounded unit of code or exposition grouped around one responsibility and designed to be referenced as a whole.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A module is a bounded unit of code or exposition grouped around one responsibility and designed to be referenced as a whole.
public_glossary.card_definition: In software, a module collects related definitions or behavior; in this site's paper-module layer, it collects a subsystem's readable explanation. The surrounding label tells which meaning applies.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the module kind before assuming that it is executable code or a paper module.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Modularity creates boundaries for ownership, testing, reuse, and navigation, but those boundaries are organizational rather than proof that the unit is independent.
public_glossary.scope_note: A module covers the material assigned to its named unit and declared responsibility.
public_glossary.example: A Lean module may contain related theorem declarations, while a paper module explains one system area.
public_glossary.non_example: Every file is not automatically a coherent module.

public_glossary.label: Morse saddle
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A saddle is a point where a surface rises in one direction and falls in another, like the middle of a mountain pass. It is a Morse saddle when the curvature there is non-degenerate, so the local picture is the standard one and the saddle is isolated.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A saddle is a point where a surface rises in one direction and falls in another, like the middle of a mountain pass.
public_glossary.card_definition: Non-degeneracy is what pins the number of directions leaving the point. An argument that assumes the wrong number of local branches at a saddle can be locally invalid while looking right globally.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Morse is a hypothesis about curvature at the point, not a description of the whole surface.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The Erdős #1041 note reports that a recent manuscript's load-bearing Proposition 12 uses an invalid three-ended local block at an interior Morse saddle. This was diagnosed here independently and matches Tao's public account of the same defect. The proposition is not refuted and may admit a repair.
public_glossary.scope_note: Applies to a critical point of a smooth real function, in the sense of Morse theory.
public_glossary.example: The origin is a Morse saddle for x squared minus y squared.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: move
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A move is one deliberate change of position, state, ownership, or strategy.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A move is one deliberate change of position, state, ownership, or strategy.
public_glossary.card_definition: The word can name a file relocation, an operational action, or a reasoning step. In each case it should identify what changes, from where, to where, and under whose authority.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a proposed move by checking its target, direction, consequences, and reversibility.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A move can preserve content while changing its location or role, but references and ownership may still need updating.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers bounded transitions in files, plans, arguments, and workflows.
public_glossary.example: Moving a definition from handwritten HTML into the governed registry changes its authority location.
public_glossary.non_example: Describing a desired destination without changing anything is not the move itself.

public_glossary.label: multiple
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis uses both ordinary senses of multiple: several items, and the mathematical divisibility relation. The surrounding grammar determines which one applies.
public_glossary.short_definition: Multiple can mean more than one item, or in arithmetic a number obtained by multiplying another number by an integer; Plectis uses both senses.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Multiple can mean more than one item, or in arithmetic a number obtained by multiplying another number by an integer; Plectis uses both senses.
public_glossary.card_definition: In system prose, multiple usually means several, as in multiple providers or files. In the mathematical papers, m is a multiple of d exactly when m = d × k for some integer k, equivalently when d divides m. The mathematical sense must be supplied by a product or divisibility context.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Resolve the sense from the noun phrase: several objects in ordinary prose, or an exact integer product in a divisibility statement.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The mathematical sense coordinates common denominators, periods, and least-common-multiple constraints. It includes zero and can include negative values under the theorem's convention; none of that structure is implied by the ordinary adjective.
public_glossary.scope_note: This entry disambiguates the ordinary quantity sense from the mathematical integer-multiple relation.
public_glossary.example: Multiple LLM providers means several providers, while 12 is a multiple of 3 because 12 = 3 × 4.
public_glossary.non_example: The phrase multiple providers is not a divisibility statement.

public_glossary.label: multiplicative order
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The multiplicative order of an integer `b` modulo `Q` is the smallest positive exponent `k` for which `b^k` leaves remainder one when divided by `Q`.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The multiplicative order of an integer `b` modulo `Q` is the smallest positive exponent `k` for which `b^k` leaves remainder one when divided by `Q`.
public_glossary.card_definition: The order exists when `b` and `Q` are coprime and measures the period of repeated multiplication by `b` modulo `Q`. It can connect a reduced denominator to the least common multiple of a set of exponents.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the modulus, base, coprimality condition, and minimality of the claimed exponent.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Verifying `b^k ≡ 1 mod Q` only shows that the order divides `k`; proving exact order also requires excluding every smaller positive divisor candidate.
public_glossary.scope_note: Multiplicative order covers one specified base and modulus satisfying the needed coprimality condition.
public_glossary.example: A finite certificate checks that the order of the base modulo the reduced denominator equals the support's least common multiple.
public_glossary.non_example: Any exponent producing remainder one is a period, but it need not be the multiplicative order unless it is minimal.

public_glossary.label: name
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A name is the human-readable word or phrase used to refer to a person, object, concept, or release.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A name is the human-readable word or phrase used to refer to a person, object, concept, or release.
public_glossary.card_definition: Names make things recognizable, but they can be ambiguous, translated, or changed. Stable identifiers and compatibility routes preserve identity when names move.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the name for communication and the stable identifier when exact identity matters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A rename changes the public handle without necessarily changing the underlying object, which is why migrations record old and new names explicitly.
public_glossary.scope_note: A name identifies its object within the language, namespace, and version where it is declared.
public_glossary.example: Plectis is the current public name; Microcosm remains a compatibility name.
public_glossary.non_example: Two objects sharing a label are not therefore the same object.

public_glossary.label: narrow
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To narrow something is to reduce its scope, possibilities, range, or level of detail under consideration.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To narrow something is to reduce its scope, possibilities, range, or level of detail under consideration.
public_glossary.card_definition: Narrowing helps make questions answerable and actions safer by excluding irrelevant or unauthorized territory. It should preserve the relationship between the smaller question and the larger one it came from.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When scope is narrowed, record the exclusions so the resulting claim is not later read as broader than it is.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A narrow result can be strong within its boundary while leaving the general case entirely open.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers reduced search spaces, claims, routes, permissions, and implementation targets.
public_glossary.example: Restricting a link check to one generated directory narrows its coverage.
public_glossary.non_example: Omitting difficult cases without stating the omission is not honest narrowing.

public_glossary.label: natural number
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A natural number is a whole number used for counting, with the convention about whether zero is included stated by the surrounding formalization.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A natural number is a whole number used for counting, with the convention about whether zero is included stated by the surrounding formalization.
public_glossary.card_definition: Different texts use ℕ for either {0,1,2,…} or {1,2,3,…}; Lean includes zero in its natural-number type. Positive natural numbers exclude zero.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the zero convention before transferring a statement between sources.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Natural numbers support induction, recursion, divisibility, and finite counting, and formal systems encode them as a specific type rather than an informal collection.
public_glossary.scope_note: Natural number covers the number type and zero convention declared by the source.
public_glossary.example: In Lean, 0, 1, and 2 are natural numbers.
public_glossary.non_example: −1 and 1/2 are not natural numbers.

public_glossary.label: navigation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Navigation means route selection across governed repository surfaces. It does not redefine physical navigation, web navigation generally, or graph search as a discipline.
public_glossary.short_definition: Navigation is the system’s browse-and-drilldown layer for moving from a question to the smallest source-backed answer surface.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Navigation is the system’s browse-and-drilldown layer for moving from a question to the smallest source-backed answer surface.
public_glossary.card_definition: Rather than opening the whole codebase to find one thing, navigation presents the system as a series of choices that can be opened in stages: a top-level map, then groups, then individual rows, then the source or evidence behind a row. Each step shows what exists and what it contains before the full text is loaded, so a path through the material can be chosen deliberately. It is the layer that makes the system inspectable in order, from overview down to a single record.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a navigation surface as a map of what is available, not the thing itself: follow it down to the underlying record before relying on what a row says.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Navigation works by compression, turning a large body of files into visible rows that can be expanded at widening levels of detail, so the system can present its own structure instead of each reader rebuilding the map from scratch.
public_glossary.scope_note: Navigation covers the orientation surfaces of the site: the architecture and area pages, contents listings, and the staged drilldowns from map to group to row to source. A reader meets it whenever they move between an overview and a specific component, paper module, or piece of evidence.
public_glossary.example: The architecture and navigation area page is one instance: it lays out how the parts of the system fit together and links onward into the specific components and records beneath each part.

example_route.label: Area: architecture & navigation
example_route.gloss: see the navigation surface that maps the parts and links down to records

public_glossary.non_example: Navigation is not a search box or a website menu bar bolted on for convenience. It is the staged map from overview to source that the system builds over its own files, and a row in it is a pointer to a record, not the record itself.

relationships.gloss: Navigation depends on routing to choose which surface to open next.
The navigation hologram is a compiled navigation surface.
