public_glossary.label: negative
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Negative describes a result, condition, value, or case that denies, fails, opposes, or falls below a chosen reference point.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Negative describes a result, condition, value, or case that denies, fails, opposes, or falls below a chosen reference point.
public_glossary.card_definition: Its meaning depends on context: a negative test expects rejection, a negative finding reports absence, and a negative number lies below zero. The surrounding noun supplies the relevant sense.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Do not treat negative as automatically bad; identify the test, sign convention, or proposition it negates.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Negative evidence can be highly useful when it rules out an unsafe input, disproves a conjecture, or narrows a search.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers evaluative, logical, testing, and numerical uses stated by the page.
public_glossary.example: A negative test verifies that malformed input is rejected.
public_glossary.non_example: A low but positive measurement is not a negative number.

public_glossary.label: negative case
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A negative case is a deliberately invalid fixture that the check is expected to reject; it is not any failed run, undesirable outcome, or negative opinion.
public_glossary.short_definition: A negative case is an input a check must reject, shipped beside passing inputs so a detector that stops discriminating fails visibly instead of quietly accepting everything.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A negative case is an input a check must reject, shipped beside passing inputs so a detector that stops discriminating fails visibly instead of quietly accepting everything.
public_glossary.card_definition: A check that only ever sees valid input cannot tell you it is working. Break it and it still passes. The negative case closes that hole: it is a deliberately bad input with a recorded expectation that the check refuses it. If a component's negative case starts passing, the component is broken even though nothing has thrown an error. This is the difference between a check that runs and a check that discriminates.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a component's negative cases to see what it can actually detect. A check with no negative case has not shown it can fail.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Negative cases are the cheapest defence against the failure mode this system is most exposed to: machinery that reports success because it has stopped looking. They are why a passing result is treated as evidence rather than as a green light - the run has demonstrated both that it accepts what it should and refuses what it should not.
public_glossary.scope_note: Negative cases bound what a check can catch. A check refuses the negatives it ships; it makes no claim about failures nobody wrote down.
public_glossary.example: A gate that must reject an overclaiming release note ships the overclaiming text as a negative case; a build in which that text passes is a failing build.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

source_refs.gloss: Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.
Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.label: Newton flow
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The Newton flow is the continuous version of Newton's method: instead of jumping in steps toward a root of a polynomial, a point drifts smoothly in the direction Newton's method would push it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The Newton flow is the continuous version of Newton's method: instead of jumping in steps toward a root of a polynomial, a point drifts smoothly in the direction Newton's method would push it.
public_glossary.card_definition: Along that flow the value of the polynomial decays in a controlled way, which turns a question about curves in the plane into a question about how those trajectories can meet.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A statement about the flow constrains the trajectories, not the polynomial's roots directly.
public_glossary.deep_definition: For Erdős #1041, Lean checks that the polynomial value decays as exp of minus t along the flow and therefore stays on one oriented ray, and formalises the resulting no-connection criterion. The global topology and the length gluing remain open.
public_glossary.scope_note: Complex Newton flow of a polynomial, in the plane. Not gradient flow in general.
public_glossary.example: Following the Newton flow from a starting point drives the polynomial's value toward zero.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: node
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A node is one uniquely identified object represented as a point in a graph.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A node is one uniquely identified object represented as a point in a graph.
public_glossary.card_definition: Nodes carry identity and attributes, while edges record their relationships. A node may stand for a page, theorem, component, term, or another artifact kind.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the node type and stable identifier before following its edges.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same real object should not become several accidental nodes merely because it appears on several pages; projections preserve a join back to one identity.
public_glossary.scope_note: A node covers the graph object and attributes attached to its identifier.
public_glossary.example: A theorem can appear as a statement node connected to the proof file that declares it.
public_glossary.non_example: A visual dot with no identity in the graph data is not a governed node.

public_glossary.label: normal form
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A normal form is a standard way of rewriting an object so that two objects are equal exactly when their rewritten versions match.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A normal form is a standard way of rewriting an object so that two objects are equal exactly when their rewritten versions match.
public_glossary.card_definition: Putting a problem into a normal form does not solve it. It moves the difficulty into a shape where the remaining obligation can be stated exactly, which is often what makes a machine check possible at all.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A normal form is a reformulation, so it carries the same difficulty as the statement it rewrites unless a separate result says otherwise.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Erdős #68 has an exact factorial-successor normal form in Lean, and Erdős #257 an exact carry-pivot normal form. Both are exact reformulations, and both problems remain open.
public_glossary.scope_note: Applies to the mathematical objects named in the papers, not to file formats or data schemas.
public_glossary.example: Writing a fraction in lowest terms is a normal form for rational numbers.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: note
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A note is a short record or explanation attached to a larger body of work.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A note is a short record or explanation attached to a larger body of work.
public_glossary.card_definition: Notes preserve context, qualifications, reminders, or observations that do not belong in the main flow. Their authority depends on who wrote them and what evidence they cite.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a note as supplementary context unless the governing surface explicitly gives it stronger authority.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Brevity does not make a note informal or unimportant, but it often means the note omits the fuller argument or evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers annotations, explanatory asides, and bounded working records shown by the site.
public_glossary.example: A note beside a result can state the version on which the measurement was taken.
public_glossary.non_example: An unsupported note does not override a checked source record.

public_glossary.label: nowhere dense
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A set is nowhere dense when it contains no interval, and neither does the set you get by adding all its limit points.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A set is nowhere dense when it contains no interval, and neither does the set you get by adding all its limit points.
public_glossary.card_definition: It is the topological sense of thin: however far you zoom in, you always find a gap. The Cantor set is the standard example.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Nowhere dense is a statement about gaps, not about size in measure. A set can be nowhere dense and still fill most of an interval in Lebesgue measure.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The achievement set studied for Erdős #257 is compact, nowhere dense, and of Lebesgue measure one at the same time. The pairing is the point: no interval sits inside it, and yet it is not negligible.
public_glossary.scope_note: Applies to sets of real numbers here, not to sequences or to sets of indices.
public_glossary.example: The Cantor set is nowhere dense.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: number
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A number is an abstract mathematical object used to count, measure, order, or represent quantities.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A number is an abstract mathematical object used to count, measure, order, or represent quantities.
public_glossary.card_definition: Different number systems include natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers, each with different operations and properties. A theorem's domain states which kind is intended.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the number system before applying divisibility, order, or approximation rules.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same written numeral can denote elements embedded across several number systems, but formal proofs keep their types explicit.
public_glossary.scope_note: Number covers the number system and role named in the surrounding expression or statement.
public_glossary.example: 3 is a natural number, an integer, a rational number, and a real number under the usual embeddings.
public_glossary.non_example: A version label containing digits is not necessarily a mathematical number used in a calculation.

public_glossary.label: number theory
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Number theory is the area of mathematics that studies integers and related structures, including divisibility, primes, congruences, and arithmetic functions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Number theory is the area of mathematics that studies integers and related structures, including divisibility, primes, congruences, and arithmetic functions.
public_glossary.card_definition: The Erdős problems on this site are largely number-theoretic, often involving sequences, reciprocal sums, denominators, and multiplicative behavior. Number theory can use tools from analysis, algebra, combinatorics, and computation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify which integer or arithmetic structure the problem is asking about.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Elementary statements in number theory can require deep proofs because simple integer operations encode strong global constraints.
public_glossary.scope_note: Number theory covers the integer and arithmetic questions in the published problem statements and proofs.
public_glossary.example: Studying Euler's totient function and multiplicative orders is number theory.
public_glossary.non_example: Ordinary data counting is not automatically a number-theory problem.

public_glossary.label: numerator
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The numerator is the top part of a fraction: in P/Q, it is P, the quantity being divided by Q.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The numerator is the top part of a fraction: in P/Q, it is P, the quantity being divided by Q.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis uses numerators when an exact finite sum is reduced to P/Q. P and Q must be tracked as a pair: cancelling a common factor changes both, and only the reduced denominator Q is later used for the order and divisibility certificates.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a paper or component writes P/Q, check whether the fraction is reduced and do not transfer a claim about Q to P.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In the finite denominator-certificate work, exact rational summation produces P/Q before the denominator is reconstructed independently from least-common-multiple and factorisation data. The numerator records the accumulated finite sum; it is not the certificate target, and its value depends on the same cancellation that determines the final denominator.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers the upper integer or expression in a stated fraction, especially the reduced rational outputs of Plectis finite-sum components.
public_glossary.example: For S_F(b)=P/Q in lowest terms, P is the numerator and Q is the denominator checked by the certificate.
public_glossary.non_example: The 5 in 3/5 is the denominator, not the numerator.

public_glossary.label: observation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis uses package for both installable software units and assembled submission or release units; the surrounding operation determines the sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: An observation is information recorded by inspecting an event, artifact, measurement, or behavior.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An observation is information recorded by inspecting an event, artifact, measurement, or behavior.
public_glossary.card_definition: Observations report what was seen under particular conditions and can become evidence for a claim. Interpretation and generalization require a separate argument.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Record the observer or instrument, conditions, time, and exact thing observed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In software work an observation may come from logs or output; in research it may come from an experiment or dataset; neither becomes a universal fact automatically.
public_glossary.scope_note: An observation covers the object, conditions, and time of the recorded inspection.
public_glossary.example: A browser screenshot can support the observation that an underline is visually faint in one rendered viewport.
public_glossary.non_example: An expectation or remembered impression is not a recorded observation.

public_glossary.label: observe
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Observe names the repository's evidence-gathering lane when used as a noun; it does not redefine the ordinary verb or imply neutral measurement without a stated method.
public_glossary.short_definition: An observe is a read-only pass that gathers structured evidence from files, probes, and responses into a bounded record before any decision or change is made.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An observe is a read-only pass that gathers structured evidence from files, probes, and responses into a bounded record before any decision or change is made.
public_glossary.card_definition: Observe is the evidence-gathering half of the observe/apply pairing the system runs. An observe pass learns, maps, compares, or probes a target and writes down what it found: the questions it asked, the files it examined, the responses it got back, a synthesis, and any validation signals. It can run locally or across a bridge of helpers, but it never mutates code or doctrine. Its job is to keep exploration separate from action so a decision rests on collected facts rather than a first guess.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read an observe pass as a record of what was examined and found, not as a completed change. The work it describes has been looked into, not yet carried out.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Keeping the observe step explicit means the evidence behind a later change is inspectable on its own, and the system does not treat its first plan as if the work were already done.
public_glossary.scope_note: Observe is a runtime activity in the system's observe/apply cycle. A reader meets it wherever the pages describe how a pass gathers evidence, runs probes, or proves a point before any application step, including the evidence and architecture surfaces.
public_glossary.example: The Tactic Portfolio Availability Probe is one concrete observe: it inspects which proof tactics are available for a target and reports what it found, without itself attempting the proof.

example_route.label: Tactic Portfolio Availability Probe
example_route.gloss: see what an observe pass actually records and proves

public_glossary.non_example: An observe is not the change itself and not a finished decision. It collects and records evidence; the separate apply step is where anything is altered.

relationships.gloss: Observe normally precedes mutation.
Observe can dispatch bridge groups.

source_refs.gloss: Observe workflow skill.
Observe plan contract.

public_glossary.label: omission receipt
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An omission receipt records what detail was deliberately excluded, why, and where to recover it; it is not an excuse for forgotten work or evidence that omitted material is irrelevant.
public_glossary.short_definition: An omission receipt is the note on a compressed row that states what was left out, why that omission is allowed at the current depth, and which command reopens the full source.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An omission receipt is the note on a compressed row that states what was left out, why that omission is allowed at the current depth, and which command reopens the full source.
public_glossary.card_definition: Pages and browse rows on this site are compressed views of a much larger body of source material. An omission receipt is the part of such a row that keeps the compression honest: it names what was dropped, such as the underlying source bodies, deeper relationships, or fuller command output, gives the reason that omission is acceptable for a quick-scan row, and points to the drilldown that recovers the complete material. It lets a row be useful for choosing what to open without quietly pretending to be the whole story.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat the omission receipt on a row as the row's own statement of its limits: it tells you what is not shown and how to reach the full source, so follow that pointer when you need the complete picture rather than assuming the short row is everything.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Its function is to stop a compact view from claiming false completeness: the row stays cheap to read, yet the receipt records exactly what was excluded, why that exclusion is acceptable at this level of detail, and which command restores the full source behind it.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers row-level truth boundaries throughout the system's compressed navigation, browse listings, and summary cards. A reader meets it wherever a short row stands in for fuller source material and carries a pointer back to that material.
public_glossary.example: The doctrine card "Preserve provenance across every boundary" is a concrete instance: it holds the rule that a compressed surface must always keep a path back to the source it summarises, which is exactly what an omission receipt records on an individual row.

example_route.label: Preserve provenance across every boundary
example_route.gloss: open the doctrine rule that an omission receipt enforces on each row

public_glossary.non_example: An omission receipt is not an error message, a disclaimer, or an admission that something is broken. It is a deliberate, structured record of what a compressed row leaves out and how to recover it.

relationships.gloss: Receipts preserve currentness and authority boundaries.
Option-surface cards use omission receipts for drilldown safety.
Profiles decide what loss is legal at a band.
Rows become safe to browse when omissions are explicit.

source_refs.gloss: Card rows carry omission_receipt fields and drilldown commands.
Navigation-row contract for drilldowns and compact row boundaries.
Compression skill that requires explicit loss and drilldown boundaries.

public_glossary.label: open problem
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An open problem is a precisely stated question for which no proof or counterexample accepted by the relevant mathematical community is currently known.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An open problem is a precisely stated question for which no proof or counterexample accepted by the relevant mathematical community is currently known.
public_glossary.card_definition: A problem can remain open despite extensive computations, conditional reductions, solved special cases, and formalized supporting theory. Those results narrow or reorganize the question but do not settle its universal statement.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a problem is marked open, distinguish the original question from the partial and conditional results reported around it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Open status is time-sensitive and source-sensitive, so a responsible statement names the problem, date or source of the status, and any claimed resolution that would need independent review.
public_glossary.scope_note: Open problem covers the exact question and formulation named by the cited problem source.
public_glossary.example: Every Erdős problem represented in the paper corpus is recorded as open.
public_glossary.non_example: A theorem proving one finite case or a stronger conditional statement does not automatically close the original problem.

public_glossary.label: operation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An operation is a defined transformation, calculation, or state change applied to specified objects or inputs.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An operation is a defined transformation, calculation, or state change applied to specified objects or inputs.
public_glossary.card_definition: Operations range from mathematical addition to file writes and API calls. Their meaning comes from the domain, operands, preconditions, and expected effect.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the operation's inputs, permitted target, and result contract before executing or reasoning from it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: An operation can be pure, producing a value without changing external state, or stateful, changing files, services, or records.
public_glossary.scope_note: An operation covers the operands, target, and semantics defined by its owning system.
public_glossary.example: Sorting registry rows by identifier is a deterministic data operation.
public_glossary.non_example: A desired outcome with no defined transformation is not an operation.

public_glossary.label: operator proxy
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An operator proxy performs one bounded task from prepared intent and context; it does not impersonate the operator or acquire the operator’s wider authority.
public_glossary.short_definition: An operator proxy is an outside worker acting on the operator's behalf for one bounded task from a prepared context-and-instruction packet, carrying the operator's intent without acquiring the operator's authority.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An operator proxy is an outside worker acting on the operator's behalf for one bounded task from a prepared context-and-instruction packet, carrying the operator's intent without acquiring the operator's authority.
public_glossary.card_definition: When the system hands a task to a separate worker, such as a chat model or coding agent, it sends a packet that holds the purpose, the relevant doctrine, worked examples, the output shape, and the constraints. The worker runs as an operator proxy: it can do real work because the packet makes the intent executable, but its remit is fixed to that one task. Choosing what context to send, validating the result, and deciding whether the output enters the system stay with the owning side, not the proxy.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat an operator proxy's output as work done to order, not as a decision made by the operator. It is bounded to the task it was given, and it becomes part of the system only after the owning side validates and admits it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The role separates how capable a worker is from how much authority it holds: a highly capable proxy can outperform a less capable owner on a well-prepared packet, yet it still cannot see context it was not given, change the system's rules, or speak as the operator.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the bounded delegation role used when the system routes a task to an external worker such as a chat model or coding agent. A reader encounters it on the pages describing how the system works with coding agents and runs prepared missions.
public_glossary.example: A concrete instance is a chat model that receives a packet defining one message-writing mission, drafts the message inside those limits, and returns it for the owning side to check and admit, never acting beyond that brief.

example_route.label: With a coding agent
example_route.gloss: see a worker run a prepared task on the operator's behalf

public_glossary.non_example: An operator proxy is not the operator and not an autonomous agent that sets its own goals or changes the system's rules. It is a worker running one prepared task within fixed limits, whose results take effect only once the owning side admits them.

relationships.gloss: Operator proxy is a Bridge role for bounded message missions.
The proxy remains Type B bounded-worker agency.
Proxy output is not raw operator voice.
A proxy packet needs schema, constraints, examples, and validation.

public_glossary.label: operator voice
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Operator voice is preserved direct human input that outranks later agent synthesis on intent; it is not a writing style, inferred preference, or agent-authored paraphrase.
public_glossary.short_definition: Operator voice is the preserved first-person record of what the operator said directly, kept separate from every later agent-authored summary or interpretation as the original human input behind the system.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Operator voice is the preserved first-person record of what the operator said directly, kept separate from every later agent-authored summary or interpretation as the original human input behind the system.
public_glossary.card_definition: Operator voice is the unmediated expression of the person who runs the system: raw seed paragraphs, spoken notes, and direct instructions, recorded as they were given. It holds authority over every later artifact, so paper modules, standards, and agent-written summaries may compress or route it but can never replace or contradict it. The raw record is kept append-only for this reason: it is the layer everything else answers to.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is marked as operator voice, treat it as the original human source, above any summary or agent rephrasing of it. If a later page conflicts with it, the operator voice is the one that holds.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It is distinct from two nearby things: a Bridge proxy acting for the operator under a prepared packet, and an agent-authored projection that compresses operator voice into doctrine. Both of those are downstream; only operator voice is the original.
public_glossary.scope_note: Operator voice covers the raw seeds, voiced paragraphs, and direct instructions that seed the system. A reader meets it behind the doctrine and component pages, which are projections drawn from it, and most directly in the loop that turns this voice into doctrine.
public_glossary.example: The Voice To Doctrine Self Improvement Loop is a concrete instance: a component that takes the operator's recorded voice and distils it into doctrine while preserving the original wording, so you can see the raw human input on one side and the compressed rule on the other.

example_route.label: Voice To Doctrine Self Improvement Loop
example_route.gloss: open the component that turns recorded operator voice into doctrine

public_glossary.non_example: Operator voice is not the polished doctrine, standards, or agent-written summaries on the site. Those are projections compressed from it. It is also not a Bridge proxy speaking on the operator's behalf: it is only what the operator himself said directly.

relationships.gloss: Operator voice is preserved in raw seed paragraphs.
Direct operator voice differs from Bridge proxy output.

public_glossary.label: option surface
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: An option surface enumerates stable selectable rows for one artifact kind before handing off to source authority; it is not merely a UI page, search result list, or command menu.
public_glossary.short_definition: An option surface is a browse layer of stable, kind-grouped, selectable artifact rows used to choose and inspect a specific item before opening the authoritative source it points to.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An option surface is a browse layer of stable, kind-grouped, selectable artifact rows used to choose and inspect a specific item before opening the authoritative source it points to.
public_glossary.card_definition: An option surface sits between the top-level Kind Atlas and the underlying source material. For a chosen kind of artifact, such as components, paper modules, or doctrine cards, it enumerates the available rows cheaply, lets one be selected by its stable id, and shows a compact card for that row that states what is and is not included and how current it is. Only after a row is chosen does it hand off to the authoritative standard, registry, skill, or paper module behind it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat an option surface as a catalogue for finding and selecting one row, not as the final authority on that row. The card it shows is a summary with its own currentness and omission notes; the binding detail is in the source it links to.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It works in bands: a cheap listing band shows many rows at a glance, and a card band expands a single selected id into more detail, including a record of any id that was asked for but not found. This keeps browsing inexpensive while keeping the path back to source explicit.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the standard-owned row-and-card browse mechanism used across the system's navigable kinds. A reader meets it wherever the public pages present a list of components, paper modules, or doctrine cards that can be opened one at a time.
public_glossary.example: The Navigation Hologram Route Plane is the routing layer in which option surfaces operate: the place where artifact rows are listed by kind and a stable id is selected before the authoritative source is opened.

example_route.label: Navigation Hologram Route Plane
example_route.gloss: open the routing plane where rows are listed and selected by id

public_glossary.non_example: An option surface is not a keyword search box and not the source files themselves. It is a fixed catalogue of rows you select from by id, sitting one layer above the authority it links to.

relationships.gloss: Each option surface is scoped by artifact kind.
A supported option surface is the rowability browse layer.
Option surfaces expose adapter-supported bands.
Cards record omitted source context and drilldown.

public_glossary.label: orbit
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An orbit is the sequence of values produced by applying the same step over and over from a starting point.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An orbit is the sequence of values produced by applying the same step over and over from a starting point.
public_glossary.card_definition: Orbits turn a question about a number into a question about long-run behaviour: does the sequence stay bounded, return, drift, or vanish. That is often easier to state exactly, and no easier to prove.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A finite stretch of an orbit is a computation. Statements about the whole orbit need a separate argument.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Erdős #243 becomes rigidity of a centred integer error orbit once denominators are cleared, and the remaining Erdős #257 targets reduce to explicit alternatives about infinite orbits. In both cases the reformulation is exact and the problem is open.
public_glossary.scope_note: Discrete-dynamics sense: iterating one map. Not the astronomical sense, and not a group orbit unless the paper says so.
public_glossary.example: Starting at 6 and repeatedly halving even numbers gives the orbit 6, 3.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: order
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Order is the arrangement of items or actions according to position, precedence, dependency, or a comparison rule.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Order is the arrangement of items or actions according to position, precedence, dependency, or a comparison rule.
public_glossary.card_definition: Order can be alphabetical, chronological, logical, numerical, or procedural. The chosen rule determines what earlier and later mean and whether the order affects validity.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When order matters, identify the ordering rule and which steps or items depend on their position.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Some collections are displayed in an order for convenience even though their underlying meaning is unchanged by permutation.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers reading order, execution order, sort order, and mathematical order relations.
public_glossary.example: Glossary entries are displayed in alphabetical order by preferred label.
public_glossary.non_example: Two items appearing adjacent in a list are not necessarily ordered by importance.

public_glossary.label: orientation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Orientation is the material meant to be read first: a short account of what this is and how to navigate it, as distinct from the evidence itself.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Orientation is the material meant to be read first: a short account of what this is and how to navigate it, as distinct from the evidence itself.
public_glossary.card_definition: Orientation is deliberately separated from evidence, because the two carry different weight. An orientation guide is the author describing the work, which is useful and is not proof of anything. Keeping the boundary visible stops a good explanation from being mistaken for a good result.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read orientation to find your way. Read records to check claims.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The separation is easy to lose, because clear description is persuasive in the same register as evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: Orientation describes the system. It establishes nothing about it.
public_glossary.example: The concise guide is orientation for an assistant that cannot accept a file upload.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: orphan
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An orphan is an item an index has failed to place: something present in the source but connected to nothing in the map built over it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An orphan is an item an index has failed to place: something present in the source but connected to nothing in the map built over it.
public_glossary.card_definition: The orphan count is how you tell an index apart from a partial index. A map with orphans is one that quietly stops covering part of its subject, and any question asked of it will return an answer that looks complete. Publishing the count is what makes coverage checkable rather than assumed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the orphan count before trusting a map's coverage. Zero is the only reassuring number.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The failure mode is silence: an orphaned declaration does not raise an error, it simply never appears in an answer, so the gap is invisible from the outside.
public_glossary.scope_note: An orphan count describes the index, not the source.
public_glossary.example: The semantic map reports 153,238 declarations indexed with zero orphans.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: output
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An output is the data, artifact, message, or state produced by a process after it consumes inputs.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An output is the data, artifact, message, or state produced by a process after it consumes inputs.
public_glossary.card_definition: Outputs should be interpreted through the producing command, source version, and contract. Generated output is usually rebuilt from source rather than edited directly.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Trace an output back to its inputs and producer before treating it as authoritative.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A process can emit several outputs with different roles, such as a human page, a machine packet, and a validation receipt derived from the same source.
public_glossary.scope_note: An output covers the product of one stated process and invocation.
public_glossary.example: The public glossary HTML is an output of the site builder.
public_glossary.non_example: A planned filename is not an output until the producing process creates it.

public_glossary.label: overview
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: An overview is a compressed account of a subject's main parts and relationships intended to orient a reader before detail.
public_glossary.reader_preview: An overview is a compressed account of a subject's main parts and relationships intended to orient a reader before detail.
public_glossary.card_definition: An overview trades completeness for navigational value. It should reveal the shape of the subject, important boundaries, and where to continue without pretending to contain all evidence.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use an overview to choose a route, then open the owning detail before relying on a precise claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Compression can omit exceptions and implementation detail, so an overview is a projection rather than exhaustive authority.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers high-level site, area, component, and research summaries.
public_glossary.example: An architecture overview names the main components and how they connect.
public_glossary.non_example: A list of titles without relationships or orientation is not a useful overview.

public_glossary.label: package
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A package is a collection prepared to travel as one unit. In Plectis it can mean an installable software package or a submission or release package of artifacts.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A package is a collection prepared to travel as one unit.
public_glossary.card_definition: A software package carries code, metadata, dependencies, and a version for package tooling. A submission package instead gathers the files and records needed for review or delivery. Neither meaning is automatically the same as an AI packet or evidence bundle, which have their own reader and provenance contracts.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use install, import, dependency, or version context for the software sense; use submit, review, or delivery context for the assembled-artifact sense.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Plectis also preserves some package identifiers for compatibility and lineage. Such an identifier can keep an old route or dependency resolvable without making that package name a current public category or product identity.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers installable dependency units, assembled submission units, and explicitly preserved package identifiers; the surrounding operation determines the sense.
public_glossary.example: A Lean project pins a Mathlib package revision, while tactic-routing work can produce a separate submission package for review.
public_glossary.non_example: Any compressed directory is not automatically a managed software package.

public_glossary.label: packet
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A packet is a single bundled file prepared for an AI assistant to read, carrying the site's content and structure in one download rather than as pages to browse.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A packet is a single bundled file prepared for an AI assistant to read, carrying the site's content and structure in one download rather than as pages to browse.
public_glossary.card_definition: An assistant reading a website page by page gets an incomplete and arbitrary slice of it. A packet removes that problem by shipping the whole public surface at once, in a form built for machine reading. Different sizes exist for the same reason: some tools refuse large files.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A packet tells an assistant what the site says. It does not let the assistant run anything.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The distinction between reading and running survives the packet. A packet improves the quality of a summary, and a summary is still not evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: A packet carries the public surface as of the build that produced it.
public_glossary.example: The landing page offers the full AI packet and a smaller reader digest of the same map.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: page
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A page is one rendered reading surface at a stable site route, presenting selected prose, data, and links from underlying source material.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A page is one rendered reading surface at a stable site route, presenting selected prose, data, and links from underlying source material.
public_glossary.card_definition: Pages are designed for orientation and reading, not as independent authority. A generated page may accurately project source data, but the page still needs a route back to the file, record, or contract that owns the underlying claim.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a page as a presentation of source material and use its links to inspect the owning record when accuracy matters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A page can combine authored prose with generated facts and relationships, so its trust boundary is field-specific rather than uniform across the whole document.
public_glossary.scope_note: A page covers the material rendered at its route and the source revision from which it was built.
public_glossary.example: The glossary page renders one expandable card for every active public vocabulary row.
public_glossary.non_example: A page is not automatically the authority for every fact it displays.

public_glossary.label: paper
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: In Plectis, a paper is the rendered PDF write-up for a project, question, or result. It is not a claim that the document is an academic publication, and it is not an ai_workflow paper module.
public_glossary.short_definition: A paper is a rendered PDF write-up that gives a human-readable account of a project, question, method, result, and evidence boundary, linked to its supporting source where available.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A paper is a rendered PDF write-up that gives a human-readable account of a project, question, method, result, and evidence boundary, linked to its supporting source where available.
public_glossary.card_definition: The Plectis paper shelf contains reader-facing rendered PDFs: short problem notes, longer working records, mathematical expositions, and systems write-ups. Calling one a paper identifies that presentation form, not peer review, journal publication, novelty, or proof authority. A paper module is different: it is an internal ai_workflow document that maps a subsystem, its owners, and its routes. For mathematical claims, the paper explains the argument while the Lean declarations and claim registry own what was checked and what remains open.

public_glossary.label: perfect set
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A set is perfect when it is closed and has no isolated points, so every point in it is approached arbitrarily closely by other points of the set.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A set is perfect when it is closed and has no isolated points, so every point in it is approached arbitrarily closely by other points of the set.

public_glossary.label: periodic

public_glossary.short_definition: A sequence is periodic when a fixed block repeats forever, and eventually periodic when such repetition begins after a finite initial segment.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A sequence is periodic when a fixed block repeats forever, and eventually periodic when such repetition begins after a finite initial segment.
public_glossary.card_definition: The period is the smallest positive shift that preserves the repeating tail. Positional digit expansions of rational numbers are eventually periodic, which makes forbidden repetition a route to proving irrationality.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check whether periodicity begins immediately or only eventually and whether the claimed period is minimal.

public_glossary.non_example: A pattern repeated several times in computed data is not proof that the sequence is periodic forever.

public_glossary.label: planted error
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A planted error is a fault introduced on purpose to check that a detector notices it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A planted error is a fault introduced on purpose to check that a detector notices it.
public_glossary.card_definition: A check that has never caught anything has not been shown to work. Planting an error and confirming it is rejected is the difference between a gate that runs and a gate that discriminates. This site records one such case: a deliberately false claim was introduced after a real failure had been repaired, and the repaired gate refused it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask what a detector has actually caught. An untested detector is an assumption.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The honest version of this reports both halves: the real failure that got through first, and the planted case that the repair then caught. Reporting only the second would make a repair look like foresight.
public_glossary.scope_note: A planted error establishes that a detector catches that error. It implies no wider coverage.
public_glossary.example: After a wording gate was repaired, a deliberately false version of the same claim was rejected.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: planted forgery
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A planted forgery is a deliberately false claim placed in a test input so that a check can be observed refusing it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A planted forgery is a deliberately false claim placed in a test input so that a check can be observed refusing it.
public_glossary.card_definition: Watching a check pass on correct input shows only that it does not object. Watching it reject a known-false input by name shows it can tell the difference, which is the harder half.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A run that plants a forgery and does not report a refusal has failed, even when it reports a pass.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The completion-faithfulness audit runs against notes carrying three planted forgeries: a fake commit claim, a fake test claim, and a fake work-record claim. The external verification job uses the same idea, running a second fixture with one statement altered and counting as passed only when the checker rejects it by name.
public_glossary.scope_note: The forgeries are synthetic test data. They are not real claims made anywhere.
public_glossary.example: A note claiming a commit that was never made is one of the planted cases.

public_glossary.label: policy
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A policy is a stated rule for choosing, permitting, restricting, or handling actions and information in recurring situations.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A policy is a stated rule for choosing, permitting, restricting, or handling actions and information in recurring situations.
public_glossary.card_definition: Policies guide decisions where raw facts alone do not determine what should happen. Enforceable policies name their scope, authority, conditions, and consequences.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate the policy choice from the evidence used to evaluate its conditions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A policy can be expressed in prose, structured data, or executable checks, but those projections should remain synchronized with one governing source.
public_glossary.scope_note: A policy covers the actors, actions, information, and conditions named by its rule.
public_glossary.example: A publication policy can require private paths to be removed from public output.
public_glossary.non_example: A one-off preference with no recurring scope or authority is not necessarily a policy.

public_glossary.label: positive integer
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A positive integer is an integer greater than zero.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A positive integer is an integer greater than zero.
public_glossary.card_definition: The positive integers are 1, 2, 3, and so on, excluding zero and all negative integers. Formal statements often use positivity to permit division, ordering, or finite counting arguments.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check whether the domain is positive integers, nonnegative integers, or all integers.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A positivity hypothesis can be essential even when it looks routine, because removing it may introduce zero denominators or sign changes.
public_glossary.scope_note: Positive integer covers the integer domain n > 0 in the stated theorem or definition.
public_glossary.example: 1 and 249 are positive integers.
public_glossary.non_example: 0, −3, and 1/2 are not positive integers.

public_glossary.label: present
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Present describes something that exists or is available in the relevant place or time, or the act of displaying it to an audience.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Present describes something that exists or is available in the relevant place or time, or the act of displaying it to an audience.
public_glossary.card_definition: The adjective is the opposite of missing within a search boundary; the verb concerns presentation. Context should identify whether presence in state or communication to a reader is meant.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When presence matters, check where, when, and under which observation method the item was found.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Presence establishes existence within the observed boundary but not correctness, relevance, or freshness.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers observed state and reader-facing display where the sentence makes the sense clear.
public_glossary.example: The requested term is present when its unique id occurs in the registry's term rows.
public_glossary.non_example: A label shown in a cached page does not prove the current source row is still present.

public_glossary.label: preserve
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To preserve something is to keep its relevant content, meaning, condition, identity, or availability through change or over time.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To preserve something is to keep its relevant content, meaning, condition, identity, or availability through change or over time.
public_glossary.card_definition: Preservation requires naming which properties must remain and which transformations are allowed. A format conversion may preserve meaning while changing bytes, layout, or metadata.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a process claims preservation, identify the invariant and the comparison that verifies it before and after the change.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Preserving one property can sacrifice another, so content, structure, provenance, and presentation should not be silently conflated.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers retention of source voice, evidence, semantics, files, identifiers, and public access.
public_glossary.example: A projection preserves a term's preferred meaning while presenting it in a different format.
public_glossary.non_example: Keeping a filename while replacing its content does not preserve the file's meaning.

public_glossary.label: prime
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A prime is a whole number greater than one divisible only by itself and one.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A prime is a whole number greater than one divisible only by itself and one.
public_glossary.card_definition: Primes appear in several of these problems as the rule generating the terms of a series, either directly or through the gaps between consecutive primes. That makes the series inherit every difficulty of the primes themselves, which is a large part of why the questions are hard.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A series built from primes is at least as hard as what is known about primes.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Results about such series are often conditional on facts about prime distribution that are themselves deep, which is why several claims here rest on stated analytic hypotheses rather than standing alone.
public_glossary.scope_note: A result about a prime-generated series covers that series.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #251 asks about the series built from the gaps between consecutive primes.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: prime gap
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A prime gap is the difference between two consecutive prime numbers.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A prime gap is the difference between two consecutive prime numbers.
public_glossary.card_definition: Prime gaps vary irregularly: most are small compared with the primes themselves, but arbitrarily large gaps occur. A series built from them inherits hard questions about how primes are distributed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check whether a statement concerns every gap, average behaviour, infinitely many gaps, or a bounded finite range.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Writing consecutive primes as a starting prime plus accumulated gaps can transform a prime-generated series into an equivalent gap-generated series with different proof handles.
public_glossary.scope_note: Prime gap covers the difference between the named consecutive primes or the corresponding indexed gap sequence.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #251 asks about a dyadic series generated from consecutive primes, equivalently from their gaps.
public_glossary.non_example: The difference between nonconsecutive primes is not the prime gap at either index.

public_glossary.label: principle
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Principle means a governed local operating rule or design constraint. It is not automatically universal, moral, scientific, or externally accepted law.
public_glossary.short_definition: A principle is a durable, doctrine-promoted operating law that constrains agent behaviour and system design, recorded under a stable `pri_*` identifier.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A principle is a durable, doctrine-promoted operating law that constrains agent behaviour and system design, recorded under a stable `pri_*` identifier.
public_glossary.card_definition: A principle states a rule that holds across many cases rather than a fix for one situation, such as "status fails closed" or "derive before you assert". Each principle carries not just the rule but the design instinct behind it: the underlying tradeoff and the reasoning a later decision should reuse when a new case differs from the one that first prompted it. Principles are more stable than a single observation and more general than a mechanism, and each is grounded in recorded evidence and a curation history.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a principle as a standing commitment the system holds itself to, and look at the rule it states and the reason given for it, not just its label.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A principle is one layer in a doctrine hierarchy: above a local note or a one-off observation, below nothing it cannot still be traced back to, and always anchored to the evidence and curation that promoted it.
public_glossary.scope_note: Principles appear throughout the doctrine and rules-and-ideas pages, where each is shown as a numbered, named rule with its rationale; they are the general laws the more specific anti-patterns, mechanisms, and components are measured against.
public_glossary.example: "Status fails closed" is a principle: it commits the system to treating an unknown or unproven status as not-passing rather than assuming success, so that absence of evidence never reads as a green light.

example_route.label: Status fails closed
example_route.gloss: open one stated principle with its rationale

public_glossary.non_example: A principle is not a passing slogan, a personal preference, or a description of one feature. It is a governed, evidence-backed rule that holds across cases, distinct from the narrower mechanisms and anti-patterns it governs.

relationships.gloss: Principles are doctrine nodes.
Skills cite and enact principles.

source_refs.gloss: Principles curation skill.

public_glossary.label: prior
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Prior describes something that existed, occurred, or was believed before the current item or update.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Prior describes something that existed, occurred, or was believed before the current item or update.
public_glossary.card_definition: A prior can be earlier work, an earlier state, or an initial belief used in reasoning. The relevant ordering may be temporal, logical, or procedural.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When prior is used, identify what it precedes and whether the comparison is about time, dependency, or belief.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Earlier material can inform current work without remaining current or authoritative after later corrections. Chronology and authority remain separate: later evidence may supersede an earlier claim while preserving its provenance.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers antecedent versions, work, evidence, and assumptions explicitly referenced by the site.
public_glossary.example: A changelog compares the current release with its prior version.
public_glossary.non_example: A source listed first on a page is not necessarily prior in time.

public_glossary.label: prior art
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Prior art is earlier published work that already contains what is being claimed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Prior art is earlier published work that already contains what is being claimed.
public_glossary.card_definition: Finding it retires a priority claim without saying anything against the work. The result stands; it is simply not first, and saying so is the honest move rather than a concession.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Failing to find prior art is not evidence that none exists. Novelty needs a positive clearance, not an absent search result.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Two cases are recorded here. Steve Fan published the two-prime reduction for Erdős #269 first, on 26 June 2026, so no priority is claimed for it. Two implications in the Erdős #243 work coincide with prior lemmas of Koizumi in canonical coordinates, and no priority is claimed over them.
public_glossary.scope_note: Used in the scholarly-priority sense here, not the patent-law sense.
public_glossary.example: A reduction published earlier by someone else is prior art for the same reduction.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: private
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Private means intentionally unavailable to the general public and accessible only under stated permissions or within a restricted environment.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Private means intentionally unavailable to the general public and accessible only under stated permissions or within a restricted environment.
public_glossary.card_definition: Private describes an access boundary, not secrecy, wrongdoing, or superior authority. Public projections may summarize allowed facts without exposing the private source material behind them.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Do not infer the contents of private material from the existence of a public projection.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A private boundary can protect personal data, unfinished work, credentials, operational state, or simply material outside the release scope, and those reasons carry different handling rules.
public_glossary.scope_note: Private covers the artifacts, services, or context withheld by the stated access policy.
public_glossary.example: The public repositories are inspectable, while the larger working environment remains private.
public_glossary.non_example: Private does not mean false, secret in the security sense, or authoritative.

public_glossary.label: probe
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A probe is a small check that establishes one narrow fact about an environment, run before the work that depends on it rather than after something has already failed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A probe is a small check that establishes one narrow fact about an environment, run before the work that depends on it rather than after something has already failed.
public_glossary.card_definition: A probe is not a test of the system; it is a question about the ground the system is standing on. Is this a fresh clone, are the declared dependencies actually present, does this command exist. Probes are cheap and specific on purpose, so a failure names one missing precondition instead of producing a long trace nobody can localise.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read what single fact a probe establishes. It is not a statement about whether the system works.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The value is in the ordering. A precondition checked first fails with a usable message; the same precondition discovered halfway through a run fails with a symptom.
public_glossary.scope_note: A probe establishes its own narrow fact at the moment it ran.
public_glossary.example: The pre-install probe on a fresh clone reports exit 0 and writes its evidence before any component is run.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: problem
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A problem is a precisely stated question or task whose answer, construction, or proof is not supplied by the statement itself.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A problem is a precisely stated question or task whose answer, construction, or proof is not supplied by the statement itself.
public_glossary.card_definition: In mathematics, a problem specifies the objects, assumptions, and conclusion to be established or refuted. “Open” means no accepted solution is currently known, not that the statement is vague or that no partial results exist.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the exact statement, hypotheses, and requested conclusion before judging whether a result solves the problem.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A problem can accumulate equivalent formulations, partial theorems, computational evidence, and failed approaches while remaining open until the full requested claim is settled.
public_glossary.scope_note: Problem covers the exact question and conditions in its cited statement or catalogue entry.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #249 asks a specific question about values derived from Euler's totient function.
public_glossary.non_example: A related theorem or useful computation is not a solution unless it establishes the problem's full conclusion.

public_glossary.label: problem note
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A problem note is Plectis’s short rendered paper for one open problem and its proved/open boundary; it is not an issue note, private work note, or full working record.
public_glossary.short_definition: A problem note is a short standalone paper on a single open mathematical problem, stating what has been formally proved, what remains open, and where the boundary between them lies.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A problem note is a short standalone paper on a single open mathematical problem, stating what has been formally proved, what remains open, and where the boundary between them lies.
public_glossary.card_definition: The notes exist because a formal proof and a readable account of it are different artefacts, and the gap between them is where overstatement lives. Each note is written for a mathematician reading cold, records the exact range proved rather than the impression it creates, and names the adjacent stronger statement that is still open.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a problem note for the boundary, not the headline. The interesting content is what it declines to claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Keeping the note honest is itself checked: the relationship between a note's public wording and the formal statement behind it is registered, so a later edit that erases a distinction fails rather than passing quietly.
public_glossary.scope_note: A problem note covers one problem and the results actually proved about it.
public_glossary.example: Each covered problem has its own note; two of them also have full reasoning papers.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

source_refs.gloss: Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.label: process
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A process is an ordered set of activities or a running program that changes inputs or state over time toward an outcome.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A process is an ordered set of activities or a running program that changes inputs or state over time toward an outcome.
public_glossary.card_definition: In workflow prose, a process means the sequence of steps; in operating-system prose, it means one executing program instance. The surrounding context should distinguish them.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify the process kind, start conditions, state, and completion rule.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Processes can be deterministic or interactive, local or networked, and short-lived or persistent, which changes how their results can be reproduced and monitored.
public_glossary.scope_note: A process covers the activities, execution instance, and lifecycle named in context.
public_glossary.example: The build process reads registries and writes generated pages.
public_glossary.non_example: A static file is not a running process.

public_glossary.label: product
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis uses two ordinary senses of product—software offering and multiplication result—and the surrounding nouns determine which one applies.
public_glossary.short_definition: In Plectis, product usually means a user-facing software offering or capability; in mathematical passages, a product is the result of multiplication.
public_glossary.reader_preview: In Plectis, product usually means a user-facing software offering or capability; in mathematical passages, a product is the result of multiplication.
public_glossary.card_definition: The site actively uses both senses. Product performance, product quality, and product authority concern a software offering and what may be claimed about it. Prime products, running-LCM products, and product formulae concern factors multiplied together. One sense supplies no evidence about the other.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the surrounding noun: performance, launch, quality, or authority indicates the software sense; factors, primes, LCM, or a formula indicates multiplication.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This is a real vocabulary collision in Plectis, not a local redefinition of either ordinary meaning. The popup therefore keeps both senses visible so mathematical language cannot silently overwrite product-governance prose.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers the two ordinary senses that appear in Plectis and exists primarily to keep them explicitly disambiguated.
public_glossary.example: “Product authority” concerns permission to judge or launch an offering; a “prime product formula” concerns multiplication of prime factors.
public_glossary.non_example: 3 + 4 is a sum, not a product.

public_glossary.label: profile gap
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A profile gap means an artifact kind exists but lacks the supported row projections needed for honest browsing; it is not an absent model profile or proof that the source artifact is missing.
public_glossary.short_definition: A profile gap is a recorded admission that an artifact kind exists but lacks the supported summary and card rows needed for honest row-by-row browsing, so navigation shows the gap instead of pretending the option surface is complete.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A profile gap is a recorded admission that an artifact kind exists but lacks the supported summary and card rows needed for honest row-by-row browsing, so navigation shows the gap instead of pretending the option surface is complete.
public_glossary.card_definition: The system arranges its artifacts into kinds and lets each kind be enumerated as stable rows that can be selected and drilled into. A profile gap marks a kind that has a registry, source files, or generated index entries but no fully supported rows yet, so it is visible at the top level without being claimed as fully navigable. It is a deliberate marker of navigation debt: a way of saying the support is incomplete rather than papering over the difference between data that exists and a surface that can honestly list it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a profile gap as an honest "not yet browsable here" sign, not a defect: the kind is real and visible, but its row-level listing has not been finished, so do not expect to enumerate or open every member of it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: It exists to stop a kind's mere presence (a registry entry, a legacy command, a generated index, or raw data bands) from being mistaken for full navigability until the navigation layer can actually enumerate and open its members by stable identifier.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the boundary between artifacts the system can see and artifacts it can list as selectable rows. A reader meets it in the navigation and architecture surfaces, where some kinds are marked as fully browsable and others carry this gap.
public_glossary.example: In the architecture map, a kind that appears in the system inventory but has no completed flag-and-card row support is shown as carrying a profile gap, which is why it is named at the top level yet cannot be drilled into member by member.

example_route.label: How it fits together (architecture map)
example_route.gloss: see where kinds become browsable and where a gap stands in

public_glossary.non_example: A profile gap is not a bug, a missing file, or a broken page. It is a recorded marker that a kind's row-level browsing has not been finished, even though the kind itself exists and is visible.
