public_glossary.label: program
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis uses program for executable software and for organized initiatives such as a bug-bounty program; the surrounding context must choose the sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: Program can mean executable computer instructions or an organized initiative such as a bug-bounty program; Plectis uses both senses.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Program can mean executable computer instructions or an organized initiative such as a bug-bounty program; Plectis uses both senses.
public_glossary.card_definition: Most component pages use program for code that a machine runs. Policy and disclosure pages can instead use program for an organized activity with participants, rules, and a purpose. The initiative does not execute merely because it shares the word.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Commands, inputs, source code, and runtime indicate the executable sense; participation, eligibility, disclosure, or administration indicate the initiative sense.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Plectis needs the distinction because a component may be a computer program while the vulnerability-disclosure page explicitly says the project is not a bug-bounty program. Conflating them turns a scope disclaimer into a claim about executable software.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers executable software and organized initiatives only where the surrounding context makes the intended sense clear.
public_glossary.example: The public-site builder is a computer program; a bug-bounty program is an organized security initiative.
public_glossary.non_example: A document describing an algorithm is not itself the executable program.

public_glossary.label: projection
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A projection is a derived view generated from one or more source artifacts to make selected facts easier to read, query, or navigate without becoming their authority.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A projection is a derived view generated from one or more source artifacts to make selected facts easier to read, query, or navigate without becoming their authority.
public_glossary.card_definition: A projection selects, reorganizes, or compresses source material into a useful surface such as a page, index, card, or report. Because it can become stale, a trustworthy projection records its inputs, builder, source fingerprint, and refresh path.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use a projection for access and orientation, then follow its source pointer when the underlying fact or authority matters.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Projection quality has two independent dimensions: fidelity to the source and usefulness to the reader; a perfectly accurate dump may be unusable, while a beautiful summary may be dangerously incomplete.
public_glossary.scope_note: A projection covers the selected source inputs, transformation, and build revision recorded for that output.
public_glossary.example: The glossary page is a projection of the governed term registry.
public_glossary.non_example: A projection is not a second source of truth and should never be hand-edited in place of its input.

public_glossary.label: projection drift
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Projection drift is what happens when a copy stops matching the source it was made from.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Projection drift is what happens when a copy stops matching the source it was made from.
public_glossary.card_definition: Every page on this site is generated from the repositories behind it, so a stale copy would say something the source no longer supports without anything visibly breaking. Drift is dangerous precisely because it is quiet.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a copy and its source disagree, the source is the authority. A copy that agrees with its source proves nothing about whether the source is right.
public_glossary.deep_definition: One group of components exists to recompute a copied projection against its source and fail when the two differ, which is also the rule the videos state: if the map and the source disagree, the source wins.
public_glossary.scope_note: Applies to generated copies of source material, including this website.
public_glossary.example: A count printed on a page that the substrate no longer produces has drifted.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: proof
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A proof is a logically valid argument showing that a mathematical statement follows from stated definitions, assumptions, and previously established results.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A proof is a logically valid argument showing that a mathematical statement follows from stated definitions, assumptions, and previously established results.
public_glossary.card_definition: A human proof communicates the reasoning to qualified readers; a formal proof encodes enough detail for a proof checker. Both establish only their exact conclusion under their exact assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the theorem statement and dependencies before treating a proof as settling a broader claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Proof validity is different from exposition quality, novelty, significance, or whether the theorem solves the motivating open problem.
public_glossary.scope_note: A proof covers the proposition it concludes under the assumptions and formal or mathematical framework it uses.
public_glossary.example: A Lean proof can mechanically verify one denominator identity used in a paper.
public_glossary.non_example: Examples, numerical evidence, and a plausible explanation are not a proof of a universal statement.

public_glossary.label: proof assistant
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A proof assistant is a program that verifies mathematical proofs mechanically, requiring every step to be justified in a form it can check.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A proof assistant is a program that verifies mathematical proofs mechanically, requiring every step to be justified in a form it can check.
public_glossary.card_definition: Writing mathematics for a proof assistant is slower than writing it for a reader, because nothing can be left to the reader. That cost buys a specific guarantee: if it compiles, the argument holds. The tool is honest about scope in a way prose rarely is, since a proof that only covers a finite range simply will not check for the general one.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a machine-checked result as settled for what it states, and no further.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Proof assistants make gaps visible rather than making authors careful. An argument with a hole does not compile, so the hole is found at writing time instead of at review time.
public_glossary.scope_note: A proof assistant establishes validity, not significance.
public_glossary.example: Lean is the proof assistant used for the formal mathematics on this site.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: proof boundary
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Proof boundary marks where the machine-checked formal statement ends and human description begins; it is not merely an incomplete proof or an open mathematical obligation.
public_glossary.short_definition: A proof boundary is the line between what a formal proof establishes and what the prose around it claims: the point where machine-checked certainty stops and ordinary description begins.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A proof boundary is the line between what a formal proof establishes and what the prose around it claims: the point where machine-checked certainty stops and ordinary description begins.
public_glossary.card_definition: A proof assistant checks that a proof establishes the formal statement written in the source. It does not check that a README or a paper describes that statement faithfully. The proof boundary is where those two diverge, and it is the gap where a correct proof can sit underneath an overstated summary without anything failing.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For any formal result, find the formal statement and read it. The prose is a description of the proof, not part of it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: This site records one real instance: an edit that erased a finite-versus-open distinction passed, because the relationship between wording and formal statement had not been registered. Registering it made a later deliberately false version fail. That is one failure and one repair, not complete claim discovery.
public_glossary.scope_note: A proof boundary marks where machine checking ends. Everything on the far side is human claim.
public_glossary.example: A Lean theorem proving a statement for a finite range sits behind a proof boundary from a README sentence implying the general case.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

source_refs.gloss: Grounds this Plectis-specific definition and its scope.

public_glossary.label: proof checker
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A proof checker is the small trusted program that accepts a formal proof only when every encoded inference follows from the system's rules and stated assumptions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A proof checker is the small trusted program that accepts a formal proof only when every encoded inference follows from the system's rules and stated assumptions.
public_glossary.card_definition: The checker does not invent the proof or judge whether the formal statement captures the intended mathematics; it verifies the derivation it receives. Keeping this trusted core small makes the result less dependent on large generators, tactics, or user interfaces.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate what the checker verified from what translators, generators, and theorem authors supplied to it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: In Lean, elaboration and automation may be complex, but accepted declarations are replayed through a compact kernel whose rules define the final formal trust boundary.
public_glossary.scope_note: A proof checker covers the formal declarations, axioms, and proof objects accepted by its recorded version.
public_glossary.example: The Lean kernel checks the corpus declarations and rejects any proof term that does not type-check.
public_glossary.non_example: A linter, test runner, or numerical calculator is not a proof checker unless it verifies derivations in a formal logic.

public_glossary.label: proposition
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A proposition is a declarative mathematical statement that has a definite truth value once its terms and assumptions are fixed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A proposition is a declarative mathematical statement that has a definite truth value once its terms and assumptions are fixed.
public_glossary.card_definition: A proposition can be a theorem, lemma, conjecture, or intermediate claim depending on whether and how it has been proved. Its wording, not its label, determines what must be established.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate the proposition's exact statement from its proof status.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Formal systems represent propositions as types whose inhabitants are proofs, making hypotheses and logical structure explicit.
public_glossary.scope_note: A proposition covers the statement and assumptions as written in its source.
public_glossary.example: “Every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes” is a proposition, currently known as Goldbach's conjecture.
public_glossary.non_example: A question or command is not a proposition because it does not assert something true or false.

public_glossary.label: prove
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To prove a claim is to establish it from accepted premises by an argument that satisfies the relevant standard of proof.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To prove a claim is to establish it from accepted premises by an argument that satisfies the relevant standard of proof.
public_glossary.card_definition: In mathematics, a proof connects premises to a conclusion through valid reasoning; in software documentation, a check may prove only a narrower operational fact. The governing standard determines what counts.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Ask what premises, method, and proof boundary support any statement that something was proved.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Proof is stronger than evidence that merely raises confidence, but it remains conditional on the formalization, premises, and checker used.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers mathematical proof and explicitly bounded verification claims.
public_glossary.example: A kernel-accepted theorem proves its formal statement relative to the kernel and imported axioms.
public_glossary.non_example: A successful example does not prove a universal claim.

public_glossary.label: provenance
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Provenance is the record of where something came from: which source a copied file was taken from, and whether it still matches.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Provenance is the record of where something came from: which source a copied file was taken from, and whether it still matches.
public_glossary.card_definition: Copies drift from their sources silently. Provenance is what makes that detectable rather than discovered later, by recording the origin alongside the copy and checking the two still agree. It is the reason a published body can be trusted to be the real implementation rather than an old snapshot of it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: For any copied artefact, ask where it came from and whether that link is still checked.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Provenance is more durable than correctness. A wrong thing with recorded provenance can be traced and repaired; a right thing without it cannot be maintained.
public_glossary.scope_note: Provenance establishes origin and current agreement, not correctness.
public_glossary.example: Each copied source body records the source it came from, and the build re-checks the digest on every run.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: public
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Public means intentionally available for anyone to inspect without private repository, account, or operator access.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Public means intentionally available for anyone to inspect without private repository, account, or operator access.
public_glossary.card_definition: Public describes access, not endorsement, completeness, peer review, or permission to infer private material. The public site and repositories expose a deliberately bounded source slice whose omissions and claim limits remain part of what is being published.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read public as an access classification and check separate fields for review status, evidence strength, license, and completeness.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A public projection may be generated from private work only when its exported content passes the public boundary; the existence of a public artifact never implies that the private whole is equivalent or available.
public_glossary.scope_note: Public covers the explicitly released pages, repositories, files, and packets at their current public routes.
public_glossary.example: The Plectis site and its linked source repositories are public; the larger working environment is not.
public_glossary.non_example: Public does not mean peer-reviewed, production-ready, security-approved, or complete.

public_glossary.label: published
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Published here means released openly to a public code repository, not accepted by a journal or peer-reviewed.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Published here means released openly to a public code repository, not accepted by a journal or peer-reviewed.
public_glossary.card_definition: The distinction is easy to lose and worth keeping. Everything here is public in the sense that anyone can read, download and run it, and none of it has been through peer review. Those are different kinds of standing: the first is about access, the second is about scrutiny, and only the first has happened.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Published means available. It does not mean reviewed, accepted, or endorsed by anyone.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The gap is why the claim registry records what is proved separately from what is asserted. Open publication removes the gatekeeper and with it the external check, so the burden of stating limits accurately moves onto the author.
public_glossary.scope_note: Publication establishes availability and a date. It carries no external validation.
public_glossary.example: The papers are published to a public repository as PDFs; none has been submitted to or accepted by a journal.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: purpose
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Purpose is the intended use, function, or reason for which something exists or an action is taken.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Purpose is the intended use, function, or reason for which something exists or an action is taken.
public_glossary.card_definition: Purpose helps evaluate fit because the same artifact can be useful for one decision and misleading for another. Stated purpose does not guarantee actual performance.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read an artifact or action by comparing its declared purpose with its design, evidence, and observed effect.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A clear purpose narrows evaluation criteria but does not excuse harms or failures outside the designer's attention when they remain foreseeable.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers declared uses and goals of pages, tools, records, and processes.
public_glossary.example: The glossary's purpose is to make site vocabulary understandable to a cold reader.
public_glossary.non_example: A side effect is not automatically the purpose of the action that produced it.

public_glossary.label: pytest
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: This registry only explains how the external term appears here. The external owner, specification, or primary source controls when exact meaning matters.
public_glossary.short_definition: pytest is the standard tool for running automated tests in Python projects.
public_glossary.reader_preview: pytest is the standard tool for running automated tests in Python projects.
public_glossary.card_definition: It reports an exit status: zero when every test passed, non-zero otherwise. A check that runs pytest and then ignores that status has learned nothing, which is a failure mode this system explicitly looks for.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Running a test suite is not the same as checking its result. Look for the exit status.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The completion-faithfulness audit runs one real pytest process and checks its exit status explicitly. That lane needs the test extra installed; a plain install leaves it nothing to run.
public_glossary.scope_note: pytest is external open-source software and is not part of this work.
public_glossary.example: The receipt records one pytest span with its exit status checked.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: question
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A question is a request for a particular piece of information, explanation, decision, construction, or proof.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A question is a request for a particular piece of information, explanation, decision, construction, or proof.
public_glossary.card_definition: A well-formed question makes the expected answer shape and relevant scope clear. The same topic can support several different questions with different evidence requirements.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Identify exactly what is being asked before selecting sources or claiming an answer.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Question routing matters because a source suitable for orientation may be insufficient for proof validity, current status, or operational permission.
public_glossary.scope_note: A question covers the information and conditions expressed in its wording.
public_glossary.example: “What does this component prove?” is different from “How do I run it?”
public_glossary.non_example: A topic heading is not necessarily a complete question.

public_glossary.label: quickstart
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The quickstart is the shortest path from nothing to a first result: clone, install, run one check, read the file it wrote.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The quickstart is the shortest path from nothing to a first result: clone, install, run one check, read the file it wrote.
public_glossary.card_definition: It exists so that the first thing a reader does is produce evidence rather than read more prose. Everything else on the site is easier to evaluate once you have run something and seen what it writes.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Run the quickstart before evaluating any claim here. It takes minutes and changes what you are able to check.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The shape is deliberate: the reader ends holding a file they produced, which is a different epistemic position from having read a description of one.
public_glossary.scope_note: The quickstart establishes that the published checks run on your machine.
public_glossary.example: The quickstart lists the dependencies and the exact commands, and ends at a result file.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: radix
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A radix is the base of a positional numeral system, so a radix-two expansion is binary and a radix-ten expansion is ordinary decimal.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A radix is the base of a positional numeral system, so a radix-two expansion is binary and a radix-ten expansion is ordinary decimal.
public_glossary.card_definition: Choosing a radix fixes which digits are available and therefore what carrying looks like. Several arguments in this corpus turn on exactly which digit values can occur.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A digit-level result is stated relative to one radix and does not transfer to another without proof.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The Erdős #269 work gives an exact running-lcm product, logarithmic cells, shell bounds, and a four-value radix at the primes 2, 3 and 5, together with a rank-two nonseparability witness. The remaining criterion is conditional and the problem stays open from three primes onward.
public_glossary.scope_note: Radix and base are used interchangeably for numeral expansions here.
public_glossary.example: In radix two the digits are 0 and 1.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: rational
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A number is rational when it can be written as one whole number divided by another.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A number is rational when it can be written as one whole number divided by another.
public_glossary.card_definition: Rationality is the property most of these problems are trying to rule out. It is a strong constraint: if an infinite sum is rational, its value has an exact denominator, and that denominator forces detectable structure. Much of the formal work here consists of showing that the required structure cannot occur.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Assuming rationality and deriving a contradiction is the standard route to proving irrationality.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The reason rationality is attacked rather than irrationality proved directly is that rationality gives you something finite to work with, and irrationality gives you nothing to hold.
public_glossary.scope_note: A rationality constraint covers the series it is derived for.
public_glossary.example: Rationality of the series forces an exact recurrence in the long division, which is where several of the constraints here come from.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: raw seed
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Raw seed means the preserved operator-voice substrate in this repository. It is not raw data, model-training data, a random seed, or public evidence by default.
public_glossary.short_definition: A raw seed is the append-only, unedited record of the operator's own words and thinking, serving as the source layer from which later summaries, doctrine, and routes are derived.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A raw seed is the append-only, unedited record of the operator's own words and thinking, serving as the source layer from which later summaries, doctrine, and routes are derived.
public_glossary.card_definition: The raw seed holds the operator's voice in its first form: the intent, the recurring phrases, the changes of mind, and the provenance of an idea, written down before any tidying. Indexes, shards, principles, and paper modules elsewhere in the system are summaries drawn from it; the raw seed is the thing they summarise, and it is never overwritten or compressed away. When a higher layer needs to be checked against what was actually meant, the raw seed is the bottom authority it answers to.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat the raw seed as the original wording and the summaries above it as maps of that wording. When the two seem to disagree, the raw seed is the record of what was actually meant.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Because it is append-only, the raw seed preserves the full history of an idea, including reversals and recurring motifs, so a later summary can be traced back to the exact source it came from.
public_glossary.scope_note: The raw seed covers the operator-voice source material that the system's doctrine, principles, and components are generated from. A reader meets it on the pages that show how recorded voice becomes structured doctrine, and in references back to source provenance.
public_glossary.example: The Voice To Doctrine Self Improvement Loop is one place the raw seed is visible in use: it takes recorded operator voice as its input and turns it into structured doctrine, so the seed is the raw material entering one end of that loop.

example_route.label: Voice To Doctrine Self Improvement Loop
example_route.gloss: open the component that turns recorded operator voice into doctrine

public_glossary.non_example: A raw seed is not a polished mission statement, a marketing narrative, or the system's final doctrine. It is the unedited source voice that those later, tidier layers are derived from.

relationships.gloss: Raw seed can seed bounded phase whiteboards.
Doctrine ultimately traces to voice and evidence.

public_glossary.label: read
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To read is to interpret written, symbolic, or structured material in order to recover meaning or data from it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To read is to interpret written, symbolic, or structured material in order to recover meaning or data from it.
public_glossary.card_definition: People read prose and interfaces, while programs read files and data structures according to parsing rules. In both cases, successful access does not guarantee correct interpretation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When the site says something reads a source, distinguish byte access, parsing, and semantic understanding.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Reading is observational unless the reader also performs a separate action that changes the material or records state.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers human comprehension and programmatic input from public or repository material.
public_glossary.example: The builder reads the registry JSON before rendering glossary HTML.
public_glossary.non_example: A program opening a file without parsing its contents has not necessarily read it meaningfully.

public_glossary.label: reader
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A reader is the person or software consumer trying to understand, navigate, or use a published artifact.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A reader is the person or software consumer trying to understand, navigate, or use a published artifact.
public_glossary.card_definition: Reader needs depend on prior context: a cold reader starts without the repository's house vocabulary, while an expert may need exact source and proof routes. Public pages try to serve both through layered definitions and drilldowns.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Choose the shallowest explanation that makes the next step clear, while preserving a route to deeper evidence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A software reader can consume structured packets and pointers that would be awkward for a person, but it still needs definitions, authority boundaries, and unambiguous identifiers.
public_glossary.scope_note: Reader covers the audience named by a page, packet, or route contract.
public_glossary.example: The glossary gives a cold reader a one-sentence definition before deeper context.
public_glossary.non_example: The author of a page is not automatically its intended reader.

public_glossary.label: reader packet
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A reader packet is a generated portable guide to public routes, summaries, sources, and limits; it is not the source authority, a complete export, or publication permission.
public_glossary.short_definition: A reader packet is a generated, portable guide that gathers routes, short summaries, source references, and scope limits so a person or AI assistant can inspect a public source slice without mistaking the guide for that source.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A reader packet is a generated, portable guide that gathers routes, short summaries, source references, and scope limits so a person or AI assistant can inspect a public source slice without mistaking the guide for that source.
public_glossary.card_definition: A reader packet is the compact starting document handed to someone, or to an automated assistant, who is opening the public slice for the first time. It carries the routes worth following, brief descriptions of components and glossary rows, links back to the underlying source files, and an explicit note of what it does and does not cover. It is reproducible and built from the source, so its job is to point at where to inspect rather than to stand in for the records it summarises.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Follow a reader packet through to the source records it links rather than treating its summaries as the final word. It tells you where to look and where its own boundaries are.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A reader packet is built to cut cold-start confusion without turning its own summary text into authority: it is compact and source-linked precisely so that its claims can be checked against the records it routes to.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers the generated digest and review artifacts that orient a reviewer at the public source slice, such as the AI reader digest and the review packet. A reader encounters it as the entry-and-orientation surface that hands off into components, routes, and source files.
public_glossary.example: The Cold-Reader Route Map is a reader packet: a single artifact that lays out the first routes a newcomer should follow into the public slice and links each one back to its source.

example_route.label: Cold Reader Route Map
example_route.gloss: open the packet that routes a first-time reader into the source

public_glossary.non_example: A reader packet is not source authority and not proof that a reviewer read or endorsed the project. It is a generated map whose summaries hold only as far as the source records they link to.

relationships.gloss: Reader packets should route to concrete records.
Reader packets summarize the public source slice.
Reader packets remain projections below source authority.

source_refs.gloss: Generated public reader digest.
Generated public review packet.

public_glossary.label: real
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Real describes something that exists or occurs in the referenced world or system rather than being merely hypothetical, simulated, or fabricated.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Real describes something that exists or occurs in the referenced world or system rather than being merely hypothetical, simulated, or fabricated.
public_glossary.card_definition: The word is contrastive and therefore needs a comparison: real data versus synthetic data, live effects versus rehearsal, or an actual source versus an invented example. In mathematics, real number is a separate defined term.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read real by identifying what alternative is being ruled out in that sentence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Reality is not the same as correctness; real observations and production data can still be noisy, misleading, or incorrectly interpreted.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers actual artifacts, events, and environments when contrasted with tests, simulations, or examples.
public_glossary.example: A defect reproduced against the deployed service is a real operational observation.
public_glossary.non_example: A plausible example invented for explanation is not real evidence of an event.

public_glossary.label: real number
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A real number is a point on the continuous number line, including every rational and irrational number.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A real number is a point on the continuous number line, including every rational and irrational number.
public_glossary.card_definition: Plectis first treats the value of a convergent series as a real number and then asks the narrower arithmetic question: is that real value rational or irrational? A decimal approximation locates the value but does not settle that exact classification.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Separate existence as a real limit from the stronger claim that the limit is rational, irrational, algebraic, or transcendental.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Finite certificate computations may live in exact rational arithmetic while the completed infinite series lives in the reals. Moving between those levels requires an explicit limit argument and, in formal work, explicit type coercions; a rational partial sum does not make the real limit rational.
public_glossary.scope_note: Covers the real-valued limits and theorem domains used by the Plectis mathematical papers and formalizations.
public_glossary.example: The binary totient series has a real value; the Erdős question asks whether that real number is irrational.
public_glossary.non_example: An arbitrary complex number with nonzero imaginary part is not a real number.

public_glossary.label: reason
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: Plectis uses series for infinite mathematical sums and ordered data observations; convergence language belongs only to the mathematical sense.
public_glossary.short_definition: A reason is a fact, consideration, rule, or inference offered to explain or justify a belief, decision, event, or action.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A reason is a fact, consideration, rule, or inference offered to explain or justify a belief, decision, event, or action.
public_glossary.card_definition: Reasons can be causal, evidential, logical, or practical. A useful record distinguishes what caused an outcome from what justifies believing or choosing it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Evaluate a reason by its relevance, truth, connection to the conclusion, and consistency with governing constraints.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Having a reason does not make it sufficient; competing reasons, missing evidence, or a broken inference can still defeat the conclusion.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers explanations and justifications in research, decisions, failures, and operational records.
public_glossary.example: Avoiding ambiguous automatic links is a reason to require explicit term markers for colliding phrases.
public_glossary.non_example: A preference stated without connection to the decision is not a complete reason for that decision.

public_glossary.label: receipt
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A receipt is the durable output that proves an action happened: the file or record a step writes, kept so the claim can be checked later rather than taken on trust.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A receipt is the durable output that proves an action happened: the file or record a step writes, kept so the claim can be checked later rather than taken on trust.
public_glossary.card_definition: Actions here are expected to leave something behind. A commit reports a hash, a deploy reports the bytes it verified live, a check writes its result record. The pattern is deliberate, because the failure it guards against is the confident report of work that did not occur. A receipt turns that from a matter of trust into something you can look up.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a step is reported as done, ask what it wrote. No receipt, no completion.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The discipline extends to failure. A refused action produces a receipt too, naming what stopped it, which is what stops a blocked step from being quietly reported as finished.
public_glossary.scope_note: A receipt establishes that a specific action ran and what it produced. It is not a judgement about whether the action was the right one.
public_glossary.example: A deploy receipt records the commit pushed, the asset hash verified live, and the paper hashes compared against public source.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: reciprocal
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: The reciprocal of a number is one divided by it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: The reciprocal of a number is one divided by it.
public_glossary.card_definition: Most of the series here are sums of reciprocals, which is why the terms shrink and the sums settle on a value at all. Taking reciprocals also inverts the difficulty: a fast-growing sequence gives a fast-shrinking sum, and the arithmetic of the sum depends delicately on how the original sequence grew.
public_glossary.reader_rule: In a reciprocal sum, how fast the underlying sequence grows controls almost everything.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The delicacy is the point: sequences that grow at similar rates can give sums of entirely different character, so growth conditions have to be stated exactly.
public_glossary.scope_note: A reciprocal-sum result covers the growth condition it assumes.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #243 concerns integer sequences whose reciprocal sum is rational under a rapid-growth hypothesis.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: recompute
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To recompute something is to calculate or derive it again from its inputs rather than reuse a previous result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To recompute something is to calculate or derive it again from its inputs rather than reuse a previous result.
public_glossary.card_definition: Recomputation can verify reproducibility, refresh a stale projection, or incorporate changed inputs. It should use a defined procedure so differences can be attributed to inputs, environment, or implementation.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When a result is recomputed, compare the inputs, method, environment, and output with the earlier run.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Recomputation is not automatically independent evidence when it uses the same sources and potentially the same defect.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers repeated calculation, building, indexing, and validation from named inputs.
public_glossary.example: The term-layer report recomputes usage counts from the current registry and generated pages.
public_glossary.non_example: Copying a stored number into a new report is not recomputation.

public_glossary.label: recurrence
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A recurrence is a rule defining each term of a sequence from the ones before it, rather than by a direct formula.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A recurrence is a rule defining each term of a sequence from the ones before it, rather than by a direct formula.
public_glossary.card_definition: Recurrences appear here on both sides of the work. Some problems ask whether a sequence must eventually satisfy a particular recurrence; elsewhere, assuming a sum is rational forces a recurrence in its long division, which then gives something concrete to contradict.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A forced recurrence is usually a proof strategy rather than a result: it is the structure the contradiction will come from.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The reason recurrences are useful in irrationality arguments is that they propagate: establish one at a single index and it constrains every later one.
public_glossary.scope_note: A recurrence result covers the sequence it is stated for.
public_glossary.example: Erdős #243 asks whether rationality of a reciprocal sum forces the sequence to satisfy Sylvester's recurrence eventually.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: reduction
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A reduction turns one problem into another, so that solving the second would solve the first.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A reduction turns one problem into another, so that solving the second would solve the first.
public_glossary.card_definition: A reduction is not progress on its own. If the new statement is no easier than the original, the problem has been restated rather than advanced. Several results in this corpus are exact reformulations and are labelled as such rather than presented as progress.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Count results, not restatements. Statements each proved equivalent to a problem are one result about that problem, not many.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The claim registry records 39 of its 103 claims as conditional reductions, and separately records that neither Erdős #249 nor Erdős #257 is settled. The Lean repository also lifts the hypotheses of its conditional theorems into standalone propositions and proves 17 of the 23 substantial ones equal in strength to the open problem they were meant to approach.
public_glossary.scope_note: Mathematical reduction between statements. Not a reduction in size, cost, or scope.
public_glossary.example: Clearing denominators reduces Erdős #243 to rigidity of an integer error orbit.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: referee
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A referee is the expert a journal asks to assess a submitted paper, usually anonymously, before deciding whether to publish it.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A referee is the expert a journal asks to assess a submitted paper, usually anonymously, before deciding whether to publish it.
public_glossary.card_definition: Refereeing is what gives a published mathematical result its standing. A correct proof and a refereed proof are different states: the second has had someone independent try to break it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Machine checking and refereeing answer different questions. A proof assistant checks the formal statement; a referee judges whether the paper says something true, correctly attributed, and worth publishing.
public_glossary.deep_definition: No referee, editor, or venue has assessed any of the papers on this site. Every one is author-released, so no result in them carries the standing such an assessment would confer.
public_glossary.scope_note: Ordinary academic usage.
public_glossary.example: A referee report can reject a paper without disputing any single line of it.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: reference
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A reference is a pointer that identifies another source, record, definition, or location relevant to the current statement.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A reference is a pointer that identifies another source, record, definition, or location relevant to the current statement.
public_glossary.card_definition: References make claims traceable by naming where supporting or explanatory material can be found. A reference may provide context without itself being evidence for the claim.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Follow the reference and inspect the role assigned to its destination.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Exact references include stable identifiers, paths, anchors, versions, or citations so later readers can resolve the same object rather than a nearby substitute.
public_glossary.scope_note: A reference covers the destination and relationship declared by the referring artifact.
public_glossary.example: A paper can reference the exact Lean theorem that formalizes one claim.
public_glossary.non_example: Mentioning a source without enough detail to locate it is not a reliable reference.

public_glossary.label: reformulation
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A reformulation restates a problem or theorem in a different representation while preserving a proved relationship to the original statement.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A reformulation restates a problem or theorem in a different representation while preserving a proved relationship to the original statement.
public_glossary.card_definition: A reformulation can expose new structure—digits instead of sums, recurrences instead of rationality, or gaps instead of primes—without solving anything by itself. Its value depends on whether the new form is equivalent, merely implied, or only heuristically related.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check the exact relation between the original and reformulated statements before treating them as interchangeable.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Productive reformulations preserve the target while moving the difficulty into objects with stronger tools, clearer barriers, or finite certificates.
public_glossary.scope_note: A reformulation covers the two named statements and the proved direction or equivalence connecting them.
public_glossary.example: A prime-series question can be reformulated in terms of consecutive prime gaps.
public_glossary.non_example: A suggestive analogy or informal change of wording is not a mathematical reformulation without a proved relation.

public_glossary.label: refuse
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To refuse is to deliberately decline an action, request, input, or inference because permission or required conditions are absent.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To refuse is to deliberately decline an action, request, input, or inference because permission or required conditions are absent.
public_glossary.card_definition: Refusal is a controlled outcome, not simply a crash or omission. A useful refusal states the boundary it protects and, when safe, the condition or route that could allow progress.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a refusal by identifying who or what declined, which rule applied, and whether the refusal changed any state.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Refusal can be evidence that a safety or authority boundary worked as designed.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers tool, policy, validation, publication, and inference refusals.
public_glossary.example: A resolver refuses to guess when one phrase belongs to two glossary concepts.
public_glossary.non_example: A process disappearing without a result or reason is a failure, not a clear refusal.

public_glossary.label: registry
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A registry is a governed collection of uniquely identified records for one kind of object.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A registry is a governed collection of uniquely identified records for one kind of object.
public_glossary.card_definition: A registry defines membership, identifiers, and required fields for a class of artifacts. Generated indexes and pages should project from it rather than maintain competing lists.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Use the registry to answer which records exist and which identifier names each one.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Registries make additions, removals, and duplicates mechanically visible, but the truth of each record's substantive claims still depends on its own evidence.
public_glossary.scope_note: A registry covers the record kind and version named by its schema.
public_glossary.example: The system vocabulary registry owns the set of glossary terms.
public_glossary.non_example: An informal list is not a governed registry unless it has an ownership and validation contract.

public_glossary.label: regression
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A regression is the return of a previously fixed failure or the loss of behaviour that an earlier version demonstrably supported.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A regression is the return of a previously fixed failure or the loss of behaviour that an earlier version demonstrably supported.
public_glossary.card_definition: A regression test preserves a concrete past expectation so later changes fail visibly if they break it again. The baseline must be real and dated; calling any new failure a regression is inaccurate when the earlier behaviour was never established.
public_glossary.reader_rule: To call something a regression, identify the prior passing evidence and the change after which it failed.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Regression protection turns a bug fix into durable system memory by keeping the smallest reproducing case and its expected outcome in the validation path.
public_glossary.scope_note: A regression applies to one previously evidenced behaviour and the versions being compared.
public_glossary.example: A test preserving plural glossary links prevents a later matcher change from dropping `declarations` while still linking `declaration`.
public_glossary.non_example: A newly discovered unsupported case is not necessarily a regression.

public_glossary.label: reject
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To reject something is to refuse its acceptance, admission, use, or continuation because stated conditions are not satisfied.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To reject something is to refuse its acceptance, admission, use, or continuation because stated conditions are not satisfied.
public_glossary.card_definition: Rejection should name the gate and the reason an input or claim failed it. A deterministic rejection is useful evidence when the same conditions reliably produce the same outcome.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When an item is rejected, inspect the rule, failing condition, and whether correction or appeal is possible.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Rejection establishes non-acceptance under one process, not that the item is worthless or false in every context.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers validation, safety, schema, proof, and publication decisions.
public_glossary.example: The builder rejects a glossary row whose definition field is empty.
public_glossary.non_example: Ignoring an item without evaluating it is not a governed rejection.

public_glossary.label: release
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A release is an intentionally published, versioned set of artifacts made available to a defined audience.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A release is an intentionally published, versioned set of artifacts made available to a defined audience.
public_glossary.card_definition: A release turns working material into a distribution with stated contents, source revision, licenses, and claim boundaries. Publication does not imply production readiness or peer review.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the release manifest and limits before treating the published set as complete.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A release may include generated pages, source repositories, papers, checks, and compatibility routes that must agree on identity and version.
public_glossary.scope_note: A release covers the artifacts, version, audience, and publication boundary declared by its manifest.
public_glossary.example: The public Plectis release includes the site, source repositories, and listed papers.
public_glossary.non_example: An uncommitted local build is not a public release.

public_glossary.label: reliability
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Reliability is the degree to which something continues to perform its stated function under specified conditions.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Reliability is the degree to which something continues to perform its stated function under specified conditions.
public_glossary.card_definition: A reliable process behaves consistently across repeated use, expected variation, and relevant failures. Reliability claims therefore need a function, environment, time span, and evidence base.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat reliability as conditional and ask what workload, conditions, and failure rate were actually measured.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Correctness concerns whether an outcome is right, while reliability concerns how dependably the process produces its intended outcome.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers repeatable operation of agents, tools, builds, checks, and public routes.
public_glossary.example: A link checker that produces the same complete result on repeated builds demonstrates operational reliability.
public_glossary.non_example: One successful run does not establish reliability.

public_glossary.label: rename migration receipt
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A rename migration receipt records whether a governed path rename landed, was blocked, or was reverted, with its obligations and evidence; it is not a commit message or automatic proof of success.
public_glossary.short_definition: A rename migration receipt is the durable proof that a storage-path rename passed its gate, recording the evidence, obligations, rollback plan, or—when blocked—the unmet precondition that prevented the change.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A rename migration receipt is the durable proof that a storage-path rename passed its gate, recording the evidence, obligations, rollback plan, or—when blocked—the unmet precondition that prevented the change.
public_glossary.card_definition: When a file or directory in the source is renamed, the receipt is the artifact that makes that rename auditable and reversible. It records the scope of the change, the evidence that the rename gate was satisfied, the post-rename tasks, and closure notes. Receipts move through fixed states, planned, blocked, in progress, completed, and reverted, so the history of a rename is legible from a single object rather than reconstructed from the file system. A completed receipt is evidence the migration happened safely; a blocked receipt is the honest record that it is not yet safe to proceed.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Check a rename migration receipt's state and its named gate evidence before treating a rename as settled. A blocked receipt means the change was deliberately not made, and it names the precondition that is still missing.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Each receipt forces the reference-impact map, stable-identifier plan, alias and redirect plan, projection-rebuild plan, verification plan, and rollback plan to be written down before the file system is touched, and the actual outcome to be recorded afterwards.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers governed renaming of storage paths across the system. Receipts live under state/semantic_naming/rename_receipts/ and follow a fixed standard; a reader encounters the concept wherever a rename is described as governed, gated, or held.
public_glossary.example: The planned receipt for renaming the EPHEMERAL.md storage path, held in a blocked state because a gate precondition was not yet met, is a concrete rename migration receipt naming the outstanding condition rather than performing the rename.

example_route.label: Proof-Derived Governed Mutation Authorization
example_route.gloss: open the rule that ties a mutation to a typed proof that its gate was satisfied

public_glossary.non_example: A rename migration receipt is not a commit message or an after-the-fact changelog note. It is a typed, governed object recorded before the rename is made, and it can carry a blocked state that records a rename deliberately not performed.

public_glossary.label: replay
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A replay is a check that re-runs a recorded scenario end to end and asserts the outcome, rather than testing a function in isolation.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A replay is a check that re-runs a recorded scenario end to end and asserts the outcome, rather than testing a function in isolation.
public_glossary.card_definition: Unit-level checks tell you a part behaves; a replay tells you a situation resolves the way it is supposed to. The scenario is committed as fixtures, including the cases that must fail, so the whole path can be re-run by anyone and compared against a recorded expectation. It is the closest this repository gets to showing a behaviour rather than asserting one.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read what scenario a replay covers. It establishes that recorded path, not the behaviour of the system around it.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Replays are where negative cases earn their place: a scenario that only ever replays its happy path proves very little, because a component that has stopped discriminating still completes it. The recorded refusals are what make the pass informative.
public_glossary.scope_note: A replay covers its recorded scenario on its committed fixtures. It makes no claim about live data or unrecorded paths.
public_glossary.example: An agent-monitor replay ships a scenario the monitor must flag and one it must not; a build where both pass is a failing build.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: report
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A report is a written account of what happened, as distinct from the record the account was drawn from.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A report is a written account of what happened, as distinct from the record the account was drawn from.
public_glossary.card_definition: Reports are useful and are not evidence. The distinction runs through everything here: a component's summary is a report, its result record is not; an agent's account of a session is a report, its transcript is not. Keeping both means the account can be checked against the thing it describes instead of standing in for it.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Treat a report as a claim about a record. Ask to see the record.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Reports are rarely dishonest and reliably lossy, in a direction that flatters the reporter. That is enough to make the underlying record worth keeping even when nobody suspects anything.
public_glossary.scope_note: A report describes a run. The run's own record is what establishes it.
public_glossary.example: A closeout report cites the commit it landed, so the report can be checked against the repository.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: repository
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A repository is a project's files together with their complete change history, hosted so anyone can copy the whole thing.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A repository is a project's files together with their complete change history, hosted so anyone can copy the whole thing.
public_glossary.card_definition: Two repositories are published here: one holding the runnable components, one holding the formal mathematics. Everything claimed on this site should be traceable to a file in one of them. The history matters as much as the files, because it shows when something was written rather than only that it exists now.
public_glossary.reader_rule: If a claim cannot be traced to a repository file, treat it as description.
public_glossary.deep_definition: History is what makes a claim of priority checkable. A file can be written at any time; a commit is dated.
public_glossary.scope_note: A repository holds what was published to it. It is not a record of everything that was done.
public_glossary.example: The components live in one repository and the Lean proofs in another; both are public.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.

public_glossary.label: reproducible
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Reproducible means another reader can use the declared source, inputs, environment, and command to obtain the same materially relevant result.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Reproducible means another reader can use the declared source, inputs, environment, and command to obtain the same materially relevant result.
public_glossary.card_definition: Reproducibility turns a reported outcome into something independently checkable. It requires enough information to rebuild or rerun the work, plus a criterion for what must match—exact bytes, the same verdict, or values within a stated tolerance.
public_glossary.reader_rule: A reproducibility claim should name the inputs, versions, command, expected output, and acceptable comparison rule.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Exact byte reproduction is stronger than semantic reproduction, but not every valid workflow can be byte-identical across platforms; the claim must state which level it promises.
public_glossary.scope_note: Reproducible applies to the declared artifact, command, inputs, environment, and comparison criterion.
public_glossary.example: A cold clone can rebuild the papers from the recorded source commit and verify their hashes.
public_glossary.non_example: A run is not reproducible when it depends on unrecorded local state or inaccessible inputs.

public_glossary.label: require
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: To require something is to make it a necessary condition for a stated action, result, rule, or dependency.
public_glossary.reader_preview: To require something is to make it a necessary condition for a stated action, result, rule, or dependency.
public_glossary.card_definition: Requirements can be logical, technical, procedural, or user-imposed. The source of the requirement determines who can change it and what evidence shows it has been met.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When one thing requires another, identify the dependency and the consequence of absence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A requirement expresses necessity within a scope, not preference or universal law. In a workflow, satisfying one requirement can unlock the next step without validating the final result.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers dependency and obligation relationships explicitly stated by the site.
public_glossary.example: Publishing the glossary requires generating HTML from the current registry.
public_glossary.non_example: A commonly chosen option is not required unless a rule or dependency makes it necessary.

public_glossary.label: required
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Required describes something that must be present, performed, or satisfied for a stated rule, goal, or process to hold.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Required describes something that must be present, performed, or satisfied for a stated rule, goal, or process to hold.
public_glossary.card_definition: Requirements can come from a specification, dependency, policy, safety boundary, or user request. They should be distinguishable from recommendations and optional enhancements.
public_glossary.reader_rule: When something is required, locate the authority or dependency that makes it mandatory and the check that verifies satisfaction.
public_glossary.deep_definition: A requirement is scoped: being mandatory for one release or proof does not make it universally mandatory.
public_glossary.scope_note: The term covers binding conditions over data, actions, validation, interfaces, and publication.
public_glossary.example: A term row requires an identifier and a public definition before the builder can publish it.
public_glossary.non_example: A preferred style is not required unless a governing rule makes it so.

public_glossary.label: research
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: Research is a systematic attempt to answer a question or produce new understanding through evidence, reasoning, or experiment.
public_glossary.reader_preview: Research is a systematic attempt to answer a question or produce new understanding through evidence, reasoning, or experiment.
public_glossary.card_definition: Research differs from casual lookup by having an explicit question, a method for gathering or testing information, and a record of what supports the result. Its conclusions may remain provisional.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read a research claim together with its question, method, sources, uncertainties, and reproducibility conditions.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Research can narrow uncertainty without closing a question, and a negative result can still add knowledge by ruling out a route.
public_glossary.scope_note: Here the term covers mathematical, software, and system investigations represented by public artifacts.
public_glossary.example: Testing several proof strategies and recording why they fail is research even before a theorem is proved.
public_glossary.non_example: Collecting links without a question or evaluation method is not yet research.

public_glossary.label: result
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: The glossary intends ordinary or domain usage. Repository-specific examples contextualize the term; they do not redefine it or certify one universal definition.
public_glossary.short_definition: A result is the outcome produced by a proof, computation, test, experiment, or decision process.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A result is the outcome produced by a proof, computation, test, experiment, or decision process.
public_glossary.card_definition: A result says what happened or was established under particular inputs and conditions. Its significance depends on the producing method, evidence, and scope.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Read the result together with how it was produced and what it is allowed to claim.
public_glossary.deep_definition: The same underlying outcome may be summarized in prose and stored in a structured result record; the record carries the inspectable provenance while the summary aids reading.
public_glossary.scope_note: A result covers the stated inputs, method, source version, and execution or proof conditions.
public_glossary.example: A check can return a passing result for one committed fixture set.
public_glossary.non_example: A desired or expected outcome is not an actual result until the producing process runs or the proof is completed.

public_glossary.label: result record
public_glossary.meaning_boundary: A result record is the durable, scoped output of one named run; it is not terminal output, the input body, or evidence for behavior beyond the recorded check.
public_glossary.short_definition: A result record is the durable file a check writes with what it tested, what it found, and the boundary of that finding, as distinct from an ephemeral message shown while the run executes.
public_glossary.reader_preview: A result record is the durable file a check writes with what it tested, what it found, and the boundary of that finding, as distinct from an ephemeral message shown while the run executes.
public_glossary.card_definition: Running a component does not just print something and exit - it writes a result record you can open, keep, and compare against a later run. This is what makes a claim on this site checkable rather than quotable: the record is the evidence, and prose describing it is not. A result record carries its own scope limit, so it states the boundary of what it establishes instead of leaving that to the reader.
public_glossary.reader_rule: Prefer the result record to any summary of it. If a claim has no record behind it, treat it as description, not evidence.
public_glossary.deep_definition: Result records are metadata-only by design: they carry the shape and verdict of a run, not the private bodies it read. That is what lets a run over non-public inputs still produce a publishable artefact. It is also why a record can be honest about a failure - an exit-1 record is as publishable as a passing one, and the repository ships both.
public_glossary.scope_note: A result record establishes what its own run checked. It is not a statement about the system around it.
public_glossary.example: The cold-clone probe writes .microcosm/cold_clone_probe.json; that file, not the terminal output, is what a reader cites.
public_glossary.non_example: Do not treat this glossary row as source authority; follow its source refs and evidence commands before making claims with the term.
